Workspaces provide a virtual space for you and your teams to collaborate, organize project-based work, manage access to environments and resources, and track team activities.
You can create Workspaces to group related Designs and Environments, define domains of responsibility for your teams, and streamline resource management.
Key Features 🔗 Resource Sharing: Workspaces allow for seamless resource sharing among team members, fostering collaboration. Logical Grouping: Within Workspaces, you can group related components such as environments and infrastructure designs. Flexibility: Workspaces support various resources like Kubernetes, Prometheus, Jaeger, Nginx, and more. Simplified Management: Managing and deploying resources is made easy within Workspaces. Access Control: Workspaces allow you to control access to resources by granting permissions to users and teams. Workspace Relationships and Restrictions 🔗 Access to Workspaces may be granted to one or more teams. As a point of collaboration to facilitate work, Workspaces may have zero or more Environments associated. A Workspace is closely associated with Teams. Teams are groups of users with varying permissions, and they are at the center of resource access and management within a Workspace. One or more teams can be assigned access to a workspace. After creating a Workspace, one of your next steps is to assign team access, create or transfer designs into the Workspace, and allocate resources that to Workspace by associating it with one or more Environments, therein making the Environment’s connections available to users of the Workspace.
Like a shared drive (or shared collection of files), Workspaces are your Google Drive, while Designs are your Google Docs.
Key Workspace Components 🔗 Environments 🔗 Environments are a central part of a workspace. They serve as a logical grouping for managing connections. A connection, in this context, can be either managed or discovered. Examples of connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger traces, Nginx servers, and more. One or more environments can be assigned to a workspace. Same environment can be assigned to multiple workspaces. Assigning Environments to Workspaces Assign any number of Environments to one or more Workspaces. See Environments section for more information. Designs 🔗 Infrastructure Designs are essential for creating reusable deployment templates. Users belonging to teams with access to a workspace can utilize these designs to deploy resources in the Kubernetes clusters associated with that workspace. Like a shared drive (or shared collection of files), Workspaces are your Google Drive, while Designs are your Google Docs. One or more designs can be assigned to a workspace. Design Ownership in Workspaces Designs belong to only one Workspace at any given time. See Designs section for more information. Teams 🔗 A Workspace is closely associated with Teams. Teams are groups of users with varying permissions, and they are at the center of resource access and management within a Workspace. One or more teams can be assigned to a workspace. Same team can be assigned to multiple workspaces. Team Access Control in Workspaces Teams offer control access to workspaces and to workspace resources such as environments and managed and unmanaged connections. See Teams. Connections 🔗 Connections refer to various resources that can be either managed or unmanaged, but are discovered and made accessible for use. Examples of Connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger services, Nginx deployments, and more. These Connections serve as a fundamental part of Workspaces, as users can deploy infrastructure designs within the context of these Connections. Connections can be assigned to one or more environments. Same connection can be assigned to multiple environments. Learn More About Connections See Connections section for more information. Best Practices 🔗 To make the most of Workspaces, here are some best practices:
Clearly define permissions in the form of team assignment to ensure proper access control. Use Infrastructure Designs to standardize resource deployments. Regularly review and update your Workspace’s resources and configurations. Workspaces enhance collaboration within your teams, providing a structured environment for sharing and managing resources. By following best practices and understanding the core components of Workspaces, you can maximize the benefits of this feature.
Looking for Practical Workspace Management? For a step-by-step guide on how to create, edit, and manage your workspaces, see the Managing Workspaces documentation. Example: Orbital Labs Workspace Setup 🔗 The following illustrates how Five and Maya set up workspaces at Orbital Labs to segment access across infrastructure and development workflows. See Meet Five and the Cast for the full seed inventory.
Workspace Inventory 🔗 Workspace Owner Org Teams with Access Environments orbital-production Orbital Labs Infrastructure only prod-aws (EKS + RDS + S3 + CloudFront + SQS), prod-gcp (GKE + Cloud SQL + Cloud Storage + Pub/Sub) orbital-staging Orbital Labs Infrastructure + Development staging-aws (EKS + S3 + ElastiCache), staging-azure (AKS + Azure Blob + Azure Service Bus) orbital-dev Orbital Labs Development only dev-local (kind + LocalStack) Creating orbital-staging 🔗 Five creates the orbital-staging workspace to give the Development team a shared environment for feature-branch testing — without handing them the keys to production.
Steps Five follows:
Navigate to Workspaces and click Create Workspace Name the workspace orbital-staging Save — the workspace is created with no team access and no environments assigned Maya then assigns team access:
Open the orbital-staging workspace settings Add the Infrastructure team — enabling Zara and Five to manage environment connections Add the Development team — enabling Rex and Jordan to deploy designs and use connections Why both teams? Infrastructure owns the environments (Zara assigns connections); Development owns the designs (Rex and Jordan deploy them). Assigning both teams to orbital-staging gives each group the access it needs without elevating Development’s access to orbital-production.

What sessions are 🔗 A session represents a user authenticated connection to Layer5 Cloud. Sessions are created each time a user successfully authenticates. Sessions expire after a period of 24 hours. Before reaching their expiration time, sessions can be refreshed by an associated refresh token, which is also automatically generated at the time a user authenticates (at the same time that the adjoining session token is generated). Refresh token have an expiration period of 36 hours. Active sessions are automatically refreshed (kept alive) by the refresh token until such time as the refresh token expires, and subsequently, the session token expires thereafter.
Layer5 Cloud sessions use OAuth 2.0 for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol for authorization and focuses on client developer simplicity while providing specific authorization flows for web applications, desktop applications, mobile phones, and so on.
Session OAuth tokens are stored in your user-agent (web browser) in a cookie. The cookie is named meshery_session and is a signed cookie. The cookie is only sent over HTTPS and is not accessible to JavaScript running in the browser.
Creating and using sessions 🔗 A session is created each time a user successfully authenticates. See all active sessions on your user account’s security sessions page.
To use a session, sign into your Layer5 Cloud user account, thereby creating a new session. Your session’s token will automatically be stored in your web browser using a cookie. To use that same session, simply use the same browser until the session expires. You can have multiple sessions active concurrently, whether on the same device or different device. Each session receives it’s own authentication token and expiry time.
In this way, it is possible to use your same account to collaborate between different sessions that you have established. For example, you may use those two different sessions to open up the same Kanvas design and you will find that your avatar shows up twice in the design (along with your mouse cursor). You can use this to collaborate with yourself or with others. We recommend collaborating with others, though.
Revoking sessions 🔗 You can revoke your sessions at any time. When you revoke a session, it is immediately invalidated and cannot be used to make requests to the API. Revoking a session also revokes any refresh tokens associated with that session.
See Sessions in Layer5 Cloud.

What tokens are 🔗 For authentication and authorization, a token is a digital object that contains information about the identity of the principal making the request and what kind of access they are authorized for. In most authentication flows, the application—or a library used by the application—exchanges a credential for a token, which determines which resources the application is authorized to access.
Access tokens 🔗 Layer5 Cloud REST API uses OAuth 2.0 for authentication and authorization. OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol for authorization and focuses on client developer simplicity while providing specific authorization flows for web applications, desktop applications, mobile phones, and so on.
Access tokens are opaque tokens that conform to the OAuth 2.0 framework. They contain authorization information, but not identity information. They are used to authenticate and provide authorization information to Layer5 APIs. Access tokens are associated with a user account. They have an unlimited lifetime and can be revoked at any time.
API Tokens are User-Scoped, Not Organization-Scoped Layer5 Cloud API tokens are scoped to your user account, not to a specific organization. This means a single API token provides access to all organizations you are a member of, similar to how GitHub Personal Access Tokens work. For users who belong to multiple organizations, see Specifying Organization Context in the REST API documentation to learn how to control which organization your API requests operate on. Creating tokens 🔗 You can create a token for your user account at any time. Tokens never expire, but can be revoked. You can also give the token a descriptive label. This label will be shown in the list of tokens on your user account’s security tokens page.
See Tokens in Layer5 Cloud.
Using tokens 🔗 To use a token to authenticate to Layer5 Cloud’s REST API, pass the token as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of your HTTP request:
Authorization:  Deleting tokens 🔗 Deleting a token is how you revoke it. A deleted token is immediately invalidated and cannot be used to make requests to the API again, and any refresh tokens associated with it are revoked along with it. There is no way to restore a deleted token; anything still authenticating with it will start failing, so replace it with a newly created token first if it is in use.
To delete a token:
Go to the Tokens page in Layer5 Cloud. Each row shows the token’s ID, Name, Purpose and Creation Date. Find the token you want to remove. The list is searchable and sortable, and shows the newest tokens first by default. Click the trash can icon in that row’s Actions column. Confirm in the Delete Token dialog, which names the token it is about to delete. Click Proceed. A confirmation notification reports the deleted token by name.
Permissions Required Deleting a token requires the Delete Token key. Without it the trash can icon is disabled. See Keys. Sessions Are Deleted the Same Way Your browser sign-ins are represented by their own tokens and are listed on the Sessions page rather than here. There the same action is presented as Logout instead of Delete, and it ends that session. See Sessions.

A component is one piece of infrastructure in a design, and its configuration is what Kanvas applies when you deploy. This guide covers placing components on the canvas, editing their configuration, and moving them around by duplicating, copying, and pasting.
You need a design open in Designer mode. Designer is the only mode that allows authoring.
Add a component 🔗 Kanvas offers several ways to place a component. All of them produce the same result: a component in the design, with its configurator open beside it.
Method Behavior Drag from the component palette The component lands where you release it. Click a component in the palette or in a dock picker The component lands at a random position near the center of the canvas. Drop a component onto another component If the pair can form a parent-child relationship, Kanvas creates it. See Create Relationships. Drop or paste a file Image and text files become objects on the canvas. Infrastructure files (YAML, JSON, and archives such as TAR, GZ, ZIP, RAR, and 7Z) start an import. Text boxes, sections, and comments are annotation objects rather than infrastructure. They have their own keys: T, S, and M. Press I to pick an image file. See Whiteboard on the Canvas.
Find the right model and version 🔗 The palette groups models by category. Open a category to list its models, then expand a model to load its components. Each model has a version selector, sorted newest first, with the first version selected by default. The dock’s compact pickers offer an “All Versions” choice and hide duplicate components, keeping the highest version.
Typing in the palette search box queries the Meshery registry after you pause for one second. Results appear in two groups, Models and Components, and an empty result reads “Sorry, no matching records found”. Search matches model and component names only. It does not match labels.
The palette applies no filter of its own for deprecated or ignored models: it lists whatever the registry returns. Components whose schema is invalid appear dimmed, but you can still drag or click them.
The Kubernetes picker in the dock lists every Kubernetes component in a grid with a version filter. It hides List kinds, such as PodList.
File drop limits 🔗 File Result Limit Image (PNG, JPG, GIF, BMP, WebP, SVG) An image object, embedded in the design as data 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) Text (.txt) A text box holding the file text 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) YAML, JSON, TAR, GZ, TGZ, ZIP, RAR, 7Z An import placed at the drop position None applied by the canvas Anything else Ignored with no message - A file over the limit is rejected with an error message. The limit is fixed and identical on every plan, although the message refers to your plan.
Edit a component’s configuration 🔗 Open the configurator with any of these:
Double-click the component (two taps within 500 ms). Select the component and use the Configure control in its floating style toolbar. The toolbar appears when you are zoomed in far enough to see component detail. Add a new component. Its configurator opens automatically. Select a validation warning badge on the component. The configurator opens with the offending field highlighted. The configurator is a panel anchored to the component, on the right when there is room and on the left otherwise. The right-click menu has no Configure item.
The header 🔗 Control Behavior Component icon Hover to see the component version. Title The component kind, in sentence case. Versions menu Appears when the component exists in more than one model version. Choosing a version swaps the component’s definition and model reference to that version. Search Narrows the form to matching fields. When nothing matches, the form says so. Help Shows the component’s own description from its schema. Expand and collapse Switches the panel width between 32 rem and 45 rem. Delete Removes the component immediately, with no confirmation. Switching versions keeps your configuration values as they are. Kanvas does not migrate them, and validation then flags any value the new version does not accept. The switch also replaces custom styling with the new version’s defaults.
The tabs 🔗 A tab strip on the left appears when two or more tabs apply to the component. Which tabs are enabled depends on the capabilities the component’s definition declares. Role permissions do not decide this. A tab that does not apply appears dimmed.
Tab What it holds Config The component’s specification, as a form built from its JSON schema. Labels Key-value maps for labels and annotations. Not offered for alias components. Json Schema A read-only view of the component definition, with an Open in Registry button. Relationships The relationships this component participates in, grouped by kind, with a Show only active switch. Comment components open a chat thread instead of tabs.
Required fields, defaults, and validation 🔗 Fields are rendered from the component’s schema, and defaults come from the schema. A namespaced kind shows a Namespace field that defaults to default. A red asterisk marks a required field. An empty required field shows “This field is required”. Kanvas enforces first-level required fields up front, and an object whose children are all optional is not treated as required. The form does not validate as you type. Kanvas validates each changed component against its JSON schema after the change. Errors appear as a small red triangle beside the field label, with the messages in its tooltip, and the field is outlined. The component also shows a validation warning badge on the canvas, so an error you scrolled past stays visible after you close the panel. See Component Badges. How edits are saved 🔗 There is no Apply button. Kanvas writes an edit to the design 300 ms after you stop typing. Each write triggers three follow-ups: the design autosaves after a 3 second pause, the component is validated, and relationships are re-evaluated. Configuration that a relationship controls can therefore change shortly after you edit a related component. See Policy Evaluation.
Undo reverses configuration changes like any other edit. See Saving Designs.
Alias components 🔗 An alias component stands for one field inside its parent component. Its form edits that field of the parent, using the field’s sub-schema, and omits the Labels tab. Deleting an alias clears that field’s configuration on the parent.
Lock, duplicate, copy, and delete 🔗 Right-click a component to open its action menu. Items appear only when they apply.
Action Shortcut Behavior Lock and Unlock - Fixes the component’s position so it cannot be dragged. Configuration, labels, and style stay editable. The lock is saved with the design. Duplicate Ctrl/Cmd+D Creates a copy offset 50 px right and 50 px down, with a new id. Relationships between duplicated components are copied too. Names do not change. Copy Ctrl/Cmd+C Copies the component. The menu item copies one component without relationships. Delete Delete or Backspace Removes the component. Relationships that touched it are marked deleted, and the next evaluation reverses their effects on configuration. Reset styles - Restores the model’s default appearance. Move Out of Parent - Detaches a component from the parent it sits in. The menu labels Delete as Ctrl/Cmd+Delete, but Delete or Backspace alone performs the deletion.
Other items appear in Operator mode, such as terminal, log, and performance sessions. See Operator.
Style a component 🔗 A floating toolbar above a selected component offers the controls the component declares: shape (24 outlines), fill color with opacity from 0 to 1, border color, style, and thickness from 0 to 25, layer order, label, external link, image, and animation (none, blink, ripple, bounce, or pulse). Each control is shown only when the component supports it.
Copy and paste across designs 🔗 Task Shortcut Select every component Ctrl/Cmd+A Select several Hold Ctrl/Cmd and drag a selection box, or Ctrl/Cmd+click each one Copy the selection Ctrl/Cmd+C Paste Ctrl/Cmd+V Undo and redo Ctrl/Cmd+Z, Ctrl/Cmd+Y or Shift+Z A keyboard copy carries the selected components with their configuration, styles, and labels, plus every relationship whose two ends are both in the selection. Kanvas writes this to the system clipboard, so you can paste into another design, another browser tab, or another Kanvas session. Paste lands at the pointer when it is over the canvas and at the canvas center otherwise. The pasted group keeps its layout, and every id is regenerated.
Browsers allow clipboard access only after a user gesture. If the browser denies access, paste does nothing and shows no message. Use the keyboard shortcuts. The full list is in Keyboard Shortcuts.
Limits and errors 🔗 A design has a maximum number of components that depends on your plan. Layer5 Cloud enforces it when you save or import, not when you add a component. A save over the limit is rejected with a 403 response. Drawn objects such as shapes and text boxes count as components. See Designs and Components for the per-plan values. When zoomed out, the canvas hides text, labels, and badges and prompts you to zoom in before interacting with elements. See also 🔗 Relationships: what the Relationships tab lists. Tool Modes: every mouse interaction available on the canvas.

body:
In this tutorial you build a small web application design in Kanvas Designer: a Deployment that runs the application, a ConfigMap that holds its settings, and a Service that exposes it. You start from an empty canvas, connect the components, and save the result. The saved design is the starting point for Deploy and Observe Your First Design.
Along the way you learn what a design is made of, how relationships express the way components depend on each other, and when and how Kanvas saves your work.
Before you begin 🔗 Open Kanvas in Designer mode, either at kanvas.new or in a Meshery you run. Either works for this tutorial. If you plan to deploy the design in the next tutorial, start in a Meshery you run so the design is already where you need it. See Where do you want to work?. Work inside a specific organization. Kanvas does not create designs while the “all organizations” scope is selected. Step 1: Start an empty design 🔗 Start a new design. Kanvas opens an empty canvas and names the design “Untitled Design”.
That default name matters. Kanvas does not save a new design that has an empty canvas and no name of its own. A new design becomes saveable as soon as it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and is not “Untitled Design”.
Give the design a name that describes its purpose, such as web-app. A meaningful name makes the design easy to find later, and Kanvas also uses it to label the design’s deploy steps and its Operator view.
What you should see: an empty canvas with your design name in place of “Untitled Design”.
Step 2: Add the application components 🔗 A component is one piece of infrastructure in your design: a single, typed resource such as a Kubernetes Deployment, Service, or ConfigMap, together with its configuration. Each component comes from a model, and many components exist in more than one version. Choose the version that matches the cluster you intend to deploy to.
Add three components from the Kubernetes model to the canvas:
a Deployment, which will run the web application, a ConfigMap, which will hold the application’s settings, a Service, which will give the application a stable network endpoint. Kanvas renders each component on the canvas as soon as you place it. Arrange them so you can see all three.
Not everything on a canvas is infrastructure. Shapes, text, and drawings that you add for explanation are annotation-only: they make the design easier to read but are not resources. A connector you draw for illustration is an annotation edge for the same reason. Use annotations freely to document a design; they do not change what the design describes.
What you should see: three components on the canvas, each showing its kind.
Step 3: Configure each component 🔗 Every component carries configuration based on its schema. Open a component’s configuration panel to set its fields. The canvas updates as you change them.
Configure the three components so they refer to each other:
On the ConfigMap, set a name such as web-app-config and add one key, for example GREETING. On the Deployment, set a name, a container image (for example nginx), and a label such as app: web-app on its pod template. Reference the ConfigMap by its name so the container reads its settings from it. On the Service, add the same label (app: web-app) and set a port. These references are the same ones you would write in Kubernetes manifests. Kanvas evaluates them to work out how the components relate.
What you should see: each component shows the name you gave it.
Step 4: Connect the components with relationships 🔗 A relationship describes how two components interact or depend on each other. Kanvas draws relationships on the canvas as edges between components, or as nesting when one component contains another. Relationships fall into families:
Edge relationships describe interaction between components. A Service in front of a Deployment is a network relationship. A Deployment that reads a ConfigMap is a reference relationship: one component refers to another by name. Hierarchical relationships describe containment and inheritance, such as a Namespace that must exist before the Pods inside it. Relationships come from two sources: configuration you set, and connections you make on the canvas. Components that carry the same label form a label-match relationship automatically, so the Service and the Deployment in this design are now related. You can also drag a connection line from one component to a compatible target to create an edge relationship yourself. Relationships describes every kind and what each one means.
Check that your design shows a relationship between the Service and the Deployment, and one between the Deployment and the ConfigMap. If one is missing, compare the names and labels you set in Step 3, or drag a connection between the two components.
In large designs, Kanvas can skip drawing some relationships of one kind once that kind passes its rendering limit. When that happens it shows a warning of the form “Skipped rendering of N <kind> relationships due to limit of M”. The relationships still belong to the design; only their drawing is skipped.
What you should see: the Deployment connected to both the Service and the ConfigMap.
Step 5: Save the design 🔗 Kanvas saves for you. Once the design is saveable, Kanvas saves pending changes 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, Kanvas retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts.
Three things happen when a design is saved:
A new version is created. Every save increments the design’s version, so a design accumulates a history of versions as you work. A new design starts as public. The first save of a new design sets its visibility to public. Later saves keep whatever visibility the design has at that point. Designs can also be private or published; Saving designs explains each. Your plan’s component limit is checked. Each plan sets a maximum number of components per design, and Kanvas checks it on every save and import. A design over the limit is not saved; Kanvas reports “Design exceeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan”. Reduce the number of components or upgrade the plan. See Layer5 pricing for the limit on each plan. This three-component design is well within every plan’s limit.
What you should see: your design saved under its new name, with no unsaved changes pending.
Optional: Merge another design into this one 🔗 You can bring an existing design into the canvas you are working on. Kanvas merges its components and relationships into the current design and leaves the original design unchanged. Use this to assemble a larger system from designs you already have. See Merging designs.
What you built 🔗 You now have a saved design named web-app that describes a web application:
three infrastructure components, each configured from its schema, relationships that record how the Service reaches the Deployment and how the Deployment reads the ConfigMap, a version history that grows with every save. You also learned the core rules of saving: a new design needs a component or a real name before it can be saved, autosave runs 3 seconds after you stop editing, a new design starts as public, and your plan limits the number of components in a design.
Next 🔗 Take this design to a cluster in Deploy and Observe Your First Design. You will validate it, dry-run it, deploy it, and watch the resulting resources in Operator mode.
description: Build a small web application design from an empty canvas, connect its components through relationships, and save it, while learning how Kanvas models and stores designs.

title: Create Your First Design

body:
A design is the unit of work in Kanvas. It is a declarative description of infrastructure that you author on a canvas, save as a versioned document, share with others, and deploy to your clusters. Components are the building blocks of a design: some represent real infrastructure that Kanvas deploys, and others are annotations that only explain the design. Knowing which is which, and how a design behaves when you save, share, and deploy it, tells you exactly what Kanvas will do with your work.
What a design contains 🔗 A design holds four kinds of content:
Components - the infrastructure resources in the design, such as Kubernetes Deployments, Services, or cloud provider resources, each with its own configuration. Relationships - the connections between components and what those connections mean. See Relationships. Configuration - the settings of each component. Annotations - shapes, arrows, text, and icons that document the design. Kanvas never deploys annotations. How designs are saved 🔗 Naming and the saveability rule 🔗 A new, unsaved design is named “Untitled Design”. Kanvas saves a new design only when it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and not “Untitled Design”. An empty, unnamed canvas is not saved. Once a design has been saved, it can always be saved again, even after you remove every component.
You cannot create a design while your organization scope is set to all organizations. Select a single organization first.
Autosave 🔗 Kanvas saves pending changes automatically 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, Kanvas retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts.
Versions 🔗 Every save creates a new version of the design. You never overwrite a previous version by saving.
Who can see a design 🔗 A design has one of three visibility values:
Visibility Meaning Public Visible beyond its owner. Every newly created design starts as public. Private Visible to its owner. Other organization members need the “View Designs” permission to view private designs. Published Listed in the catalog. Unpublishing a design sets its visibility back to private. Saving an existing design never changes its visibility. Non-owners read private and published designs only when the design is shared with them or when they hold administrator rights.
Components 🔗 Components in Kanvas fall into two categories, distinguished by whether Kanvas can orchestrate them during deployment.
Semantic components (orchestratable) 🔗 Semantic components represent actual infrastructure resources. They map directly to real infrastructure elements, so Kanvas can create, configure, and manage their lifecycle during deployment. Examples include:
Kubernetes resources (Pods, Services, Deployments) Cloud provider resources (AWS S3 buckets, Azure Functions) Infrastructure components (load balancers, databases) Semantic components are either built in, like the Kubernetes components, or custom components that you create.
Non-semantic components (annotation-only) 🔗 Non-semantic components are visual and organizational elements that document and organize your design. They do not represent deployable resources, and Kanvas ignores them during deployment. Examples include:
Text boxes and comments Shapes and containers for grouping Arrows and lines Labels and tags Visual distinction rule Semantic components have a background, which marks them as real infrastructure resources. Non-semantic components have a transparent background, which marks them as visual aids only. Both kinds support visual customization. You can change a Kubernetes Pod’s color, modify its shape, or replace its background logo without changing what Kanvas deploys.
How components are organized 🔗 Kanvas draws semantic components from integration models. Kubernetes is the most common, and every integration model, such as KEDA, Prometheus, or AWS, provides components with the same orchestratable capabilities. Kanvas organizes them in a three-level hierarchy:
Categories - high-level groups, such as “Cloud Native Network” or “Database”. Integration models - specific technologies, such as Prometheus or Kubernetes. Components - the deployable building blocks within a model. For the full list of technologies Kanvas integrates, see the integrations directory.
Kubernetes component conventions 🔗 Kubernetes components follow a consistent visual system, so you can identify a resource kind at a glance.
Color and structure
Kubernetes component icons use a distinctive blue background. Every icon has the same structure: an outer shape filled with blue that encloses a white inner symbol. The white inner symbol identifies the specific Kubernetes kind. Shape as an indicator
The outer shape identifies the component’s role:
Triangles mark core networking resources, such as Service and APIService. Hexagons mark foundational workload controllers, such as StatefulSet. Unique polygons mark specialized resources, such as Endpoints, PriorityClass, or ValidatingWebhookConfiguration. Non-semantic palettes 🔗 Kanvas provides four palettes of annotation-only components. None of them is ever deployed.
Generic shapes cover general-purpose diagramming.
Arrows show direction or create simple visual annotations. They are static shapes for illustration only. To represent a functional relationship between semantic components, such as network traffic or a dependency, use an edge instead; see the edges shape guide.
Flowchart shapes document a design’s logic and flow with standard flowchart symbols.
Simple Line Icons add icons for annotation and visual emphasis.
One component, several representations 🔗 A semantic component looks different depending on where it appears. The Deployment component is a good example:
On the canvas, it has its distinctive shape and badge.
In a component selection panel, it appears as an icon.
In a cluster resource overview, it appears as a resource entry.
To practice reading designs, see interpreting Meshery designs in the Layer5 Academy.
Limits as shipped 🔗 The limits below describe Kanvas as it ships today. Current plans and their entitlements are listed at layer5.io/pricing.
Components per design 🔗 Kanvas enforces a maximum number of components per design whenever you save or import a design. The limit depends on your organization’s plan and is the same for monthly and annual billing.
Plan Components per design Personal 100 Team Designer 200 Team Operator 100 Enterprise 300 When a design exceeds the limit, the save or import is rejected with HTTP 403 and the message “Design exceeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan”, where N is your plan’s limit. To proceed, reduce the number of components in the design or upgrade your plan.
If your organization is not entitled to add components to a design at all, the save fails with HTTP 500 and the message “Org is not entitled to adding components to a design”.
Files dropped on the canvas 🔗 You can drop files directly onto the canvas:
Image and text files up to 500 KB are accepted. Larger files are rejected. The rejection message says “Your current plan allows files up to 500 KB”, but the 500 KB limit is the same on every plan. Infrastructure-as-code files, such as Kubernetes manifests, are imported as a design. How a design maps to deployed resources 🔗 When Kanvas deploys a design, every resource it creates carries the identity of its source design:
Metadata Key Value Label design.meshery.io/id The id of the source design Annotation design.meshery.io/version The version of the design that was deployed Annotation component.meshery.io/id The id of the component in the design A resource that carries the design id label is managed by Meshery. Because the label is a standard Kubernetes label, you can also select a design’s resources with your own tooling.
This metadata powers Operator’s per-design view. A design’s view is named “<design name>-View” and shows only the resources whose design id label matches that design, so you see exactly what one design produced across your clusters. See Operator.
description: What a Kanvas design is, how it is saved, versioned, and shared, what components are, and how a design maps to the resources it deploys.

body:
In this tutorial you build a single NGINX Pod in Kanvas, deploy it to a live cluster, expose it with a NodePort Service, and inspect the running Pod in Operator: its details, a shell inside its container, and its log stream. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, and every workload controller you meet later (Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs) exists to create and replace Pods. Working with a bare Pod first shows you exactly what those controllers automate.
The Pod in this tutorial is standalone: no controller watches it, so if it fails or is deleted, nothing recreates it. That trade-off suits learning and does not suit production.
What you will learn 🔗 A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network address and are scheduled together onto one node. A Kanvas component is a Kubernetes object in design form: its configuration is the object’s manifest, and Deploy turns it into a live object. Labels identify objects, and a Service’s selector uses labels to find the Pods it sends traffic to. Deploying a design again updates the cluster in place instead of creating duplicates. Operator shows what actually runs in the cluster, which is the ground truth when it differs from the design. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed environment. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. An environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See Environments. Operator mode for the inspection phases. Operator reads the cluster through Meshery Operator and MeshSync, which must run in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object. A unique prefix. Playground is shared with other users. Pick a short prefix, such as your handle, and use it in every name and label. This tutorial uses alex. You need basic familiarity with containers and Kubernetes manifests. You do not need to write YAML.
The scenario 🔗 You build two objects in one design:
Service alex-nginx-np type NodePort, port 80, selector app=alex-nginx | | Network relationship (traffic flows from the Service to the Pod) v Pod alex-nginx label app=alex-nginx +-- container nginx image nginx:latest, port 80 You deploy the Pod first, inspect it, then add the Service and deploy again.
Build the Pod 🔗 Create a new design and name it alex-pods. Kanvas saves the design automatically as soon as it has a name or a component; there is no Save button. Add a Pod component. The Kubernetes icon in the dock lists every Kubernetes kind, and the component palette search finds it too. The component’s configurator opens as soon as the Pod lands on the canvas. Set the Pod’s name to alex-nginx and leave the namespace as default. Add one entry to the Pod’s containers: name nginx, image nginx:latest, and a container port of 80. Containers is a list, so each entry opens in its own form. In the configurator’s Labels tab, add the label app with the value alex-nginx. What just happened. The configurator form is generated from the Pod’s schema in the Meshery registry, so its fields are the Kubernetes API fields. Required fields carry a red asterisk. Each edit is written to the design after a short pause; Kanvas then checks the changed component against its schema and marks problems beside the field. Those marks are warnings and never block you. The component you built is equivalent to this manifest:
apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: alex-nginx namespace: default labels: app: alex-nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:latest ports: - containerPort: 80 Check your work. The Pod sits on the canvas without a warning badge. If a badge with an error count appears on the component, select it to see each error; it leads to the field that needs attention.
Check the design before deploying 🔗 Run Validate from the design’s Actions menu. Run Dry Run from the same menu. What just happened. Validate runs in your browser. It checks each component against its schema and never contacts the cluster, so it cannot catch cluster-side problems such as a missing namespace or a name already in use. Its errors are advisory. Dry Run sends each object to the cluster’s API server as a server-side dry run: the API server applies its full validation and admission checks and persists nothing. Dry Run from the Actions menu targets the clusters selected in Meshery’s context selector.
Check your work. Validate reports No validation errors. and Dry Run reports No deployment errors. A Pod without any container fails the dry run with a Field Value Required error on the containers field; add the container and run it again.
Deploy and verify 🔗 Run Deploy from the Actions menu. The Deploy workflow has five steps: validation, choosing deployment targets, a dry run, a final review, and a summary. Select the environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Selecting an environment targets every Kubernetes connection assigned to it. Continue past the dry run once it reports no errors, then confirm the deployment. What just happened. Meshery Server turned each component into a Kubernetes object and sent it to every selected cluster. For each object it creates the object, or replaces it in place if an object of that kind and name already exists. It labels every object it applies with design.meshery.io/id=<design id> and records the design version and component id as annotations. That label is how Operator finds the objects that came from this design.
Check your work. The summary lists Deployed Pod "alex-nginx", and a notification reads Deployment completed for design 'alex-pods'. Read the per-object rows, not only the notification: the notification reads “completed” even when individual objects failed, and failures appear only as Failed to deploy rows with an error card. If the summary spinner never finishes, the request failed before it reached the cluster, most often because your session expired; reload Kanvas, sign in, and deploy again.
Inspect the Pod in Operator 🔗 Switch to Operator, either with the mode switch or with Open In Operator on the deploy summary. With the design open, Operator shows a view scoped to this design: only objects that carry this design’s id label. Select the alex-nginx Pod to open its details panel, and switch the panel from Summary to Details to see every field. What just happened. Operator draws the objects that MeshSync reports from the cluster, not the objects in your design. For a Pod, the details panel shows its phase as a status chip, the Pod IP, the host IP of its node, its QoS class, restart count, and each container’s image, ports, start time, and image pull policy. The QoS class is BestEffort because the container sets no resource requests or limits. The view is a snapshot: Operator loads it when you open a view, change a filter, or change the selected cluster, and it does not update on its own. To see later changes, change a filter or switch back to Operator.
Check your work. The status chip reads Running. A Pending Pod is not scheduled yet or is still pulling its image; load a fresh snapshot after a few seconds. If it stays Pending, the container status shows why, for example an image pull failure caused by a mistyped image name. If the canvas reads No data available for the current view, the snapshot found no objects with this design’s label: MeshSync has not reported the Pod yet, or the deploy failed. If it reads No Kubernetes context selected, select your cluster in Meshery’s context selector.
Open a shell and stream logs 🔗 Start a terminal on the Pod with Initiate Terminal Session, which is in the Pod’s right-click menu and in the details panel header. A terminal panel opens with one tab per container in the Pod. Run hostname. It prints alex-nginx, because a Pod’s name is the hostname of its containers. Run cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html to read the page NGINX serves. Start a log stream on the same Pod with Initiate Log Session. A log tab opens in the same panel. What just happened. Kanvas asks MeshSync, inside the cluster, to open /bin/sh in the container through the Kubernetes exec API, the same mechanism kubectl exec uses. The shell runs with MeshSync’s cluster permissions. The terminal sends each line when you press Enter and Ctrl+C sends an interrupt, so line-based commands work and full-screen programs such as vim, top, and less do not. Images without /bin/sh, such as distroless images, cannot open a shell.
The log tab shows the last 1,000 lines from every container in the Pod and then follows new output. Each line starts with [alex-nginx:nginx] and a Kubernetes timestamp; stdout and stderr are combined. NGINX’s container entrypoint writes its startup messages here. Closing the panel hides it without ending the sessions; the trash icon on a tab ends that session.
Check your work. The shell prints the Pod name and the HTML page. If the terminal tab stays blank, the session did not start, and Kanvas does not display the reason. The usual causes are a container without /bin/sh, a Pod that is not Running, or MeshSync not connected. When a Pod is deleted, its log stream stops without a notice.
Expose the Pod with a NodePort Service 🔗 Switch back to Designer and add a Service component named alex-nginx-np. Set the Service type to NodePort and add one port with port 80 and target port 80. Leave the node port empty so Kubernetes assigns a free one from the node port range (30000 to 32767 by default). On a shared cluster, a fixed node port that someone else holds fails the dry run. Set the Service’s selector to app: alex-nginx, the same label the Pod carries. Draw a Network relationship from the Service to the Pod. Edge handles appear when you hover a component; choose the network option and drag to the Pod. Compatible targets show a green outline while you drag, and releasing anywhere else creates nothing. Run Deploy again with the same environment. What just happened. Kubernetes routes Service traffic by the selector alone: every Running Pod whose labels match the selector becomes a backend of the Service. The Network relationship records the same connection in the design so that readers of the diagram see where traffic flows, and its edge shows the port values it reads from both components. Kanvas evaluates relationships after every change, and a relationship’s registry definition can copy designated fields from one component to the other. The selector you set is what Kubernetes acts on, so confirm it in the Service’s configurator after you draw the edge.
Deploying the same design again creates objects that are missing and replaces objects that already exist. The Service is created; the Pod is submitted unchanged and keeps running. Kubernetes treats almost every field of a running Pod as immutable, so changing a Pod beyond its container image means deleting it and creating it again, one of the reasons real workloads use Deployments.
Check your work. The summary lists Deployed Service "alex-nginx-np". Switch to Operator and select the Service. Its details show the service type NodePort, a cluster IP, the selector app=alex-nginx, and, under its connections, the ports including the node port Kubernetes assigned. The Service is reachable at http://<node IP>:<node port> from any machine that can reach the node; the Pod’s host IP is one such node address. In Playground, node IPs are often not reachable from your browser. The assigned node port still confirms that Kubernetes exposed the Pod.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu and select the same environment. The Undeploy workflow has the same five steps as Deploy, and its dry run checks the deletions.
Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind, name, and namespace: here, the Pod and the Service. It matches by name, not by the design label, so an object with the same kind, name, and namespace that someone else created is deleted too. That is another reason to use unique names on a shared cluster. Namespaces are removed only when the design contains a Namespace component. If an object is already gone, the dry-run step reports it as not found; select the bypass option to continue, because the real undeploy ignores missing objects.
The design itself stays in your account. Delete it from the design’s file menu if you no longer need it. Deleting a design never removes objects from a cluster, so undeploy first.
What you learned 🔗 A Pod is one or more containers that share a hostname and network address. A standalone Pod has no controller, so nothing replaces it. Each Kanvas component maps to one Kubernetes object, and its configurator edits that object’s manifest. Validate checks schemas in the browser; Dry Run asks the cluster’s API server; Deploy creates or replaces each object and labels it with the design id. A Service finds its Pods by label selector. The Network relationship documents the connection in the design. Operator shows a snapshot of what runs in the cluster, and it is where you open a shell and stream logs. Next steps 🔗 Continue with Explore Deployments to let a controller manage your Pods. Read Deploying designs for every option in the Deploy workflow. Read Operator to understand how Operator sees a cluster, and Interactive terminal and Log streaming for the full session behavior.

Plans 🔗 The matrix has one column for each of the four Layer5 plans: Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise. Entitlements follow your organization’s plan. Current pricing and plan details are listed at layer5.io/pricing.
Reading the matrix 🔗 A check mark means the plan includes the capability. A dash means the plan does not include it. Each table covers one category of capability. The What it does column describes the capability in one sentence. The matrix is refreshed automatically from the Layer5 product feature list. It lists the capabilities that have a documentation page. A capability that does not appear here is not necessarily unavailable; check the page that documents it.

Powered by Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDT), this feature ensures seamless, low-latency synchronization of cloud native designs, configurations, and operational workflows, even in complex multi-cluster Kubernetes and public Cloud environments. -Not included -Not included -Not included ✓Included Collaboration Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Team Design Review Multiple users to simultaneously edit a document, leave comments directly on specific text sections, and track changes made by others, enabling efficient collaboration and feedback loops during the review process. -Not included ✓Included -Not included ✓Included Collaborative Infrastructure Design Create and collaborate in online designs in real-time. -Not included ✓Included -Not included ✓Included Public and Private Designs Invite any user to collaborate on your public or private designs. -Not included ✓Included -Not included ✓Included Collaborative Infrastructure Views Simultaneously manage your infrastructure using shared views in real-time. See the status of your deployments, monitor performance, and troubleshoot issues. Views provide tools for interacting with your cluster, such as terminal access and log streaming. -Not included -Not included ✓Included ✓Included Public and Private Views Invite any user to collaborate on your public or private views. -Not included -Not included ✓Included ✓Included Performance Management Capability What it does Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Load Generation and Performance Testing Continuous visibility across all of your clusters and workloads. Single or multiple results in standardized format. ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included ✓Included Performance Profiles Define, name, and save performance profiles. Share performance profiles and test results with individual users or teams. -Not included -Not included ✓Included ✓Included Comparative Testing Visual comparison of performance test results. -Not included -Not included ✓Included ✓Included Capacity, soak, and burst testing Protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, gRPC with configuration duration, concurrency -Not included -Not included ✓Included ✓Included Availability depends on more than your plan 🔗 A capability is available to you only when all of the following hold: your plan includes it, your role grants it, your provider supports it, and your Kanvas deployment can reach a cluster when the capability needs one.
Your role 🔗 Your organization assigns you roles, and each role grants a set of permissions. Kanvas checks a permission before it offers Validate, Dry run, Deploy, Undeploy, Share, and Publish. An action your role does not grant is not offered, even when your plan includes it. See Permissions by Role for which role holds which permission.
Your provider 🔗 Kanvas stores designs, views, the catalog, and sharing records with a remote provider, Layer5 Cloud. Meshery can also run with a local provider, which has no remote service behind it. Under the local provider, every provider-bound feature, including views, the catalog, sharing, and support requests, returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. Run Meshery with a remote provider to use these features.
Where you run Kanvas 🔗 The hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new is for authoring designs. Every capability that needs a cluster requires a Meshery deployment that you run: the Meshery Playground or your own self-hosted Meshery.

Share and Publish open a sign-in prompt when you are not signed in. For why the hosted site differs, see How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud.
Limits by plan 🔗 Each plan caps the number of components in a single design, and Kanvas enforces the cap whenever you save or import a design. The limit for each plan and the error you receive when a design exceeds it are in Components per design.
Support by plan 🔗 The support channels and response commitments each plan includes are listed in Support channels by plan.

body:
Kanvas turns cloud native infrastructure into a design you can see, check, and deploy. This section takes you from an empty canvas to resources running in a Kubernetes cluster. Along the way you learn the four ideas that every other Kanvas page builds on, and which parts of Kanvas need a Meshery deployment of your own.
What you will learn 🔗 How a design is built from components, relationships, and configuration, and how Kanvas saves it. How Kanvas checks a design before it touches a cluster. How a design becomes running resources, and how Kanvas tracks them afterward. Which capabilities work on hosted Kanvas and which need a Meshery you run. The model in four steps 🔗 Design. In Designer mode you describe infrastructure as a design: components (such as a Kubernetes Deployment or Service), the relationships between them, and their configuration. Validate. Kanvas checks the design against each component’s schema and attaches every error to the component and field that caused it; a dry run then checks the design against a real cluster without changing it. Deploy. Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes clusters you select and labels every resource it creates with the design’s identity. Operate. In Operator mode you see the recorded state of your clusters and can filter it to the resources that belong to one design. Where do you want to work? 🔗 Kanvas runs in two places. Both use the same Designer, but only a Meshery you run can reach your clusters.
Capability Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new Meshery you run (Playground or self-hosted) Create and edit designs Yes Yes Share and publish designs Yes, after you sign in Yes, after you sign in, when Meshery uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider Validate a design No Yes Dry-run, deploy, and undeploy a design No Yes Connect and view Kubernetes clusters No Yes Operator mode No Yes On kanvas.new, validating, deploying, undeploying, connecting clusters, and opening Operator mode open a prompt that points you to a Meshery you run instead of performing the action. You have two choices:
Meshery Playground at playground.meshery.io is a hosted Meshery you can use without installing anything. Self-hosted Meshery runs in your own environment and connects to your own clusters. See the Meshery installation guide. A Meshery you run must use Layer5 Cloud as its remote provider for the features that live in Layer5 Cloud: sharing, the catalog, and Operator views. With the local provider, Meshery reports those features as not implemented.
Start on kanvas.new if you only want to design. Start on the Playground or your own Meshery if you plan to complete both tutorials below.
Sign in 🔗 You can open Kanvas and start designing without an account. Sharing and publishing a design require sign-in: when you are anonymous, these actions show a “Sign in to” prompt with a single Sign in action. Signing in takes you to the Layer5 Cloud sign-in page and returns you to the page you were on.
If sign-in cannot start because the provider address is malformed, Kanvas shows the notification “Sign-in could not start” followed by the reason.
Your first path 🔗 Complete these two tutorials in order. The second one starts from the design you save in the first.
Create Your First Design - build a small web application design from an empty canvas, connect its components, and save it. Deploy and Observe Your First Design - validate, dry-run, and deploy that design, then find its running resources in Operator mode and remove them. After the first design 🔗 Import designs from Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, Docker Compose files, and existing Meshery designs. Create relationships between components and learn how Kanvas interprets them. Work with components to configure, copy, and arrange them on the canvas. Embed designs in your own documentation so diagrams stay in step with the design they describe. Browse the Tutorials for longer, scenario-based walkthroughs. Read the Concepts to understand designs, relationships, and the Kanvas architecture in depth.

body:
Import turns an existing configuration into an editable design. Kanvas identifies the format from the file content, converts it to a Meshery design, and saves it as a new design in your account. The original file is not kept for download, so exporting later produces a new file from the current design.
Import works in Designer mode. The import action is hidden in Operator mode.
Choose how to import 🔗 Method Accepts Result Import dialog, File Upload One local file New design, or merge into the open design Import dialog, URL Import One direct http or https URL to a single file New design, or merge into the open design Drag or paste onto the canvas One or more files One new design per file, or a merge prompt if the canvas is not empty Catalog clone or open A published design Copy of the design, see Clone a Design GitHub integration in Layer5 Cloud Files and folders in a connected repository One private design per valid file The URL must point at a file, not a repository, a chart repository, or a directory. Folders cannot be imported directly: compress a Kustomize project or Helm chart into a single archive first.
The import dialog takes a name (1 to 255 characters, default “Untitled Design”). Names are not required to be unique. If you leave the name empty, Kanvas uses the name inside the file, and drops use the file name.
Supported formats 🔗 Kanvas accepts .yml, .yaml, .json, .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz, .gz, and .zip. Any other extension is rejected. Archives are extracted safely and entries that try to escape the archive directory are refused.
Kanvas decides the format by content, not by the file name, and takes the first match in this order:
Meshery design. A YAML or JSON design file, or an OCI image archive (.tar, .tgz, .zip) whose layers contain a design file. Only the first design in an archive is taken. An OCI archive without a design file fails. Kubernetes manifest. A .yml or .yaml file with one or more documents. Unknown resource kinds are kept as generic objects. Helm chart. A packaged chart archive. An uncompressed .tar is reported as needing gzip compression. Individual chart files such as Chart.yaml cannot be imported, and values overrides are not an import option. Docker Compose. Compose services are first converted to Kubernetes resources, so the design contains Kubernetes components. Kustomize. A single kustomization file, or an archive that contains kustomization.yaml and every file it references. The full matrix is in Supported Import and Export Formats.
Import a file as a new design or merge it 🔗 When the canvas is empty, import loads the new design. When a design is open, the dialog offers Import as new and Merge into current.
Import as new saves the file as a design and opens it. If the open design has unsaved changes, the browser asks you to confirm before leaving. Declining cancels the load, but the imported design stays saved in your account. Merge into current saves the file as its own design, then appends its components and relationships to the open design. Files dropped on a non-empty canvas raise a Merge Design prompt that names the incoming design and its component count. It offers Cancel, Open as new, and Merge into current. Cancel does not delete the design the import already saved.
Dropping several files imports each as a separate design. The import dialog processes a single file at a time.
How a merge behaves 🔗 Merging happens in the editor and changes only the open design.
Identity. Every component and relationship in the incoming design receives a new identifier. Kanvas does not match or de-duplicate against existing components, so merging the same design twice doubles its components. Preserved. Names, kinds, configuration, styles, and the internal layout of the incoming block. Placement. The block’s top-left corner moves to the drop position when you dropped a file. Otherwise it lands 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from its original coordinates, and it can overlap existing components. Not carried over. The incoming design’s name, id, version, visibility, catalog data, layer preferences, and workspace. The open design keeps its own. After the merge. Relationship evaluation runs as for any edit, and autosave persists the result after three seconds. If the merged design exceeds your plan’s component limit, the save fails and the merged components remain unsaved on the canvas. See Save Designs. Merging needs no permission key, but the incoming design must be one you can read: your own, public, published, or shared with you.
Where the imported design lands 🔗 The imported design is owned by you, placed in your selected workspace, public, at version 0.0.1, and records its detected source type. Imports from a GitHub repository are the exception: each file becomes a private design named after the file, and the connection records its repository, path, and branch. Invalid files in a selection are reported per path and do not stop valid files from importing.
The components-per-design plan limit applies to URL imports and to every save. GitHub imports are not checked at import time. They are checked the first time the design is saved.
URL import limits 🔗 The server fetches a URL under these limits:
Only http and https, checked again on every redirect, with at most 5 redirects. 10 seconds to connect and 30 seconds for the request. 16 MiB maximum body. Destinations that resolve to loopback, private, or link-local addresses are refused. Failures 🔗 Every failed import shows the same message, Failed to import design "<name>", whether the cause is an unrecognized format, an invalid archive, a plan limit, or an unreachable server. Nothing is saved when the server rejects the file. A failed merge shows Failed to merge design: <reason>.
Files dropped on the canvas follow separate rules. Images and .txt files become canvas objects, not designs, and files over 500 KB are rejected whatever your plan. Archive types RAR and 7Z pass the drop check but fail at import. Other file types are ignored without a message.
Related 🔗 Save Designs covers plan limits and failures after an import. GitHub Integration covers connecting a repository.

body:
The interactive terminal opens a shell inside a running container without leaving the Operator canvas. Use it for last-mile diagnosis that logs and status cannot answer: testing connectivity from inside a pod, reading a mounted file, or checking an injected environment variable. It is a browser-based equivalent of kubectl exec, scoped to the resource you selected.
Before you start 🔗 Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. See How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud. A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and a message broker in the cluster. MeshSync executes the shell, and Meshery Server relays input and output through the broker. If any of the three is unavailable, the terminal does not connect (see Failure modes). A running container whose image contains /bin/sh. Distroless images have no shell and cannot be used. Open a session 🔗 The action is named Initiate Terminal Session and is offered on Pod and Container resources only. Right-click the resource on the canvas, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The session starts immediately and the terminal panel opens at the bottom left of the canvas. There is no separate connect step.
What opens depends on what you selected:
You select Sessions opened A pod One session per container in the pod’s containers list, each in its own tab. Init and ephemeral containers are not included. There is no prompt to choose a container. A container One session for that container. A node with an active session shows a terminal badge. Selecting the badge reopens the panel.
Work in the terminal 🔗 Each tab is one shell session. The panel is draggable, minimizable to a dock icon with a session count, and keeps its scrollback (10,000 lines). Closing the panel with the close button hides it and leaves the sessions running. The trash icon on a tab ends that tab’s session and removes the tab. Leaving Operator mode closes the panel.
The terminal edits your input in the browser and sends it to the container when you press Enter:
Key Behavior Printable keys, Backspace Edit the current line locally. Enter Sends the whole line to the shell. Up, Down Walk the history of lines typed in this tab. Ctrl+C Sends an interrupt to the running command. Tab Inserts four spaces. It does not trigger shell completion. Other Ctrl, Alt, and Meta combinations Ignored. Because input is line-based and the remote terminal is not resized when you resize the panel, commands that take over the screen, such as vim, top, and less, do not work. Use commands that print and exit: ls, cat, env, ps aux, curl, nslookup.
The search icon in the panel header opens a search field with next and previous controls for finding text in the scrollback.
Limits and scope 🔗 Item Behavior Sessions per container One live session per container per user. Starting a second session for the same container does nothing and opens no new tab. Concurrent sessions overall No limit is enforced. Different users Each user gets an independent session, even on the same container. Shell Fixed to /bin/sh with a terminal attached. No bash fallback and no shell selection. Identity in the container The exec call runs with MeshSync’s own Kubernetes access, not a per-user Kubernetes identity. Anyone who can open a terminal has the reach of the workload’s container, so treat access to this action as access to the container. Idle timeout, maximum duration None. Reconnect None. If the connection between your browser and Meshery Server drops, the tab stays on screen but is dead. Close the tab and start a new session. Who can use it 🔗 Kanvas does not hide or disable the action based on role or plan. The permission model lists View Interactive Terminal as an Operator capability for the Team Operator plan and above. See Permissions by Role and Feature Availability for the current role and plan matrix.
Failure modes 🔗 Symptom Cause and fix Panel shows Failed to create terminal session with a reason The Kanvas extension could not be loaded by Meshery. The reason names the cause, for example a plugin built for a different Meshery version than the one you run. Install matching versions. Toast No container found to create term session The selected component lists no containers. Empty tab, no prompt Meshery Server could not reach MeshSync. Confirm the cluster shows as connected and that the broker is connected. Kanvas does not display the server’s error text for terminal sessions. Prompt never appears, or the shell prints an error The container has no /bin/sh, is not in the Running phase, or was deleted. Errors raised while MeshSync opens the shell print in the terminal itself. Session goes quiet after exit or a pod restart The session ended on the cluster. Kanvas shows no closed message. Close the tab and start a new session. For cluster connection problems, see Troubleshoot Kanvas.
Related 🔗 Stream Container Logs opens in the same panel as terminal sessions. Operator explains where this data comes from. Resource Details lists the actions available for every resource kind.

body:
Sharing opens a private design to the people you name. Each grant is for one person, and it has no access level: a person who can open the shared design can also edit it and comment on it. You can also change a design’s visibility to make it open to everyone, and you can copy a link that points people to it.
This guide covers the task. For the reasoning behind the access model, read Collaboration Model. For a worked example with two people, follow Collaborative Editing.
Before you start 🔗 Requirement Detail Signed-in account Anonymous visitors to kanvas.new can design without signing in, but sharing asks them to sign in first. Layer5 Cloud also refuses a share from an anonymous session. Share Design permission Kanvas hides the Share action without it, and Layer5 Cloud checks it again when the request arrives. Layer5 Cloud checks it in the organization that owns the design’s workspace. A design that is in no workspace is checked in an organization the design’s owner belongs to. View All Users permission The people picker searches users through this permission. Without it the search is rejected, and the dialog does not find anyone. A loaded, non-empty design Share is unavailable while a design is empty, and while it is still loading. A new design has no link until its first save assigns it an id. An unpublished design Share is hidden for a published design. A remote provider Under the local provider, sharing returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. See Feature Availability by Plan. Views use the same dialog and the same grant model. Sharing a view needs the Share Views permission instead of Share Design. See Views.
Visibility levels 🔗 Visibility decides who can open a design without a grant.
Visibility Who can open it Who can edit it Private The owner, provider administrators, and people you grant access The same people Public Anyone with the link or the design id, including anonymous visitors Any signed-in user Published Everyone, through the Layer5 Cloud catalog The owner, provider administrators, and people with a grant A newly saved design is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Make a design private before you put sensitive architecture in it. A design cannot change visibility while it is published. See Publish Designs for the published state.
Changing visibility saves like any other edit: it raises the design’s version and counts against the plan’s components limit.
Give people access 🔗 Open Share for the design. It is in the design’s top bar, and in the menu of a design in your list of recent designs. Search for the person and add them. The search covers every user on Layer5 Cloud your role may search, not only your organization. It returns ten matches at a time and nothing for an empty search. Confirm the person appears in People with Access. The grant takes effect immediately. The person opens the design with the link, and it also appears in their list of designs.
What a grant allows 🔗 A grant carries no access level. It lets a person open a private design, edit and save it, comment on it, clone it, and download it. What else they can do depends on their own permissions, not on the grant: deploying, validating, and sharing each check the person’s role.
Action Owner Person with a grant Open and edit the design Yes Yes Comment, resolve, and reopen threads Yes Yes Clone and download Yes Yes Share it onward With the Share Design permission With the Share Design permission Change visibility Yes Layer5 Cloud does not restrict it to the owner Revoke access Yes With the Share Design permission Delete the design Yes, and provider administrators No Transfer ownership Not supported Not supported Most accounts hold the Share Design permission, because the default Organization Admin role includes it. Expect a collaborator to be able to share the design onward unless your organization has changed its roles. See Permissions by Role.
Rules for grants 🔗 The owner cannot be granted access, and the owner’s access cannot be revoked. A person can be granted access once. A second grant for the same person is rejected. Grants and revokes in one request are applied independently. If one half fails, the other half stays in place, and the failure names the half: “access could not be granted” or “access could not be revoked”. Layer5 Cloud sends an invitation email to a newly granted person only when the request asks for one. The email links to the design in the Meshery Playground. Each share request is recorded as an event. Grant access to people in another organization 🔗 A grant does not compare the person’s organization with the design’s. You can share a design with a user from any organization on the same Layer5 Cloud. There is no provider setting that enables or blocks this. The cross-organization tutorial walks through it.
Share a link 🔗 Copy Link produces a link that opens the design in Kanvas. It works for private and public designs.
Public design: anyone with the link can open it and, if signed in, edit it. Private design: the link only points to the design. The person also needs a grant, or an administrator role. Without one, Layer5 Cloud refuses the request, and an anonymous visitor cannot open it. The link carries the design’s id. Anyone who learns the id of a public design can open it.
Revoke access 🔗 Remove the person from People with Access. The change applies at once. Their clones and any copies they made stay theirs. Comments they wrote remain in the design, because comments are part of the design.
Deleting a design removes every grant for it.
What does not grant access 🔗 Teams. The dialog finds individual users only. Layer5 Cloud accepts a grant for a team through its API, but no access check honors it, so team members gain nothing from it. Workspaces. Adding a design to a workspace, and assigning teams to that workspace, does not open a private design to those teams. Layer5 Cloud checks the owner, provider administrators, and the design’s own grants. See Workspaces for what a workspace does control. Organization membership. Being in the owner’s organization does not open a private design. To give a whole team access, grant each member.
Messages and failures 🔗 Message Cause What to do Unable to share: this design could not be loaded. Try again once it has loaded. Share was opened while the design was still loading, or after its load failed. Wait for the design to load, or reopen it, and open Share again. Failed to load the list of people with access. The owner or the access list could not be fetched. Kanvas shows this error instead of an empty list. Close and reopen Share. An empty list does not mean nobody has access while this error shows. Failed to update visibility. The visibility change was rejected. Retry. Changing visibility is not supported for this kind of item. The item has no visibility control. Keep its current visibility. A single error naming the parts that failed A grant, a revoke, or the invitation email did not complete. Parts that succeeded stay in place. Reopen Share, check People with Access, and repeat the missing part. After any grant or revoke, check People with Access before you rely on the change.
The Share dialog: add people, review who has access, set visibility, and copy the link. Related 🔗 Collaboration Model explains how access, live editing, and comments fit together. Review a Design with Comments covers feedback on a shared design. Delete a Design explains who can delete and what disappears with a design.
