body:
Validation checks the configuration of each component in a design against the schema of that component’s definition. It runs in your browser, needs no cluster, and changes nothing. Run it while you build to catch missing or malformed fields before a dry run or a deployment spends time on them.
Before you start 🔗 Environment. Validation runs in a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run it and shows a self-hosted-feature prompt instead. A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled while the design has no components. An unsaved design validates; Kanvas validates the design as it is on the canvas. Permission. On mobile, the Validate Design permission gates the action. See Permissions by Role. What validation checks 🔗 Checked Not checked Each component’s configuration against the JSON schema of its registered definition, with all errors collected per component Relationships between components Required fields, types, and formats, including 32-bit and 64-bit integers and integer-or-string values Dependencies, namespaces, and cross-references Anything in the target cluster Annotation components (text, shapes, and other visual elements) carry no infrastructure and are skipped. They are counted separately in the summary.
Two cases pass silently, so a clean result does not prove every component was checked:
A component whose definition cannot be fetched from the registry is skipped as valid. A design whose schema version is not a supported design version reports 0 components, 0 annotations, and no errors. Read the results 🔗 The results show a summary line, <N> component(s) and <M> annotations, and an error count. With no errors the result reads No validation errors.
With errors, each component that has them appears as an expandable row with its name and error count. Each error names the field by its dotted path, for example Field "spec.ports" must have required property 'apiGroup'. When the path is empty, the line shows the message alone. Errors are warnings: they never block you from continuing.
To fix an error, open the component and go to the field named in the path. A missing required property names the field you need to fill in.
Validation runs fresh each time you open it, so results always reflect the current design.
Results on the canvas 🔗 Validation also marks the canvas. A component with errors shows a circular badge at its lower left holding the total number of errors, schema and dry-run errors combined. Selecting the badge expands it to two counts: a yellow triangle for schema errors and a red octagon for dry-run errors. Each opens the matching results, scrolled to that component.
Badges appear only when the Validation Warnings and Deployment Errors entries in the Layers panel are on and the render mode is Full. They are hidden in Wireframe, Medium, and View-only modes. A new validation or dry run replaces them, and loading another design clears them. Editing a component does not clear its badge, so run validation again after you fix something.
The event it records 🔗 Validating the whole design records an informational event in the event log:
Validation completed for ‘’ with error(s) found.
The event carries the design name, the total error count, and per-component results. Validating a single component records nothing.
Validate and dry run compared 🔗 Validate Dry run Checks against Each component’s schema The Kubernetes API of each target cluster Needs a cluster No Yes Catches Missing or malformed configuration Everything the cluster’s admission and schema checks reject Speed Immediate One request per cluster Validate is the fast loop while you build. Run a dry run before you deploy, because it is the only check that involves the cluster you are deploying to. The deploy and undeploy flows run validation as their first step.

body:
Kanvas Snapshot posts a picture of your infrastructure as a comment on each GitHub pull request. Reviewers see which components a Kubernetes manifest, Docker Compose file, or Helm chart defines, and how they connect, before they read the YAML. The comment updates on every push to the pull request.
The snapshot runs in a GitHub Actions workflow on GitHub-hosted runners. It never touches your cluster. For how a snapshot is built and what it can and cannot do, see Kanvas Snapshot.
You can set it up two ways. The Layer5 GitHub App path installs the workflow for you. The direct path has you add the action to a workflow you own. Both produce the same comment.
Before you start 🔗 A Layer5 Cloud account. A repository on github.com that holds the infrastructure file. GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab, and Bitbucket are not supported. Permission to install a GitHub App on the repository, and to add repository secrets and commit to the default branch. A plan that includes GitOps Snapshots. See availability by plan. Set up with the Layer5 GitHub App 🔗 The Connect wizard for GitHub in Layer5 Cloud walks through seven stages. Running it again later updates the connection.
Stage What happens Connect GitHub opens so you can install the Layer5 GitHub App on your user or organization and choose repositories. Select repositories Lists only repositories where the App is installed. To add one, install the App on it again. Import designs Scans the selected repositories for Helm charts, Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files, and Meshery designs, and imports what you pick. Import failures are counted per repository. Select a design for the snapshot You choose at most one file per repository. Cloud stores its path for that repository. At least one repository needs a selection to continue. Configure secrets Cloud generates a Layer5 Cloud API token and shows it once. You add it to each repository as a secret named MESHERY_TOKEN. Configure workflows Cloud commits the workflow to each selected repository. Clear the checkbox to skip this stage and install nothing. Finish Shows which repositories received the workflow. Cloud never writes the secret for you. Add MESHERY_TOKEN to each repository yourself, with that exact name, and confirm the checkbox in the wizard. The wizard generates a new token each time the secrets stage opens, and it cannot show an earlier one again. Generate tokens in Layer5 Cloud and revoke them there; see Tokens.
What the installed workflow does 🔗 The wizard commits .github/workflows/kanvas.yml to the default branch of each repository, with the commit message Install Kanvas workflow. If that file already exists, the wizard replaces it.
Setting Value Name Kanvas Screenshot Service Triggers pull_request when opened, synchronized, or reopened. Also workflow_call, with an optional fileName input that overrides the stored path. Runner ubuntu-latest Token permissions actions: read, contents: write, security-events: write, statuses: write, pull-requests: write, id-token: write Authentication secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to comment, secrets.MESHERY_TOKEN for Layer5 Cloud Input file The path you selected for that repository Input type Kubernetes Manifest, always Two behaviors matter after install:
The input type is always Kubernetes Manifest. If the file you chose is a Docker Compose file or a Helm chart, edit application_type in the committed workflow to Docker Compose or Helm Chart. The workflow is built from the latest template at install time. Installing the same repository twice on different days can produce a different workflow. Review the committed file before you rely on it. Per-repository install results are:
Result Meaning Workflow added with a commit link The file was committed. Workflow already exists, try deleting it first at ./.github/workflows/kanvas.yml GitHub rejected the write because of the existing file. Delete or edit the file in the repository, then run the stage again. unable to install workflow in <repository> The request failed or timed out after 30 seconds. Run the stage again. repository must be in "owner/name" form The repository identifier is malformed. If you uninstall the App 🔗 Cloud checks whether the App installation still exists. When GitHub reports that it does not, Cloud deletes the stale GitHub connection. Run the wizard again to reconnect.
Use the action in your own workflow 🔗 Skip the wizard when you want to choose the triggers, run snapshots from a workflow you already maintain, or authenticate with a personal access token instead of the App.
Generate a Layer5 Cloud API token and store it as a repository secret, for example MESHERY_TOKEN. Add a workflow. The action needs its own repository checked out to a folder named action, and the same token permissions the installed workflow uses. name: Kanvas Snapshot on: pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened] permissions: actions: read contents: write security-events: write statuses: write pull-requests: write id-token: write jobs: snapshot: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: path: action repository: layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot - uses: layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot@v0.2.44 with: githubToken: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} mesheryToken: ${{ secrets.MESHERY_TOKEN }} prNumber: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} application_type: "Kubernetes Manifest" filePath: manifests To snapshot a file that is hosted at a public URL, such as a packaged Helm chart, replace filePath with application_url and set application_type to Helm Chart. Pin the action to the latest release tag; v0.2.44 is current at the time of writing.
Action inputs 🔗 Input Required Default Behavior githubToken Yes - Posts the pull request comment. The built-in GITHUB_TOKEN or a personal access token that can write pull request comments. mesheryToken Yes - Layer5 Cloud API token. application_type Yes - Kubernetes Manifest, Docker Compose, or Helm Chart. filePath No - A file, or a directory of manifests, in the checked-out repository. application_url No - A public URL of the source file. designID No - The id of an existing design. Overrides filePath and application_url. prNumber No 0 The pull request to comment on. With 0, no comment is posted. skipComment No false Set to true to render without commenting, for manual or scheduled runs. assetLocation No - Where the rendered image is stored. email No - See known limitations. When you give filePath a directory, the action merges the .yaml and .yml files directly inside it into one document. It does not read subfolders. Point it at the folder that holds the manifests, or at a single file.
The action outputs resource_url, the URL of the rendered image. When no image URL comes back, the action does not post a comment.
Choose other triggers 🔗 The comment needs a pull request number, so only pull request runs post one. Use any other workflow event, such as push, schedule, or workflow_dispatch, to render a snapshot without a comment and read resource_url in a later step. Leave prNumber at 0 or set skipComment to true for those runs.
What the pull request comment contains 🔗 The comment shows the rendered image, linked to itself, with links to the generated design in the catalog and to an editable copy in the Playground. The workflow keeps one comment per pull request and replaces its content on each run.
Alongside the comment, each run uploads debug logs, screenshots, and a video of the render as workflow artifacts, whether the run succeeds or fails. Open them from the workflow run when a snapshot looks wrong.
Change or remove snapshots 🔗 To Do this Snapshot a different file Run the wizard again and select another file, or edit filePath in the workflow. Add a repository Install the App on it, then run the wizard again. Upgrade the action Change the version tag after layer5labs/kanvas-snapshot@ in the workflow. Check the release notes when application_type or input names change. Rotate the token Generate a new API token, update the MESHERY_TOKEN secret, and revoke the old token. Remove snapshots Delete .github/workflows/kanvas.yml, delete the MESHERY_TOKEN secret, and revoke the token. Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause and fix The workflow runs and no comment appears The run had no pull request number, skipComment is true, or the render produced no image URL. Open the uploaded workflow artifacts to see why the render failed. The snapshot shows nothing, or only some resources A directory path reads only the YAML files directly inside it. Point filePath at the folder that holds them. The snapshot treats a Helm chart or Compose file as a manifest The wizard sets application_type to Kubernetes Manifest. Edit it in the workflow. Authentication fails MESHERY_TOKEN is missing, misspelled, or revoked, or the repository does not share the secret with the workflow. The wizard lists no repositories The App is not installed on them. Install it, then run the wizard again. Known limitations 🔗 Email delivery. The email input does not deliver mail today. The action sends its request in a shape the Layer5 Cloud endpoint rejects, and the workflow continues without a failure. Use the pull request comment or resource_url. No diffs. A snapshot shows the current file only. It does not compare against the base branch. Single design per repository in the wizard. To snapshot more than one file, add the action to a workflow of your own for each file. GitHub.com only. The App and the install flow work against github.com.

body:
Relationships record how components connect, and Kanvas keeps related configuration in sync once they exist. You create some relationships by hand and Kanvas creates others when it evaluates the design. This guide shows which is which, how to create each kind, and how to remove or hide them.
Relationships work only in Designer mode. For what each kind means, read Relationships.
Kind You create it by You remove it by Edge (network, mount, reference, and other edge subtypes) Picking an edge from a component’s handle and dragging to a target Selecting the edge and choosing Delete Hierarchical, inventory Dropping a component onto a compatible parent Dragging it out, or choosing Move Out of Parent Hierarchical, wallet Dropping a component onto a compatible host Deleting the component, or choosing Move Out of Parent Hierarchical, alias Kanvas creates it during evaluation Deleting the alias component TagSets (shared labels) Giving components matching labels Changing the labels so they stop matching Annotation edge Drawing with the Pen tool Selecting the edge and choosing Delete Create an edge relationship 🔗 Edge relationships connect components that exchange traffic or depend on one another, such as a Service and a Deployment.
Hover a component to reveal arrow handles on its bottom, left, and right sides, then select one. A circular menu opens. Pick a relationship from the menu. It lists every edge relationship in the registry that can start from this component, with the subtype in a tooltip. A binding relationship lists one item per component that can sit between the two ends. Drag from the source to a target. Compatible targets in view get a green outline, and incompatible components dim to half opacity. Kanvas checks only the components visible in the viewport. Release on a compatible target. Releasing on an incompatible component, a non-component, or empty canvas cancels the creation without a message. A binding relationship also places its binding component between the two ends.
The edge shows an arrow and a label. Network edges label the source and target ports and protocols, read from the configuration the relationship manages.
Nest components in a parent 🔗 Drag a component onto another and release. Valid targets are the components that form an inventory or wallet relationship with it, and Kanvas outlines them in green while you drag. The same drop works when you drag a component from the palette onto an existing component.
Inventory. The child is drawn inside the parent. For example, a Pod dropped on a Namespace becomes its child. You can collapse and expand parents. Wallet. The child is absorbed into the host and shown as a green badge at the host’s bottom-right corner with the item count. Select the badge to list the items, then select an item to open its configurator. A sidecar attached to a workload is an example. A component has at most one parent. Dropping it into a new parent replaces the old relationship, and dropping it on empty canvas removes it.
Let labels form TagSets 🔗 You never draw a TagSet. When components carry labels or annotations that match under a registry relationship definition, the next evaluation creates a TagSet and draws a translucent region around the group. See Work with Tags.
Remove a relationship 🔗 Edge. Select the edge and choose Delete in its toolbar. Kanvas marks the relationship deleted, and the next evaluation reverses its effects on configuration. Inventory. Drag the child out of the parent, or right-click it and choose Move Out of Parent. Wallet. No control deletes a wallet relationship by itself. Delete the component, or choose Move Out of Parent. TagSet. No control deletes a TagSet. Change the labels so they no longer match, or hide the layer. Style an edge 🔗 Select an edge to open its toolbar. It offers line color, line style (solid, dashed, or dotted), curve and arrow style, a label, and an animation (none or marching ants). Styling changes only appearance.
Hide a kind of relationship 🔗 The Layers panel lists eight relationship kinds, each with a count and a show or hide toggle: hierarchical inventory, wallet, and alias; TagSets; and edge mount, network, annotation, and reference. Open the panel with the backslash key or from the design toolbar.
Hiding a kind removes it from the canvas. It does not stop evaluation. Kanvas still evaluates the whole design, so configuration that a hidden relationship manages keeps syncing. The toggles are stored in the design, so they are saved with it, restored when it reopens, and shared with collaborators. Everything is visible by default.
Configuration sync 🔗 When two components are related, the registry definition names which fields on each side are linked, and Kanvas writes values across them each time it evaluates the design. For example, changing a Service’s port updates the matching container port on a related Deployment. The relationship definition decides the direction, so it can differ by kind. See Policy Evaluation.
Limits 🔗 Kanvas draws at most 30 TagSets. Beyond that, it shows the warning “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30”. TagSets render only in Full render fidelity. No other kind has a rendering limit. See also 🔗 Add and Configure Components: the Relationships tab lists each component’s relationships.

In this tutorial, an Organization Admin at one company asks an engineer at another company to review a private design. By the end, you will have given someone outside your organization access to one design, held a review in a comment thread, and removed that access. Along the way, you will learn what a grant gives someone, where Kanvas checks permissions, and why the review itself has to happen in comments.
The cast is the same one used across these docs (see Meet Five and the Cast). Marcus Webb is the Organization Admin at Stellar Dynamics. Five is a Platform Engineer at Orbital Labs, a separate organization.
Before you begin 🔗 Marcus holds the Share Design permission in Stellar Dynamics. Kanvas checks it in the organization that owns the design’s workspace, so a grant from another organization does not count. Marcus holds the View All Users permission. The people picker in the Share dialog depends on it. Five holds View All Users as well, so he can @mention Marcus in a comment. Both accounts exist on the same Layer5 Cloud. The design is saved and private. A design gets a link only after its first save gives it an id. Kanvas hides Share for empty designs and for published designs. The scenario 🔗 Marcus owns a saved design called stellar-saas-platform. It models Stellar Dynamics’ Azure SaaS stack: an AKS cluster, Azure SQL, API Management, Azure AD, Event Hub, and the connections between them. Before his team runs it in production, he wants Five to review the architecture.
Step 1: Marcus grants Five access 🔗 Marcus opens the Share dialog on stellar-saas-platform and searches for Five by name. The search covers every user Marcus’s role lets him search, not just members of Stellar Dynamics, so Five appears even though he belongs to Orbital Labs. Marcus adds Five, and Five now appears in the list of people with access.
Here is the model to remember. A private design opens for its owner, for provider administrators, and for each person who holds a grant on it. A grant links one person to one design. It has no access level and never checks organizations. Kanvas does not compare Five’s organization with the design’s, and you do not need any provider-level trust setting.
An invitation email goes out only when the share request asks for one, so Marcus copies the design link and sends it to Five himself.
Result: Five holds a grant on stellar-saas-platform.
Step 2: Five opens the design 🔗 Five follows the link while signed in to his Orbital Labs account. The design loads with every component and connection Marcus drew. It also appears in Five’s list of designs shared with him.
Five gets this one design and nothing else. The grant does not make him a member of Stellar Dynamics. Other private designs in the same workspace remain closed to him, because each private design checks its own grants. Assigning a team to the workspace would not open them either.
Result: Five sees the design Marcus sees.
Step 3: Five comments and mentions Marcus 🔗 Five places a comment next to API Management and writes:
@Marcus Webb You’re missing a WAF in front of API Management.
Typing @ followed by part of a name brings up matching users. Choosing one stores a real mention, not plain text.
The comment is a component in the design, so it saves and travels with the design. If Marcus has the design open, the comment shows up on his canvas right away. Because Five mentioned him, Marcus also gets an email with the design’s name, a snapshot, and the thread, unless he has turned off comment emails in his account preferences.
Result: An open thread on the design names Marcus.
Step 4: Marcus responds, edits, and resolves 🔗 Marcus replies in the thread. Five wrote an earlier message in it, so Five receives an email about the reply. Marcus then adds an Azure Application Gateway in front of API Management and connects the two. Kanvas autosaves the change.
Marcus resolves the thread. The comment leaves the canvas but stays in the comments panel under the Resolved filter. Resolving sends no email. If anyone posts again in the thread, it reopens.
Result: The fix is in the design, and the thread records why it was made.
What this means for review 🔗 Kanvas has no view-only or comment-only grant. A grantee can do anything an editor can do. Five can open the design, save edits, comment, clone it, download it, and switch it between private and public. He can only re-share it if his role gives him the Share Design permission in Stellar Dynamics’ organization. Five cannot delete the design, and he cannot take over ownership.
The rules of the review therefore live in the comment thread, not in the permission system. Marcus has two tools for keeping it that way:
Remove the grant when the review ends. Access lasts exactly as long as the grant does. Offer a clone. If Five wants to experiment, a clone gives him an independent copy, and the original stays untouched. For live co-editing during a review, see Collaborative Editing.
Step 5: Marcus revokes access 🔗 Once the review is done, Marcus removes Five from the list of people with access in the Share dialog. When Five opens the link again, Kanvas refuses it, and the design leaves his shared list.
Five’s comments stay in the design. Comments are part of the design, so removing a person does not remove what they wrote. A clone is a separate design, so revoking access to the original does not affect any clone Five made.
Result: Only Marcus and provider administrators can open stellar-saas-platform.
Access at a glance 🔗 This table applies to a private design. Provider administrators can open and delete any private design.
Person Open the private design Edit it Comment Re-share Delete Marcus (owner) Yes Yes Yes Yes, with the Share Design permission Yes Five (grantee) Yes Yes Yes Only with the Share Design permission in the design’s organization No Someone with no grant No No No No No Next steps 🔗 Share a Design covers granting, revoking, and changing visibility. Review a Design with Comments covers comment threads, mentions, filters, and notifications. Collaboration Model explains how sharing, comments, and live editing fit together. Permissions by Role lists every permission that controls these actions.

In this tutorial you take the design you saved in Create Your First Design to a live Kubernetes cluster. You validate it, dry-run it against the cluster, deploy it, and then switch to Operator mode to see the running resources that belong to the design. You finish by undeploying it.
Along the way you learn the difference between checking a design against its schemas and checking it against a cluster, how Kanvas chooses where to deploy, and how Kanvas keeps track of the resources a design creates.
This tutorial needs a Meshery you run Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new cannot validate, dry-run, deploy, or undeploy designs, and it does not offer Operator mode. On kanvas.new these actions open a prompt that sends you to a Meshery you run instead. Use the Meshery Playground or install Meshery in your own environment, then open your design there. Before you begin 🔗 You need:
The web-app design from the previous tutorial, saved and open in Designer mode. A Meshery you run, either the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery, signed in with Layer5 Cloud as its provider. Operator views are stored in Layer5 Cloud, so the local provider cannot show them. A connected Kubernetes cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. Meshery Operator installs MeshSync and Meshery Broker in the cluster; MeshSync streams the cluster’s live state to Meshery Server, and that stream is what Operator mode displays. See Operator. Permissions in your organization for each action. Validate Design permits both validation and dry runs, Deploy Design permits deploying, and Undeploy Design permits undeploying. When you lack one of these permissions, the matching action is not available to you. Step 1: Validate the design 🔗 Validate the design from the design’s action toolbar. Kanvas shows “Validating design” and opens a dialog titled Validate design "web-app".
What Kanvas does: validation checks every component in the design against that component’s schema. It does not contact any cluster. Each error is attached to the component and the field that caused it, so you fix problems where they are, not in a separate list. When validation of the whole design completes, Kanvas records a validation event in your Layer5 Cloud event log.
What you should see: no errors for this design. If validation finds problems, Kanvas shows “Design validation error” and marks the affected components. Open each marked component, correct the field, and validate again.
Step 2: Dry-run the design against the cluster 🔗 Start a dry run. Kanvas opens a dialog titled Dryrun design "web-app".
What Kanvas does: a dry run sends the design to the target cluster for checking without applying anything. It catches problems that schemas cannot, the ones only the cluster knows about. Dry-run errors attach to components in the same way as schema errors, so both kinds appear side by side on the affected component.
Validation answers “is this design well formed?”. A dry run answers “would this cluster accept it?”. Run both before every deployment.
What you should see: a dry run that completes without errors. Nothing has changed in the cluster yet.
Step 3: Deploy the design 🔗 Deploy the design. Kanvas opens a dialog titled Deploy design "web-app" that walks you through the deployment.
What Kanvas does: Kanvas applies the design to the Kubernetes contexts you select. If you do not select any, Kanvas deploys to all connected clusters. Choose your target deliberately when more than one cluster is connected.
Every resource Kanvas creates carries the design’s identity:
Metadata Key Value Label design.meshery.io/id The design’s ID Annotation design.meshery.io/version The design version that was deployed Annotation component.meshery.io/id The ID of the component the resource came from The label is what makes a resource “managed by Meshery”. It also lets you find the design’s resources with your own tools, for example kubectl get all -l design.meshery.io/id=<design-id>.
What you should see: the deployment completes, and the Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap exist in the cluster.
Step 4: Observe the design in Operator mode 🔗 Switch from Designer to Operator mode.
If the design has unsaved changes, Kanvas asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?” before it switches. Confirm only if you are ready to lose those changes; otherwise stay, let the design save, and switch again.
What Kanvas does: Operator mode shows the recorded state of your clusters through views. A view is a saved set of filters. A new, empty view shows Nodes and Namespaces across the clusters you select. A design’s view is named after the design, web-app-View, and filters on the design’s design.meshery.io/id label, so it shows only the resources this design created.
What you should see: in the design’s view, the running Deployment, Service, and ConfigMap from your design, and nothing else from the cluster.
Step 5: Undeploy the design 🔗 Return to Designer mode and undeploy the design. Kanvas opens a dialog titled Undeploy design "web-app".
What Kanvas does: undeploy removes the design’s resources from the Kubernetes contexts you select. As with deploy, selecting no context targets all connected clusters. You can dry-run an undeploy first to see what it would do.
What you should see: the undeploy completes and the resources are removed from the cluster. The design itself stays saved, ready to deploy again.
If something goes wrong 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix A prompt says Operator mode is not available on kanvas.new. Hosted Kanvas cannot validate, deploy, undeploy, connect clusters, or open Operator mode. Open the design in the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery. Validate, dry run, deploy, and undeploy are disabled. The design is empty. These actions need at least one component. Add components to the design, or open the saved web-app design. One of the actions is not available to you. Your role in the organization lacks the matching permission: Validate Design, Deploy Design, or Undeploy Design. Ask an organization administrator to grant the permission. “Design validation error” appears. One or more components fail their schema. Open each marked component, correct the field the error is attached to, and validate again. A dry run reports errors on components. The target cluster would reject part of the design. Correct the marked components, then run the dry run again before you deploy. Kanvas asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?” The design has changes that are not saved yet. Cancel, let autosave finish or save the design, then switch modes. Resources appeared in clusters you did not intend. No Kubernetes context was selected, so the action targeted all connected clusters. Undeploy from the unintended clusters, then select contexts explicitly before you deploy again. What you learned 🔗 Validation checks a design against component schemas; a dry run checks it against a cluster. Neither changes the cluster. Deploy and undeploy act on the contexts you select, and on every connected cluster when you select none. Every deployed resource is labeled with the design’s ID, which is how Operator mode filters the cluster inventory down to one design. Switching modes with unsaved changes asks for confirmation. Each action is gated by its own permission. Next 🔗 Validating designs Dry-running a design Deploying designs Undeploying designs Operator, to explore views and live cluster state beyond a single design.
description: Validate and dry-run your first design, deploy it to a Kubernetes cluster, find its running resources in Operator mode, and undeploy it.

body:
A dry run submits every component in the design to the Kubernetes API server of each target cluster as a server-side dry-run request. The API server validates the object exactly as it would on a real apply, including schema, field values, and admission, and then discards it. Nothing is created, updated, or persisted, so you can repeat a dry run as often as you like.
Before you start 🔗 A connected cluster. Meshery must hold at least one connected Kubernetes context. With none, the request fails with error meshery-server-1096, Kubernetes cluster is unavailable. A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design. Permission. Dry run is gated by the Validate Design permission. See Permissions by Role. A Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run dry runs. Meshery Server performs the dry run with the kubeconfig it holds. Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and the broker are not required.
Run a dry run 🔗 You reach a dry run in two ways.
On its own. Choose Dry Run from the design’s Actions menu. This opens Dryrun design "<name>" and runs a deploy-type dry run against your current cluster selection, or against all connected clusters when none is selected. There is no cluster-selection step.
Inside a deploy or undeploy. Step 3 of both steppers is a dry run against the environments you chose in step 2. In the deploy stepper it simulates creating the resources. In the undeploy stepper it simulates deleting them. See Deploy a Design and Undeploy a Design.
On mobile, Dry Run runs without a modal and shows its results as badges on the canvas.
What the server does 🔗 Stage Behavior Components Annotation components are dropped. Each remaining component becomes a Kubernetes object. Clusters The object goes to every selected cluster. Deploy-type A create with strict field validation and field manager meshery. Undeploy-type A delete by name. Namespace The component’s own metadata.namespace. Otherwise default for namespaced kinds, and none for cluster-scoped kinds. Persistence None. The dry run does not create namespaces. Read the results 🔗 The summary shows <N> component(s) and <M> annotations and the error count. With no errors it reads No deployment errors.
Each failing component is an expandable row, <name> (<count>). A component fails when any selected cluster returns a Kubernetes failure for it. Each error shows a bold type and field path, then the message the API server returned:
The type is the Kubernetes cause in words: Field Value Required, Field Value Invalid, Field Value Not Supported. Anything else shows as Failure. The path reads <component> > settings > <field>. Metadata name, namespace, labels, and annotations map to those names. When Kubernetes names no field the path is unknown. When the API gives no causes, its status messages appear as plain text. If the whole call fails rather than a component, a structured error block appears with the entry type RequestError, not a per-component row.
Selecting an error closes the results and opens the component’s configuration at the field. Errors also feed the red octagon badge on the canvas. See Validate a Design for where badges appear.
Each dry run records an event: Dry Run completed for design '<name>'. at informational severity, even when components failed, or Failed to dry-run design '<name>'. at error severity when the call itself failed. A dry run does not change the design’s deployment count.
Common errors 🔗 Error Cause Fix Field Value Invalid A value is outside what Kubernetes accepts, for example a Service port of 0 where 1 to 65535 is required. Correct the value in the component’s configuration. Field Value Required A required field is empty. Fill in the field. Resource not found for a component of a kind with an irregular plural See the limits below. Bypass the error if the kind is correct. Missing custom resource definition The design uses a custom resource whose definition is not on the cluster. Install the definition on the cluster first, then run the dry run again. Limits of a dry run 🔗 Irregular plurals. Dry run builds each resource name from the lowercase kind plus “s”. Kinds with irregular plurals, such as Ingress, NetworkPolicy, StorageClass, and Endpoints, can return a not-found error even when the component is correct. Namespaces the design creates. A dry run never creates a namespace. A component placed in a namespace that the same design would create reports an error, because the namespace does not exist yet. Undeploy-type runs. Deleting an object that is absent returns NotFound. Dry-running the undeploy of a design that was never deployed, or is already removed, shows an error for every component. A real undeploy ignores objects that are already absent. The Include Dependencies option. The dry-run step shows an Include Dependencies checkbox. It has no effect on the dry run. Bypass errors 🔗 In the deploy and undeploy steppers, when a dry run reports errors, the step shows a checkbox, Bypass errors and initiate deployment. Next stays disabled while the dry run is running, or while errors exist and the checkbox is off. Use the bypass when you know the errors are false positives from the limits above. The cluster raised each of them, and the real deployment may fail for the same reason.

body:
In this tutorial you build an NGINX Deployment with two replicas, deploy it, scale it to three, and roll it to a new image version, inspecting the result in Operator after each change. A Deployment is the controller most stateless applications run under: you declare how many Pods you want and what they look like, and Kubernetes keeps that many running and replaces them gradually when the template changes. Seeing the ReplicaSets and Pods appear and change shows you what the controller does on your behalf.
What you will learn 🔗 A Deployment owns ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet owns Pods built from one version of the Pod template. The Deployment’s selector must match its Pod template’s labels, and Kubernetes never lets you change the selector afterward. Scaling changes how many Pods run without creating a new ReplicaSet; changing the template starts a rolling update with a new ReplicaSet. Deploying a changed design from Kanvas replaces the object in place, which is how you update a running workload. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed environment. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. An environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See Environments. Operator mode for the inspection phases, which needs Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object. A unique prefix. Playground is shared. Use your own prefix in every name and label; this tutorial uses alex. The Pods tutorial. Explore Pods introduces the configurator, Validate, Dry Run, Deploy, and Operator, which this tutorial uses without re-explaining. The scenario 🔗 Deployment alex-web replicas 2, selector app=alex-web, label app=alex-web | +-- ReplicaSet alex-web-<template hash> (created by Kubernetes) +-- Pod alex-web-<template hash>-<id> (created by Kubernetes) +-- Pod alex-web-<template hash>-<id> You design only the Deployment. Kubernetes creates the ReplicaSet and Pods from it.
Build the Deployment 🔗 Create a new design named alex-deployments and add a Deployment component. The configurator opens as soon as the component lands on the canvas. Set the name to alex-web and leave the namespace as default. Set replicas to 2. Set the selector’s match labels to app: alex-web. In the Pod template, set the template’s metadata labels to app: alex-web, the same pair as the selector. In the Pod template’s spec, add one container: name web, image nginx:1.27, container port 80. In the configurator’s Labels tab, add the label app: alex-web to the Deployment itself. You use it later to find everything the Deployment owns. What just happened. The Deployment’s configuration mirrors its manifest. The selector tells the Deployment which Pods belong to it, and the template is the blueprint for those Pods. Nested objects such as the selector and the template open in their own forms. The component is equivalent to:
apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: alex-web labels: app: alex-web spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: alex-web template: metadata: labels: app: alex-web spec: containers: - name: web image: nginx:1.27 ports: - containerPort: 80 Check your work. Run Validate and then Dry Run from the Actions menu. Validate checks the schema in your browser; Dry Run asks the cluster’s API server, which also checks rules the schema cannot express. If the selector and the template labels differ, the dry run fails with a Field Value Invalid error on the template labels, stating that the selector does not match the template labels. Fix the pair and run the dry run again.
Deploy and see what Kubernetes created 🔗 Run Deploy from the Actions menu, select the environment that holds your cluster’s connection, and confirm once the dry run reports no errors. Switch to Operator. With the design open, Operator shows a view scoped to this design: the objects that carry this design’s id label. Select the alex-web Deployment and switch its details panel to Details. Select the app=alex-web label chip in the details panel. This adds the label to the view’s filter, and the view reloads. What just happened. Kanvas sent one object, the Deployment, and labeled it with the design id. The Deployment controller then created a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet created two Pods. Those objects come from the controller, not from Kanvas, so they carry the template’s labels (plus a pod-template-hash label that Kubernetes adds) instead of anything Kanvas applies. Label filters in a view match objects that carry any of the listed labels, so adding app=alex-web brings the ReplicaSet and the Pods into the view alongside the Deployment.
The names show the ownership chain: the ReplicaSet is named after the Deployment plus a hash of the Pod template, and each Pod is named after its ReplicaSet plus a random suffix.
Check your work. The Deployment’s details show pods 2 / 2 (available out of desired), the selector app=alex-web, and the image nginx:1.27. The view holds one ReplicaSet and two Running Pods. Operator shows a snapshot, so if Pods are still starting, change a filter or switch back to Operator to load a fresh one. If the summary reported Failed to deploy Deployment "alex-web", open its error card; on a shared cluster the most common cause is a name another user already deployed.
Scale the Deployment 🔗 Switch to Designer and change replicas from 2 to 3. Run Deploy again with the same environment. Switch to Operator to load a fresh snapshot. What just happened. Deploy replaced the existing Deployment in place with your new configuration; it did not create a second one. The controller saw that the desired count rose to three and told the existing ReplicaSet to create one more Pod. Scaling does not touch the Pod template, so no new ReplicaSet appears.
Check your work. The Deployment shows pods 3 / 3, and the same ReplicaSet now owns three Pods. Two Pods keep their original names and ages; the new one is younger.
Roll out a new image 🔗 Switch to Designer and change the container image from nginx:1.27 to nginx:1.28. Run Deploy again. Switch to Operator and look at the ReplicaSets and Pods. What just happened. Changing the Pod template gave it a new hash, so the controller created a new ReplicaSet and shifted Pods to it gradually. With the default rolling update strategy, Kubernetes starts new Pods before removing old ones and keeps at least three quarters of the desired Pods available throughout. The old ReplicaSet stays at zero replicas so that Kubernetes can roll back to it.
Check your work. The view holds two ReplicaSets: the new one owns three Pods with fresh names, and the old one owns none. The Deployment’s details show the image nginx:1.28. A snapshot taken mid-rollout shows Pods under both ReplicaSets; load a fresh snapshot to see the finished state. If you mistype the image tag, the new Pods cannot pull it and stay not ready, the rollout stalls, and the old Pods keep serving. Correct the tag and deploy again.
A change to a field Kubernetes treats as immutable, such as the Deployment’s selector, does not apply, and the Deploy summary still reports Deployed. To change the selector, undeploy the Deployment and deploy it again.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu and select the same environment. Undeploy deletes the alex-web Deployment by kind, name, and namespace; Kubernetes garbage collection then removes the ReplicaSets and Pods it owns. Undeploy matches by name, not by the design label, so a same-named Deployment created by someone else in the same namespace is deleted too. If the dry-run step reports the Deployment as not found, it is already gone; select the bypass option to finish.
The design stays in your account until you delete it from the design’s file menu. Deleting a design never removes cluster objects.
What you learned 🔗 You declare a Deployment; Kubernetes creates the ReplicaSets and Pods and keeps the desired count running. The selector must match the template labels and is immutable once deployed. Scaling reuses the existing ReplicaSet; a template change creates a new ReplicaSet and rolls Pods over to it, keeping the old one for rollback. Deploying a changed design replaces the object in place, and a label filter in Operator reveals objects that Kubernetes created on your behalf. Next steps 🔗 Continue with Explore Services to put a stable address in front of these Pods. Read Deploying designs for every option in the Deploy workflow. Read Operator to understand views, filters, and snapshots.

A design is a single record in Layer5 Cloud. It has one owner, lives in one workspace, and carries a visibility (private, public, or published) and a version. These guides cover each way a design enters, changes state, and leaves that record.
Two defaults shape everything below. A design saved for the first time is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Every save of an existing design raises its patch version by one (0.0.1, 0.0.2, and so on).
Goal Guide Bring in a manifest, Helm chart, Compose file, Kustomize project, or design, or merge one design into another Import and Merge Designs Understand autosave, the save indicator, Save as, and plan limits Save Designs Start from a public or published design Clone a Design Back up a design or hand it to other tools Export Designs Show a design on another site Embed Designs Make a design available in the catalog Publish Designs Remove a design permanently Delete a Design For the exact formats Kanvas accepts and produces, see Supported Import and Export Formats. To share a design with specific people, see Share Designs.
Where designs go 🔗 Every new design lands in exactly one workspace: the workspace you have selected for the current organization, or the first workspace you can see in that organization. If the organization has no workspace, saving, importing, and cloning fail. Creating a design is refused while the organization selector is set to all.
Anonymous users on kanvas.new can create, save, and import designs. Those designs move to the account when the user signs in. Sharing and publishing require an account.

Layer5 Cloud offers a range of user-configurable preferences that allows you to control the types of email notifications you receive.
To change the notification preferences 🔗 Sign into Layer5 Cloud
Visit Account > Preferences
Under “Notifications,” choose what notifications you want to receive:
Acknowledgment: You’ll receive notifications about badges you’ve been awarded and related updates.
Approval Requests: You’ll be notified about Workspace, Account, Permissions, Catalog
Organization Activity: When this is checked, you’ll be notified when
you’re added or invited to a new organization you’re removed from an organization a new user is added, invited to, or removed from your organization (provided that your organization admin has enabled notifications for these updates to be sent to organization members). Workspace Activity: You can choose to be notified about:
Changes to Designs Comments on Your Designs: Check this box to receive notifications for all new comments on your designs. Unchecking this box will disable all comment notifications. If you prefer to keep this box checked but wish to stop receiving notifications for a specific comment thread, you can directly mute notifications for that thread in the comment modal. You can learn more about this feature. Deployment in environments Membership Changes: team membership, user account creation/deletion Participating, @mentions in comments: Learn more Weekly summary Click Save Preferences
You can opt out of all email notifications by toggling the button located on the right side of the Notifications.

This page tells you which Kanvas actions require a permission, which default roles grant each permission, and which actions are limited by something other than a permission. Use it to find out why an action is missing for a user and which role grants it.
How permissions work 🔗 A permission is a named key, such as Deploy Design, that allows one action. Keys are grouped into keychains, and a role bundles one or more keychains. Your organization assigns roles to users. Before Kanvas offers certain actions, it checks whether the user holds the matching key. Kanvas uses the shared Layer5 permission set and defines no permissions of its own. See Roles and Keychains.
Where Kanvas checks a permission 🔗 Kanvas checks a permission before it offers each of the following actions:
Action Permission checked Also note Validate and Dry run Validate Design One permission controls both actions. Disabled while the design is empty. Deploy Deploy Design Disabled while the design is empty. Undeploy Undeploy Design Disabled while the design is empty. Share Share Design Also hidden while the design is empty or published. Publish Publish Design Anonymous users get a sign-in prompt instead. Operator mode None The provider enables Operator mode. When the provider does not enable it, the Operator switch is disabled. When a user does not hold the permission, Kanvas does not offer the action: the toolbar hides it or shows it disabled, and the action sheet on small screens omits it.
Layer5 Cloud also enforces permissions when it receives a request, independently of the Kanvas interface. It checks Share Design when a design is shared, View Designs when a user reads other members’ private designs, the workspace permissions when designs or views are assigned to or removed from a workspace, and Share Views when a view is shared.
Default role access 🔗 The tables below show which default roles grant each design and view permission. They are refreshed automatically from the Layer5 permission list.
A check mark means the role grants the permission. A check mark with an asterisk means the role grants the permission only on resources the user owns. A dash means the role does not grant the permission. Design lifecycle Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin Validate Design Validate a design ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Deploy Design Deploy a design -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Undeploy Design Retract all resources used in a Meshery design from the cluster -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Share Design Share design with anyone within your organization, and make your design easily accessible to all relevant team members. ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Publish Design Publish a design ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unpublish Design Unpublish a design ✓*Allowed on resources the user owns ✓*Allowed on resources the user owns ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Clone Design Clone any published design to customise it according to your use cases ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View Designs View all public and published designs of other team members and private of signed-in user ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Designs to Workspaces Assign designs to workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Remove Designs from Workspaces Remove designs from workspaces -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Views and clusters Permission What it allows UserTeam AdminWorkspace AdminOrg AdminProvider Admin View Views See all views within a workspace ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Assign Views to Workspace Add new views to workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Unassign Views from Workspace Remove views from workspace -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Add cluster Add Kubernetes cluster -Not granted -Not granted ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed View All Kubernetes Clusters View all configured Kubernetes clusters ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed ✓Allowed Org Admin is the Organization Admin role. The roles not shown, Org Billing Manager and the Academy roles, hold none of these permissions. Provider Admin holds every permission.
Anonymous users 🔗 A user is anonymous when no one is signed in or the signed-in account has anonymous status. An anonymous user authors and edits designs. Sharing or publishing a design opens a sign-in prompt that names the feature and offers a single Sign in action.
Anonymous users receive the anonymous role. It holds the same canvas permissions as the User role, plus Screenshot Canvas and View help center. It does not hold the Operator terminal, metrics, or component details permissions.
On kanvas.new, Validate, Dry run, Deploy, Undeploy, connecting a cluster, and Operator mode open a prompt that directs the user to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery deployment. This applies to signed-in users on kanvas.new as well. See Feature Availability by Plan.
What is not gated per action 🔗 Canvas editing 🔗 Kanvas does not check a permission for individual canvas edits: adding, deleting, cloning, copying, locking, and styling components, shapes, text boxes, sections, and comments; undo and redo; and the pen and pencil tools. Roles carry permissions with these names, but removing them from a role does not prevent the edit. Three things limit canvas editing instead:
Mode. Designer mode allows authoring. Operator mode does not. Node kind. Live nodes, the resources Kanvas reads from a connected cluster, are read-only in every mode. Design ownership and sharing. A user edits a design they own or one that is shared with them. Operator mode 🔗 Operator mode blocks canvas authoring: dropping, editing, duplicating, deleting, and renaming nodes are not allowed. Operator mode is not read-only, though. From Operator, a user still opens terminal and exec sessions and generates load.
Terminal, log streaming, and performance tests 🔗 The Kanvas interface does not check a permission before it opens a terminal session, streams container logs, or runs a performance test. Layer5 Cloud defines the permissions Stream container logs, Perform performance test in Operator, and Select performance profile in Operator. By default, only Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold them.
Customizing access 🔗 Enterprise plans can define custom roles built from keychains, so you can grant a group exactly the permissions it needs, such as Validate Design without Deploy Design. In the Kanvas interface, a custom role changes what is offered only for the actions listed in Where Kanvas checks a permission; Layer5 Cloud applies its own checks to sharing, private designs, and workspace assignments. See Roles.

A relationship records how two components connect: one runs inside the other, one sends traffic to the other, one mounts the other’s storage, or both carry the same label. Relationships do more than draw lines. Each relationship definition names the configuration fields on both sides that must agree, so Kanvas can write values from one component into the other and keep the design consistent as you edit. The definitions come from the Meshery registry, not from Kanvas, so the set of relationships available to you depends on the models you use.
Kinds of relationship 🔗 The Layers panel lists eight kinds of relationship, which fall into three families.
Edge relationships 🔗 An edge is a line between two components that interact. You draw it by hand. Kanvas lists the edges the registry allows from the component you start on, and highlights the targets that are compatible.
Subtype Meaning Example Network Traffic can flow between the components. The edge labels source and target ports and protocols. A Service gives a stable endpoint to a Deployment’s replicas. Mount One component gives storage or files to another, through a binding component placed between them. A PersistentVolume mounted into a Pod. Reference One component points to another by name, identifier, or scope. It declares a dependency and does not itself grant access or carry traffic. A Pod that references a ConfigMap or a Secret. Annotation A line you draw with the Pen tool to explain flow. It has no effect on configuration. A traced request path on a diagram. The registry can define other edge subtypes. They appear in the edge picker when they can start from the selected component.
Hierarchical relationships 🔗 A hierarchical relationship nests one component in another. A component has at most one parent.
Inventory. The child is drawn inside its parent, as a Pod sits inside a Namespace. Because the Namespace’s name is the Pod’s namespace, the parent’s configuration flows to the child. Wallet. The child is absorbed into its host and shown as a count badge on the host, as a sidecar is attached to a workload. Alias. The child stands for one field inside its parent. Editing the alias edits that field of the parent. TagSets 🔗 Components that carry matching labels or annotations form a TagSet. Kanvas never asks you to draw one. It appears when the labels match and disappears when they stop matching. See Work with Tags.
How relationships form 🔗 Three mechanisms create relationships:
Mechanism Kinds You create them: drag an edge, drop a component into a parent, or draw with the Pen Edge, inventory, wallet, annotation Evaluation creates them from the registry definitions TagSets, alias, and any relationship the definitions say should exist Paste or duplicate copies them with the components Any relationship whose two ends are both in the copied set Deleting a component marks the relationships that touched it as deleted. The next evaluation then reverses their effects on configuration.
Relationships keep configuration in sync 🔗 Evaluation is the process that applies relationship definitions to a design. It runs shortly after a change, writes values across related fields, and can add or remove components and relationships. The direction of a write depends on the definition and the kind.
Kind Typical direction Example Inventory Parent to child The child takes its namespace from the parent Namespace. Edge Source to target A Service’s port is written into the related Deployment’s container port. Wallet Attached item to host The host takes the item’s configuration. Treat these as typical. The relationship definition is the authority, and Kanvas does not hard-code a direction. Policy Evaluation explains when evaluation runs and why results can change after you stop editing.
What relationships mean at deploy time 🔗 Annotation edges, TagSets, and the drawing of any relationship never change what Kanvas deploys by themselves. What gets deployed is the configuration of each component. Relationships matter because they decided what that configuration is.
Related pages 🔗 Create Relationships: create, remove, and hide relationships. Designs and Components: what a design contains.

A comment is a note on the canvas that holds a threaded conversation. Use comments to give feedback, record the reason behind a configuration choice, or ask a teammate a question next to the component it concerns. A comment is part of the design: it saves with the design, appears live to everyone who has the design open, and travels with clones and exports.
For how comments fit with live editing and access, read Collaboration Model.
Who can comment 🔗 Anyone who can open a design can comment on it. The role catalog lists separate permissions for adding, resolving, deleting, and styling comments, but Kanvas does not enforce them. Whoever can edit a design can do every comment action. Comments work in Designer mode only.
Because new designs are public, a comment on a public design is visible to anyone who opens it. To limit who sees your review, make the design private and share it with the reviewers. See Share a Design.
A comment thread on the canvas. Add a comment 🔗 Add a comment in any of three ways:
Drag the Comment tool from the dock onto the canvas, or click it to drop a comment near the center. Right-click the canvas and choose Add Comment. The comment lands where you clicked. Press M. The comment appears near the center of the canvas, and you can drag it into place. A comment is an annotation component, so it moves, locks, groups, copies, and deletes like other annotations. See Canvas Objects. The Annotations toggle in the Layers panel hides all annotations, comments included, on your canvas. Hidden comments still sync.
Hold a conversation 🔗 Each comment holds one thread. Type a message and press Enter to send it. Press Ctrl or Cmd with Enter to add a line break. A message cannot be empty. A thread shows its first message and offers to show the rest when it has more than one.
A message can contain:
Mentions. Type @ and the start of a name. The picker searches every user on the platform, not only people with access to the design, and shows up to seven matches. A bare @ shows none. The search needs the View All Users permission. If it fails, Kanvas shows an error instead of “no users”. Links. URLs become links. Emoji. Type : and part of an emoji name to pick one. Messages cannot be edited, and a single message cannot be deleted. Deleting a comment removes the whole thread. Resolve a thread instead of deleting it when you want to keep the record.
Resolve and reopen 🔗 Resolve a thread when the discussion is done. A resolved comment leaves the canvas but stays in the design with all its messages. Reopen it to bring it back. Adding a message to a resolved thread reopens it. Resolving and reopening send no notification.
Find threads in the comments panel 🔗 The Comments panel lists every comment that has at least one message, newest activity first. Filter it by:
Filter Shows All Every comment with a message Open Threads that are not resolved Resolved Resolved threads For me Threads where any message mentions you The panel uses the same thread control as the canvas, so you can read, reply, resolve, reopen, and mute from it.
Reuse a comment 🔗 Copy, paste, and duplicate create a new comment with the original’s messages, timestamps, and name. The new comment is independent: editing or deleting the original does not change it. Copying or duplicating sends no notification. A reply to the copy notifies participants in the copy’s thread. Pasting a comment into another design does not change who can open that design, so participants from the original thread may be unable to open the copy’s design.
Notifications 🔗 Kanvas sends comment notifications by email when a message is added. Resolving and reopening a thread send nothing.
Kanvas emails these people, after removing the author of the new message:
Recipient Receives email when Mentioned users The new message mentions them Thread participants They wrote an earlier message in the thread, or an earlier message mentioned them The design owner Someone other than the owner added the message A request is sent only when the message mentions someone, or the thread already has an earlier message by or mentioning another person. A first comment that mentions nobody emails nobody, including the design owner. Mention the owner when you need them to see a new comment.
An email goes out only if the recipient’s account preferences allow it. Two preferences apply: comments on your designs, which governs the owner’s email, and participating and mentions in comments, which governs the other two. See Notification Preferences.
Kanvas does not check that a recipient can open the design before it emails them. The email shows the thread and links to the design in the Meshery Playground, whichever Meshery the design is stored for.
If a message posts but the emails fail, Kanvas shows “Comment posted, but the mentioned users could not be notified” and the reason. The comment stays.
Kanvas does not track which messages a person has read. Someone who misses an email learns of the comment only from a later notification or by opening the design.
Mute a thread 🔗 Use the bell in a thread to stop mention and participant emails to you for that thread. The bell toggles your mute. The mute is stored in the thread, so it saves with the design and every collaborator can see the list of people who muted it.
Muting affects only the thread where you set it. Mentions in other threads and designs still reach you. The owner’s email is decided by the commenter’s mute list, not the owner’s: a thread the owner muted still emails the owner, and a thread the commenter muted does not.
Account preferences apply to every design. A disabled preference stops those emails everywhere.
Review practices that match how Kanvas works 🔗 Mention the person you need. Mentions are the dependable notification path. Resolve instead of delete. Resolution keeps the discussion for later. Review in a private, shared design. Everyone with access can also edit, so agree who changes the design and who comments. Use the For me filter after time away. It lists threads that mention you. Related 🔗 Collaboration Model Share a Design Collaborative Editing Canvas Objects Keyboard Shortcuts

Kanvas saves a design for you. There is no Save button and no Save shortcut. Every change that alters the design, such as adding, moving, configuring, or deleting a component, renaming, editing a relationship, or merging, queues a save. The request is sent 3 seconds after your last change. Changes made while a save is in flight queue a new save when it finishes.
Saving needs a signed-in user or a guest session on kanvas.new, and an organization. It does not check a permission key.
What triggers a save, and what does not 🔗 A new design with no id is saved only once it has at least one component, or a name that is neither empty nor “Untitled Design”. A design that was saved before is always saved.
Kanvas does not save when you load a design, when the server assigns the id after the first save, when you open a component configurator, or when collaborators’ document updates arrive.
The first save creates the design, and the address bar updates to ?mode=design&design=<id>. If you edit again before the first save returns, Kanvas holds the second save until the id arrives, so no duplicate design is created.
Read the save indicator 🔗 The cloud icon in the top bar reports the state and doubles as a manual save trigger.
State Indicator Saving Animated icon and “Saving…” Saved “Saved” for 3 seconds, then a tooltip reading “All changes saved” with the time Failed Red cloud-off icon and “Unable to save. Retrying…” The tooltip on any saved design includes View Save History.
Save a copy 🔗 Save as saves the open design as a new design with a name you enter. It proposes <current name>-copy. The copy gets a new id, you as owner, your selected workspace, public visibility, and version 0.0.1, then Kanvas loads it. The original is unchanged. Save as is disabled on an empty canvas. The name is required but not checked for length or uniqueness.
A new blank design is named “Untitled Design” until you rename it.
Versions and history 🔗 Each save raises the patch number of the design’s version: the first save is 0.0.1, the next 0.0.2, and so on. Autosaves, visibility changes, and catalog data edits all count, so the version tracks how often the design was saved, not meaningful releases. Cloning and imports reset the version to 0.0.1. There is no way to bump the major or minor number.
View Save History opens a list titled “Design Version History”. It is an event log of who changed the design and when. You cannot restore, diff, or export an earlier version from it. If you need a version you can return to, export a copy at that point. See Export Designs.
Concurrent edits 🔗 Saving sends the whole design and the server overwrites the stored copy. The last save wins. Collaborators editing the same open design are reconciled live in the editor by the collaboration session, not at the storage layer.
Plan limit: components per design 🔗 The server rejects a save when the design has more components than your plan allows.
Plan Components per design Personal 100 Team Designer 200 Team Operator 100 Enterprise 300 These are the seeded plan values. A deployment can differ. The limit applies to every save, to Save as, to merges, and to URL imports. It does not apply to cloning. A cloned design that exceeds your limit opens normally but fails its first save.
The server answers 403 with the message “Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan” (the misspelling ships) and an upgrade remediation. Kanvas does not show that message. You see only “Unable to save. Retrying…” and the edits stay on the canvas, unsaved. Reduce the component count below the limit to save again. An organization with no active subscription that grants the feature gets “Org is not entitled to adding components to a design”.
For the other limits Layer5 lists per plan, see Feature Availability. Plan limits other than components per design are not enforced when you save.
When a save fails 🔗 Message Meaning Failed to reach the cloud. Any changes made may not be saved. The server was unreachable (HTTP 503). Failed to save Design with name: Any other failure, including the plan limit. Failed to save Design with name: Design is invalid or empty The design payload was empty or invalid. After a failure the editor enters an error mode: the top bar is tinted, and design-changing actions are ignored until the next command resets it. Autosave retries with exponential backoff, waiting 3 seconds times 2 to the power of the attempt number (6, 12, 24 seconds, and so on), up to 100 attempts. Any new edit resets the count.
Closing the tab or switching designs with unsaved changes asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?”
Who can save what 🔗 Anonymous users save normally into a guest account with its own organization and workspace. On sign-in, guest designs migrate to the account.
Updating an existing design keeps the original owner, visibility, and source type when the update does not state them. Operator mode blocks design edits, so it never saves a design. See Manage Designs for the defaults.

body:
The Kanvas Snapshot Helm plugin renders a Helm chart as a Kanvas design image from your terminal. Use it to see what a chart deploys before you install it, or to put a picture of a chart in a review, a ticket, or a README. It needs no repository, no cluster, and no Layer5 Cloud account.
You give the plugin the URL of a packaged chart. The plugin imports the chart as a design, starts a render, and then prints the image URL or emails you when the image is ready.
Before you start 🔗 Helm installed on your machine. A packaged chart (.tgz) at a URL that the snapshot service can download without credentials. The plugin submits the value of -f as a URL, so a local file path is not a supported input. For email delivery, an address in lowercase. Install the plugin 🔗 helm plugin install https://github.com/meshery/helm-kanvas-snapshot The install downloads a prebuilt binary for your platform. Confirm the install and update it later with:
helm plugin list helm plugin update helm-kanvas-snapshot The list shows the plugin as helm-kanvas-snapshot. Helm runs a plugin by its name, so the command is helm helm-kanvas-snapshot.
Generate a snapshot 🔗 helm helm-kanvas-snapshot -f <chart-url> [--name <name>] [-e <email>] For example:
helm helm-kanvas-snapshot -f https://meshery.github.io/meshery.io/charts/meshery-v1.0.20.tgz --name meshery-chart Flag Required Behavior -f, --file Yes URL of the packaged chart. --name No Name of the design that the plugin creates. Without it, the plugin uses the file name without its extension and prints a warning that it did. -e, --email No Email address to notify when the snapshot is ready. The plugin rejects any address that contains uppercase letters or does not look like an address, and exits with an error. What happens 🔗 The plugin imports the chart as a saved design and prints Successfully created Meshery design. ID: <id>. The plugin starts the rendering workflow. The plugin prints the result and exits. Without --email, the plugin prints the snapshot URL. The image takes three to five minutes to appear at that URL, so an immediate request can return nothing. With --email, the plugin prints a confirmation and the service emails you when the snapshot is ready.
Privacy and ownership 🔗 The plugin ships with Layer5’s service credentials, so it works without signing in. That has three consequences:
The service downloads your chart from the URL you give. Use only a chart that you are willing to expose to that service. The image sits at a public URL named after the design id. Anyone who has the URL can open it. The plugin saves the design with the service’s credentials, not under a Layer5 Cloud account of yours. To work on a chart as your own design, import it into Kanvas instead. See Import and Merge Designs. Errors 🔗 The plugin exits with status 1 and prints an error code.
Code Meaning kanvas-snapshot-900 The chart URI is invalid. kanvas-snapshot-901 The plugin could not create the design. kanvas-snapshot-902 The plugin could not start the render. kanvas-snapshot-903 An HTTP request failed. kanvas-snapshot-905 A response could not be decoded. kanvas-snapshot-906 A request returned an unexpected status. The message carries the status and the response body. kanvas-snapshot-907 A required field is missing. kanvas-snapshot-908 The email address is not valid. kanvas-snapshot-909 GitHub rejected the request to start the render with a 401 or 403 status. If the image never appears, check that the chart URL opens in a browser without signing in, then run the command again. For pull request snapshots, see Visualize Pull Requests with Kanvas Snapshot.

body:
Log streaming live-tails the output of a pod’s containers inside the Operator canvas. Each stream starts with the most recent lines and then follows new output as it is written, so you can watch a rollout, a crash loop, or a request path next to the topology that produced it.
Before you start 🔗 Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. A connected cluster with Meshery Operator deployed. MeshSync reads the logs and Meshery Server relays them through the broker, the same path the terminal uses. See Operator. Containers that exist. Logs come from the Kubernetes log API, so a container that has not started has nothing to stream. Start a stream 🔗 The action is named Initiate Log Session and is offered on Pod and Container resources only. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel. The stream opens in the same bottom-left panel as terminal sessions, as a tab.
You select Tabs opened A pod One tab for the pod that combines every container in its containers list. Each line is prefixed with [<pod>:<container>] in a per-container color. A container One tab for that container. Several pods, one after another One tab per pod. Kanvas does not merge different pods into one tab. Starting a stream for a pod that already has a tab does nothing. To stream only some of a pod’s containers, use the container selector in the panel header. Choosing different containers restarts that tab’s stream.
Read and control the stream 🔗 Backlog. Each container starts with its last 1,000 lines. Kanvas requests timestamps, so every line begins with an RFC 3339 time. Standard output and standard error arrive combined. Scrollback. The browser keeps the last 10,000 lines per tab. Search. The search icon in the panel header opens a search field with next and previous controls. It highlights and jumps between matches. It does not hide non-matching lines. Copy. Select text in the stream to copy it. There is no Clear, Copy-all, or Download control. Stop. The trash icon on a tab stops the stream and removes the tab. Closing the panel with its close button only hides it; streams keep running. Empty lines are dropped. Very long lines can be split across messages and display broken.
Limits and scope 🔗 Item Behavior Initial backlog 1,000 lines per container, fixed. Previous container logs Not available. Streams read the current container only. Follow Always on. Reconnect None. If the connection drops, the tab stops updating with no message. Close it and start a new stream. Container exits or pod is deleted The stream ends with no message. Resource names Pod, namespace, and container names must be valid Kubernetes DNS labels. Other names are rejected by the server. Changing the container selection Requests the 1,000-line backlog again, so lines can repeat in the tab. Who can use it 🔗 Kanvas does not hide or disable the action by role or plan. The permission model lists Stream container logs as an Operator capability for the Team Operator plan and above, granted to workspace administrators, organization administrators, and provider administrators. See Permissions by Role and Feature Availability.
Failure modes 🔗 Symptom Cause and fix Panel shows Failed to create terminal session with a reason The Kanvas extension could not be loaded by Meshery, for example because it was built for a different Meshery version. Install matching versions. Toast No container found to create log session The selected component lists no containers. Empty tab, no lines The pod has produced no output, or Meshery Server cannot reach MeshSync. Confirm the cluster shows as connected and that the broker is connected. Kanvas does not display the server’s error text for log streams. For cluster connection problems, see Troubleshoot Kanvas.
Related 🔗 Run a Performance Test to see how a service holds up under load while the stream is open. Operator explains the data path from the cluster to the canvas.
