body:
A Kanvas tutorial is a guided path to a realistic outcome. You build something real, such as a shared design, a cloud architecture, or a running application, and you learn how Kanvas works by doing it. Each tutorial explains what Kanvas does at every step, so you finish with both the result and the mental model behind it.
Tutorials are for learning. When you already know what you want to do, other parts of the Kanvas docs serve you better:
New to Kanvas? Start with Getting Started to reach your first design quickly. How-to guides accomplish one specific task for a reader who knows the basics. Concepts explain how Kanvas works and why it behaves the way it does. Reference lists exact options, limits, permissions, and shortcuts. The scenario 🔗 The collaboration and GCP tutorials follow two fictional organizations: Orbital Labs, a cloud-native startup on the Team plan, and Stellar Dynamics, their enterprise client on the Enterprise plan. Both organizations are managed under the Constellation Cloud provider. A cast of named characters builds, shares, and reviews designs, so you see how permissions, workspaces, and cross-organization access work together in practice. The cloud deployment and Kubernetes tutorials do not use this scenario.
Info Meet Five, Maya, Zara, Marcus, Dr. Aiko, and the full cast at Meet Five and the Cast. Collaborate on a design 🔗 These tutorials teach how people work together on one design. Neither deploys anything, so they run anywhere Kanvas runs.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Collaborative Editing A design that you and a teammate edit at the same time, ending with a review resolved in a comment thread. You learn the four mechanisms behind collaboration: the live session, access, comments, and saving. A Kanvas account and a teammate with their own account. Share a Design Across Organizations A private design that a reviewer in another organization can open, a review held in comments, and the removal of that access when the review ends. You learn what a grant gives someone and where Kanvas checks permissions. A Kanvas account in your organization and a reviewer with an account in a different organization. Model a cloud architecture without deploying 🔗 This tutorial teaches design as documentation. You model an architecture in Designer and share it, without connecting a cluster or a cloud account.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Build a GCP Data Pipeline Design A design of a GCP data pipeline: Pub/Sub ingests events, Dataflow processes them, BigQuery stores results, and Cloud Storage archives raw payloads, all on GKE. You place components, connect them with relationships or annotation lines, group them into sections, add labels, check the design with Validate, and share it. A Kanvas account and a workspace. No cluster and no GCP account. Deploy cloud resources from Kubernetes 🔗 These tutorials provision real cloud resources by deploying a cloud provider’s Kubernetes operator to your cluster and then deploying resource definitions that the operator turns into cloud infrastructure.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Deploy AWS EC2 Instances EC2 instances managed from Kubernetes through AWS Controllers for Kubernetes. A self-hosted Meshery with your own connected Kubernetes cluster, AWS credentials, and awareness of the cost of the instances you create. Deploy Azure Resources Azure resources managed from Kubernetes through Azure Service Operator. A self-hosted Meshery with your own connected Kubernetes cluster, Azure credentials, and awareness of the cost of the resources you create. Warning Never run the AWS or Azure tutorials on Meshery Playground. Both tutorials store real cloud credentials in a Kubernetes Secret, and Playground is a cluster shared with other users. Use your own cluster, and delete the cloud resources when you finish so they stop accruing charges. Run Kubernetes workloads 🔗 These tutorials teach core Kubernetes objects by building them in Kanvas, deploying them to a live cluster, and inspecting the result in Operator.
Tutorial You build Before you begin Kubernetes tutorials A learning path from a single Pod through Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets, and CronJobs to complete multi-tier applications. Meshery Playground, or a self-hosted Meshery with at least one connected Kubernetes cluster. The Kubernetes request flow explanation describes what happens inside the cluster when those objects receive traffic. Read it before the Services tutorial.
Choose where to run 🔗 Hosted Kanvas at kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, Undeploy, and Operator prompt you to use Meshery Playground or self-host Meshery instead. Only the design-only tutorials run there in full. Meshery Playground is a shared live cluster for the Kubernetes tutorials. The AWS and Azure tutorials need your own cluster.
Tutorial group Hosted kanvas.new (designing only) Meshery Playground Self-hosted Meshery with your own cluster Needs cloud credentials Deploys to a cluster Collaborate on a design Yes Yes Yes No No Model a cloud architecture (GCP) Yes Yes Yes No No Deploy cloud resources (AWS, Azure) No No, never Yes Yes Yes Run Kubernetes workloads Drawing only, no deploy Yes Yes No Yes What every tutorial assumes 🔗 You can sign in to Kanvas. You have a workspace. Every design belongs to one workspace, the one selected in your current organization. Kanvas saves designs automatically. A design saves after a 3 second pause in editing, and a new design saves once it has a name or a component. Your plan limits the number of components in a design. Kanvas enforces the limit when it saves the design, and it cannot save a design that exceeds the limit.

body:
In this tutorial you follow Zara Osei, Team Admin of the Orbital Labs Infrastructure Team, as she models the team’s Google Cloud data pipeline in Kanvas. The pipeline ingests events through Pub/Sub, processes them with Dataflow, writes analytical results to BigQuery, archives raw payloads to Cloud Storage, and runs alongside a GKE cluster. The result is a design named data-pipeline-gcp: a reviewable, shareable model of the architecture that lives in the team’s workspace instead of in a slide deck.
This is a design-only tutorial. It ends with a validated design shared with a teammate, and it deploys nothing. Deploying Google Cloud resources from a design needs a controller running in the target cluster that reconciles those resources against Google Cloud, the same pattern the AWS and Azure tutorials walk through. Without that controller, a deploy creates objects that nothing acts on.
What you will learn 🔗 A Kanvas component is a resource definition from the Meshery registry, and its configuration form is generated from that definition’s schema. Relationships between components come from the registry. Where the registry defines none, an annotation line documents the flow without changing any configuration. Labels carry metadata on a component, while sections group components visually. Neither changes how the components are configured. Validate checks each component against its schema and reports problems as warnings that never block you. Sharing grants a named person full editing access, and collaborators see each other’s changes live. Before you begin 🔗 A Kanvas environment that supports Validate. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io) or a self-hosted Meshery. Validate runs entirely in your browser and needs no cluster, but hosted kanvas.new offers no cluster actions: its Validate opens a prompt to use Meshery Playground or self-host instead. Playground is shared with other users, so never enter real cloud credentials there. This tutorial needs none. A workspace. Kanvas creates a new design in your currently selected workspace in the current organization. Zara uses orbital-production. Select yours before you start. Permission to share designs. Sharing requires the Share Design permission in the organization that owns the workspace. The Organization Admin role carries it by default. See Permissions. A teammate with an account. You share with a named user. Zara shares with Five. Your plan’s component limit. Each plan limits the number of components in one design, and Kanvas enforces the limit when it saves the design. This design holds well under a dozen components, plus a few annotation objects. See Feature availability. You need a working knowledge of the Google Cloud services involved. You do not need a Google Cloud project or credentials.
The scenario 🔗 At the end, the design contains five Google Cloud components, grouped into four sections by layer, with the data flow drawn between them:
[ Ingestion ] [ Processing ] [ Storage ] Pub/Sub topic ---> Dataflow job ---> BigQuery dataset events-ingest stream-processor analytics-store | +-------------> Cloud Storage bucket raw-archive [ Compute ] GKE cluster pipeline-cluster Each component also carries a layer label (ingestion, processing, storage, or compute). The design is validated and shared with Five, who leaves a review comment.
A note on environments 🔗 The design does not name a cluster or an environment, and it does not need to. Kanvas stores no environment on a design. You choose environments when you deploy: the Deploy stepper asks which environments to target, and deploys to the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. That separation lets one design go to staging and production unchanged. See Environments.
Phase 1: Create the design 🔗 Create a new design and name it data-pipeline-gcp.
Kanvas saves the design automatically: a new design is saved once it has a name or a component, and every later change is saved after a short pause in editing. There is no Save button. The design lands in your selected workspace, orbital-production in Zara’s case.
What just happened. A design is a single document that holds every component, relationship, and annotation you add. Autosave writes that document after each pause, and the save is where your plan’s component limit is checked: a design over the limit cannot be saved. Placing the design in a workspace organizes it; it does not give the workspace’s teams access to it. Access comes from sharing, which you do in Phase 6.
Phase 2: Add the Google Cloud components 🔗 Add one component for each service in the pipeline:
Name Service Role in the pipeline events-ingest Pub/Sub topic Entry point for incoming event streams stream-processor Dataflow job Reads events and writes them downstream analytics-store BigQuery dataset Long-term store for processed records raw-archive Cloud Storage bucket Raw payloads kept for replay and compliance pipeline-cluster GKE cluster The team’s Kubernetes cluster for the pipeline’s supporting services Find each one by typing the service name into the component palette search. The search runs against the Meshery registry after you pause typing for about a second, and returns matching models and components. Pick the Google Cloud component for each service, not a similarly named component from another model. If a model offers several versions, the palette lists the newest first.
Give each component the name from the table, and arrange the components left to right in the direction data flows.
What just happened. Every component in the palette comes from a model registered in the Meshery registry. The component’s name, its available versions, and every field in its configuration form come from that model, so they can differ between registry versions and between Meshery deployments. That is why this tutorial names services rather than exact component kinds or fields: match what your registry shows. When a component lands on the canvas, its configurator opens with a form generated from the component’s schema.
Phase 3: Fill in required configuration 🔗 Open each component’s configurator (double-click the component) and fill in the fields its schema marks as required. Required fields carry a red asterisk. Set the values your team actually uses, such as the project, region, or resource name the form asks for.
You do not have to complete every field now. Phase 5 lists anything required that is still missing.
What just happened. Each edit is written to the design after a short pause. Kanvas checks the edited component against its schema and marks problems beside the field. Those marks are warnings: Kanvas never stops you from saving an incomplete component, because a design is often a work in progress.
Phase 4: Draw the data flow 🔗 Draw three connections: events-ingest to stream-processor, stream-processor to analytics-store, and stream-processor to raw-archive. How you draw them depends on what the registry defines for each pair.
Try a relationship first. Hover over the source component to reveal its edge handles, and open the handle menu. The menu lists only the edge relationships the registry defines that can start from that component. If one fits, pick it and drag to the target. Compatible targets in view get a green outline. Releasing on a compatible target creates the relationship; releasing anywhere else creates nothing.
Fall back to an annotation line. If the menu offers nothing that connects the two services, document the flow with the Pen tool (Ctrl/Cmd+E toggles it, Escape exits). Pen places points where you click and draws an annotation line between each consecutive pair, so you can trace the path from one component to the next.
Whichever kind you draw, select the line and use Rename in the edge toolbar to label it. Zara labels the first connection subscription-pull so reviewers see the consumption pattern at a glance, and the others processed-records and raw-payloads. The same toolbar sets line color, line style, and an animated marching-ants effect, which suits a data flow.
What just happened. The two kinds of line look alike but behave differently. A registry relationship is part of the model: Kanvas evaluates it after each change and can write values from one component’s configuration into the other’s. An annotation line is a drawing. It is saved with the design and seen by collaborators, but it changes no configuration and is never deployed. Whether the registry offers a relationship between two Google Cloud services depends on the models your registry holds, so check the handle menu rather than assuming either way. See Relationships.
Phase 5: Organize by architectural layer 🔗 Give the design two kinds of structure: metadata on each component and a visual grouping on the canvas.
Labels for metadata. In each component’s configurator, open the Labels tab and add the key layer with the value for that component: ingestion for events-ingest, processing for stream-processor, storage for analytics-store and raw-archive, and compute for pipeline-cluster. Labels are free-form key-value pairs, so add others your team relies on, such as an owner or cost center.
Sections for visual grouping. Press S to add a section, size it around a group of components, and name it for its layer. Create four: Ingestion, Processing, Storage, and Compute.
What just happened. Labels and sections answer different questions. A label is data on the component, carried in its configuration. A section is an annotation object on the canvas that groups components for the reader’s eye; like every annotation, it is saved with the design and never deployed. Kanvas does not filter the design canvas by label.
You may also see a translucent shaded region appear around components that share labels. That region is a TagSet, and Kanvas draws it automatically only when a registry relationship defines a label match for those components. You cannot draw a TagSet yourself, and many models define none.
Phase 6: Validate the design 🔗 Run Validate from the Actions menu. Kanvas opens a validation report for data-pipeline-gcp.
The report states how many components and annotations it found and how many errors. With no errors, it reads “No validation errors.” Otherwise it lists each component that has errors, with a count, and each error names the field path and the problem, for example a required property that is missing.
Resolve each required field the report lists by opening that component’s configurator and filling in the value, then run Validate again. Components with errors also show a warning badge on the canvas in Full render mode; selecting the badge opens the configurator at the offending field.
What just happened. Validate runs in your browser against each component’s schema from the registry. It checks configuration only: it skips annotation objects such as sections and Pen lines, and it does not check relationships, namespaces, cross-references, or any cluster. Its findings are warnings and never block saving or sharing. A clean report means every component’s configuration matches its schema. It does not mean the pipeline would deploy successfully; a Dry Run against a cluster tests that.
Phase 7: Share the design for review 🔗 Open Share and add Five by searching for his name or email. Share is not available until the design has content, so it appears once you have added components.
Five now has the same access to the design as any editor: he can open, edit, comment on, and clone it, and he can share it with others. Kanvas has no read-only or comment-only share level. When you and Five have the design open at the same time, each of you appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and you see each other’s cursors and changes live.
Five reviews the topology and presses M to place a comment next to stream-processor: “Do we need a dead-letter topic for events Dataflow cannot parse?” Zara replies in the same thread.
What just happened. A share is a grant to one named user, not to a team or a workspace, and it carries no permission level. Share only with people you trust to edit. Comments are Comment components stored in the design itself, so the review conversation is saved with the design, syncs live, and travels with it when someone clones or exports it. See Collaboration.
Verify 🔗 Open data-pipeline-gcp and confirm:
Components. Five Google Cloud components, named events-ingest, stream-processor, analytics-store, raw-archive, and pipeline-cluster. Data flow. Three connections from Pub/Sub to Dataflow and from Dataflow to BigQuery and Cloud Storage, each either a registry relationship or a Pen annotation line, labeled subscription-pull, processed-records, and raw-payloads. Sections. Four sections, Ingestion, Processing, Storage, and Compute, each enclosing its components. Labels. Each component’s Labels tab shows the layer key with the correct value. Validation. Validate reports “No validation errors.”, or lists only fields you have deliberately left for later. Sharing. The Share dialog lists Five among the people with access, and his comment thread appears beside stream-processor. Workspace. The design appears in orbital-production. Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix Palette search for a Google Cloud service returns “Sorry, no matching records found”. The registry in your Meshery deployment does not hold that model, or the search term does not match its name. Try another form of the service name. If nothing matches, the model is not registered in this deployment; ask your Meshery administrator to import it. The edge handle menu offers nothing that connects two components. The registry defines no edge relationship between that pair. Draw an annotation line with the Pen tool and label it. Releasing a drag on the target creates no edge. The target is not compatible with the relationship you picked. Release only on a component with a green outline, or use the Pen tool. Validate lists missing required properties. Required fields in a component’s schema are empty. Open the component’s configurator, fill in each listed field, and validate again. Validate opens a prompt instead of a report. You are on hosted kanvas.new, which has no cluster actions. Open the design in Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery. The Actions menu is disabled. The design is empty. Add at least one component. Share does not appear. The design is empty, or it is published to the catalog. Add components first. A published design is not shared from this dialog. Five cannot open the design. He was not granted access, or the grant failed. Workspace membership alone does not grant access. Share the design with Five by name and confirm he appears in the access list. Changes stop saving and Kanvas reports an error. The design exceeds your plan’s components-per-design limit. Annotation objects such as sections and comments are components in the design too. Remove components or annotations you do not need, or move to a plan with a higher limit. A shaded TagSet region appears or disappears as you edit labels. A registry relationship matches those labels, and evaluation redraws the group after each change. This is expected. Change the labels if you do not want the grouping, or hide TagSets in the Layers panel. Where to go next 🔗 Deploy AWS EC2 instances and Deploy Azure resources show the controller pattern you need before a cloud design like this one can be deployed. Configuring components covers the configurator, its tabs, and the Labels tab in depth. Whiteboarding covers the Pen tool, sections, text boxes, and other annotation objects. Relationships explains how the registry defines relationships and how Kanvas evaluates them. Designs explains how designs, workspaces, and autosave fit together. Info Meet Zara and the rest of the team at Meet Five and the Cast.

body:
Everything on a Designer canvas is an object, and every object answers to the same small set of actions: add, select, copy, duplicate, lock, restyle, resize and delete. This page lists each object kind, each action, every style option and the limits that apply. Edges - the lines that connect objects - have their own section at the end.
Designer mode only. In Operator mode you cannot add, edit, duplicate, delete or rename objects, and live nodes discovered from a cluster are read-only in every mode. See Designer for how the two modes differ.
Object kinds 🔗 Object What it is Configurable Added from Component A piece of infrastructure under management, such as a Deployment, an S3 bucket or a Lambda function. Yes. It carries configuration and is part of what gets deployed. The Components and Kubernetes pickers in the dock, a file import, or a drop Shape A visual primitive: a circle, an arrow, a flowchart symbol or a cloud-provider glyph. No The Shapes picker in the dock Section A labeled frame that fences off a region. Objects dropped inside it become its children and move with it. No The Section tool in the dock, or S Textbox A resizable box whose content is text. No The Textbox tool in the dock, or T Image A picture embedded in the design. No I, the Image tool in the dock, or a file drop Comment A threaded note pinned to the canvas. See Reviewing Designs. No M or the Comment tool in the dock Pencil stroke and pen point Freehand drawings and the joints of drawn lines. See Tool Modes. No The Pencil and Pen tools Every object except a component is an annotation. Kanvas stores annotations in the design alongside components, but treats them differently:
Behavior Annotation Configurable component Layers panel toggle Annotations Configurable Components Kind name appended to the on-canvas label No Yes Has configuration to edit No Yes Counts toward the components-per-design limit of your plan when the design is saved Yes Yes The plan limit counts every entry in a design, drawn objects included, so a heavily annotated design can reach the limit sooner than its infrastructure alone suggests. See Feature Availability by Plan.
Adding objects 🔗 Method Result Drag from a dock picker onto the canvas The object lands where you release it. Click an icon in a picker The object lands at a random position near the center of the canvas. M, T, S Adds a comment, textbox or section near the center of the canvas. A textbox opens ready for typing. I Opens a file picker for an image. Drop or paste a file See the file rules below. Paste a copied selection Adds the copied objects and the relationships between them at the pointer. A newly added component opens its configurator beside the node. A textbox starts inline text editing on double-click. Shapes accept body text too, so double-click a shape to type in it.
Shapes 🔗 The Shapes picker lists the shape libraries registered in Meshery, with search across all of them. A default installation includes libraries for cloud providers (Amazon Web Services, Azure, Google Cloud Platform), developer icons, arrows, flowchart symbols, general-purpose shapes and line icons. The libraries come from the registry, so the list can differ between installations. Pin a library to the dock to keep it one action away - see Pinning a Model to the Dock.
The Shapes picker lists every shape library available to your design A shape library expanded Sections 🔗 A section draws its label along its top edge instead of through its middle, so the region it encloses stays readable. Drop other objects inside it and they move with the section. Deleting the section does not delete them.
Textboxes 🔗 A textbox carrying a caption Files dropped or pasted on the canvas 🔗 File Result Limit Any image type the browser recognizes An image object. The picture is embedded in the design as data, not linked. 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) Plain text (.txt) A textbox holding the file text. 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) YAML, JSON, TAR, GZ, TGZ, ZIP, RAR, 7Z An infrastructure-as-code import at the drop position. See Importing Designs. Import rules apply Any other type Ignored with no message - Files over the size limit are rejected with an error message. The limit is fixed and is the same on every plan. A file with no browser-reported type is classified by its extension.
Selecting objects 🔗 Gesture Effect Click Selects one object and shows its style toolbar. Ctrl/Cmd + click Adds or removes one object from the selection. Ctrl/Cmd + drag on empty canvas Draws a selection box. Box selection is off in Pan, Pen and Pencil modes. Ctrl/Cmd + A Selects every component on the canvas. Dragging selected objects moves them together. Locked objects do not move.
Actions on objects 🔗 Right-click an object, or press and hold on it, to open its menu. Each entry appears only when its condition holds.
Action Shortcut Appears when Behavior Copy Ctrl/Cmd + C Designer mode, object is not a group Menu: copies that one object. Keyboard: copies the whole selection and every relationship whose two ends are both selected. Duplicate Ctrl/Cmd + D Designer mode, not a group Adds a copy to the same design. Lock - Designer mode, not a group, not locked Fixes the object’s position. Unlock - The object is locked Releases the position. Delete Delete or Backspace Designer mode, not a group Removes the object. The keys delete the whole selection. Reset styles - The object supports style changes Restores the object’s default styling. Group - A multi-selection Turns the temporary selection group into a permanent group. Ungroup - A permanent group Dissolves the group. Move Out of Parent - Designer mode, the object sits inside a parent Takes the object out of its parent. The context menu open on a selected object Every change an action makes, restyling included, is a change to the shared design, so Ctrl/Cmd + Z reverses it. See Canvas Actions.
Copy and paste 🔗 Copy writes the object data to your system clipboard. Paste with Ctrl/Cmd + V into the same design, a different design or another browser tab running Kanvas.
Pasted objects land at the pointer when it is over the canvas, otherwise at the canvas center, and keep their relative layout. Every pasted object receives a new identifier. Styling travels with the copy. The browser must allow clipboard access. If it refuses, nothing happens and no message appears. Duplicate 🔗 Duplicate skips the clipboard. It places the copy 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from the original, gives it a new identifier and copies the relationships between members of the duplicated set. Duplicating a section together with its children reproduces the whole arrangement. Names are unchanged.
Lock 🔗 A lock fixes position only. A locked object can still be selected, restyled, configured and deleted, but it cannot be dragged, directly or inside a selection. The lock is stored with the object, so it survives a reload and applies to collaborators. Locking a section does not lock the objects inside it.
Delete 🔗 Deleting an object also removes the relationships that touch it. Kanvas marks those relationships as deleted rather than discarding them, so the next policy evaluation can undo any configuration they had applied. Deleting a section leaves its children on the canvas. Deletion is immediate and has no confirmation, but it can be undone.
Style options 🔗 Selecting one object shows a style toolbar above it. The toolbar edits the selected object; it does not apply a change to a multi-selection. Each control appears only when the object’s definition declares that capability, so the controls you see vary by object. The toolbar appears only when the canvas is zoomed in past a detail threshold; zoomed out, the canvas shows a hint to zoom in.
Property Options Shape 24 outlines: ellipse, triangle, round-triangle, rectangle, round-rectangle, bottom-round-rectangle, cut-rectangle, barrel, rhomboid, diamond, round-diamond, pentagon, round-pentagon, hexagon, round-hexagon, concave-hexagon, heptagon, round-heptagon, octagon, round-octagon, star, tag, round-tag, vee. Changing the outline keeps the content. Fill 13 swatches including transparent, and an opacity slider from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. Border Color from the same swatches, style (solid, dotted, dashed, double) and thickness from 0 to 25. Layer order Move To Front, Move Forward, Move Backward, Move To Back. Label The name drawn with the object. Link An external URL. A link adds an External Link badge, which opens the URL in a new tab. See Component Badges. Image A background image, set by URL or by upload, with a reset to the default. Animation None, blink, ripple, bounce or pulse. Text Color, weight (Regular, Medium, Semi Bold, Bold, Black), decoration (none, underline, line-through), horizontal alignment (left, center, right), vertical alignment (top, center, bottom) and size. Configure Opens the configurator. Components only. See Configuring Components. The default text style is gray, 12 pixels, regular weight and centered. Sections carry their label on the top edge rather than body text.
Restyling changes only how an object is drawn. It never changes a component’s configuration or what gets deployed.
Reset styles 🔗 Reset styles re-applies the styling recorded in the object’s definition and discards every change made in the style toolbar. It restores the definition, not an earlier state, so it is not an undo. Position, lock state, configuration and relationships are untouched.
Resizing 🔗 Select a single object and Kanvas draws eight handles around it, one at each corner and one at the midpoint of each side.
Drag a corner or side handle to resize. Hold Shift while dragging to keep the aspect ratio. Objects that contain other objects, such as a parent component or a section with children, show no handles. Resizing needs the object’s definition to declare the resize capability. The new size is saved with the design.
Edges 🔗 An edge is a line between two objects. Each edge is a relationship in the design, and relationships come in two kinds.
Edge kind What it represents Effect Semantic A relationship defined in the registry, such as a network connection or a volume mount. Kanvas updates the configuration of the components it joins as you draw it, and re-evaluates it as the design changes. See Relationships. Annotation A line you draw with the Pen tool to explain a flow or a dependency. Visual only. It is non-binding and configures nothing. Select an edge to open the edge toolbar.
Control Options Line Color The same 13 swatches as fills. The arrowhead takes the same color. Line Style Dotted, Solid, Dashed. Arrow/Curve Style A curve style and an arrowhead, listed below. Name A text label drawn on the edge. Edge Animation None, or marching ants: a dashed line that travels along the edge. Delete Removes the edge. Works on any edge. Curve styles 🔗 Curve style Shape Bezier A smooth curve. The default. Straight A direct line. Segments A line with two bends. Round segments Segments with rounded corners. Taxi Right-angle routing. Round taxi Right-angle routing with rounded corners. Haystack A short line that starts and ends inside the nodes. Unbundled bezier A curve with one adjustable control point. Multi unbundled bezier A curve with two control points. Straight triangle A straight line drawn with a triangular profile. Choosing a curve style applies its default geometry. Choosing Round taxi does not apply its default corner radius.
Arrowheads 🔗 Vee (the default), triangle, circle, square, diamond, triangle-cross, tee, triangle-tee, circle-triangle, triangle-backcurve and chevron. An arrowhead is drawn at the target end only.
Edge defaults 🔗 A new edge uses a dotted line, a vee arrowhead, a bezier curve, a width of 1.5 pixels and a light gray color. A selected edge draws at 4 pixels. Edges that carry TCP traffic draw as a solid gold line with a triangle-cross arrowhead.
Permissions 🔗 Kanvas gates canvas actions by mode and by object capability, not by role. The permission catalog in Layer5 Cloud lists a key for each shape, section, textbox and component-styling action (add, copy, clone, lock, delete, configure styles, reset styles and resize), and organization administrators can include them in roles and keychains. Kanvas does not check those keys on the canvas today, so withholding one does not hide a control.
The permissions Kanvas does enforce on the toolbar are Validate Design, Deploy Design, Undeploy Design and Share Design. See Permissions by Role.
Action Gate When the gate fails Add, duplicate, copy, paste, delete, lock Designer mode The control is not offered in Operator mode. Edit a live cluster node Never allowed Live nodes are read-only in every mode. Style, reset styles, resize The object’s definition declares the capability The control is hidden. Pen and Pencil The Enable Pen and Enable Pencil options The dock icons are hidden. Limits 🔗 Item Limit Image file 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB), same on every plan Text file 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB), same on every plan Border thickness 0 to 25 Fill opacity 0 to 1 Components per design Set by your plan and enforced when the design is saved. Annotations count. Image count per design No limit Related reading 🔗 Tool Modes - select, pan, pencil and pen. Whiteboarding - a task guide to drawing on a design. Keyboard Shortcuts - every shortcut. Layout and Layers - arranging and hiding objects.

body:
Cloning copies a design into your own workspace so you can change it freely. The clone is an independent record: later changes to the source never reach it, and edits to the clone never reach the source.
What you can clone 🔗 The server clones only designs whose visibility is public or published. A request for any other design fails with 403 “unauthorized to clone design”. That includes your own private designs. To copy one of those, open it and use Save as. See Save Designs. A missing source design returns 500 “could not find design”.
Where to start a clone 🔗 Kanvas has no Clone item for the design that is open. You clone from these places:
The catalog. The catalog modal’s Clone action, and catalog design cards in Layer5 Cloud. A catalog link. Opening a link with mode=design&type=catalog&id=<id> clones that design and opens your copy. Tutorials. Opening a tutorial’s design clones it. The client names a catalog clone <design name> (Copy), and a tutorial clone <tutorial title> (Copy). The server stores whatever name it receives and rejects an empty request body with 400. When the clone completes, Kanvas loads it. If the open design has unsaved changes, you confirm first.
Layer5 Cloud shows the Clone action only to roles with the Clone Design permission. The server checks visibility, not the key. See Permissions.
What carries over 🔗 Carried over Reset or changed Components, relationships, styles, configuration, annotations, and preferences, converted to the current design format New id The origin of the source design Version 0.0.1 Catalog data (compatibility, type, info, caveats, content class, published version, snapshot URLs) Owner is you Visibility private Workspace is your selected workspace Source file and usage counters are not copied Cloning is the only path that creates a private design. Every other new design is public.
Limits and failure behavior 🔗 Cloning does not check your plan’s components-per-design limit. A clone from a larger plan can exceed yours and then fail its first autosave with a plan-limit error. See Save Designs.
Kanvas shows Cloning design "<name>" while the clone runs. It shows no failure message. Because the clone copies the catalog data block, a private clone can display catalog metadata even though it is not published.

body:
Deploying applies the components in a design to the Kubernetes clusters in the environments you choose. Meshery Server does the work with the kubeconfig it holds: it creates each object, or updates it in place when it already exists. Deploying the same design again is safe and idempotent.
Before you start 🔗 A Meshery you run, with a connected cluster. The hosted kanvas.new site does not deploy; it shows a self-hosted-feature prompt. Meshery needs at least one connected Kubernetes context that belongs to an environment in your organization. A non-empty design. The Actions menu is disabled for an empty design. An unsaved design deploys as it stands on the canvas. Permission. The Deploy Design permission gates the action. See Permissions by Role. Selecting environments from the empty state also needs the Create Environment and Edit Environment permissions. A provider session. Without a signed-in session the request fails before any event is raised. Deploying does not need Meshery Operator, MeshSync, or the broker. Those make the result visible in Operator mode.
Validate and dry-run the design first. See Validate a Design and Dry-run a Design. The deploy flow runs both for you.
The deploy flow 🔗 Choose Deploy from the design’s Actions menu. The Deploy design "<name>" stepper has five steps, with Back and Next throughout.
Step What it does 1. Validate Design Runs validation inline. Next is always enabled, because validation errors are warnings. 2. Identify Environments Lists your organization’s environments as cards. Ticking an environment selects all of its Kubernetes connections. You need at least one. 3. Dry Run Runs a deploy-type dry run against the selected clusters. Next stays disabled while it runs, or when errors exist and the bypass checkbox is off. 4. Finalize Deployment Shows the environments you chose and the component count, excluding annotations. The button reads Deploy. A Schedule Deployment checkbox is shown disabled. 5. Finish Starts the deployment and shows the results. Step 2 shows only Kubernetes connections. When your organization has no environments, it shows No environments found. Add a new environment. When an environment has no connections, it shows No connections configured. Add a connection to get started. Your selection persists for the session. A cluster that belongs to two selected environments is listed twice and targeted twice.
Targets 🔗 The stepper always sends the explicit clusters you selected. Where no selection exists, such as a one-click action or the mobile sheet, the target is all. The server expands a lone all to every connected Kubernetes context. Otherwise it keeps only the ids that match a connected context and silently drops unknown ones. If none remain, the request fails with meshery-server-1096.
Clusters are deployed in parallel.
How components are applied 🔗 Aspect Behavior Ordering Components form a dependency graph. A component starts when every component it depends on has succeeded. Independent components run in parallel. Kanvas applies no other ordering, so deploy custom resource definitions before the resources that use them. Failed dependency A component whose dependency failed is withheld: Withheld <component>: <dependency> did not deploy successfully (meshery-server-1480). Invalid dependencies A malformed, unknown, ambiguous, or circular dependency fails the whole request before anything is applied (meshery-server-1475 through 1479). Existing objects The object is replaced in place. An update to an immutable field, or an attempt to unset a Service’s cluster IP, is reported as success but does not take effect. Namespaces A missing target namespace is created before the object is applied. A namespaced component with no namespace goes to default. Annotation components Never applied. Dependencies of non-Kubernetes models 🔗 For a component whose model is not the built-in Kubernetes model and whose registrant is an Artifact Hub source, Meshery installs the model’s source Helm chart into the component’s namespace, creating the namespace if needed. This brings in the custom resource definitions and operators the component needs. The step is fail-forward: if the chart fails, Meshery still applies the component and adds a row to the results, error deploying dependent helm chart for <component>.
Meshery always processes these dependencies. The Include Dependencies checkbox in the dry-run step does not change this.
What Meshery marks on applied objects 🔗 Mark Value Label design.meshery.io/id The design’s id Annotation design.meshery.io/version The design’s version Annotation component.meshery.io/id The component’s id Operator’s per-design view filters on the design-id label. A component carrying it is shown as managed by Meshery.
Read the results 🔗 Every deployment raises an event from Meshery Server. It appears as a toast and as an entry in the notification center. In the Finish step, a summary lists one row per component and cluster: Deployed <Kind> "<name>", or Failed to deploy <Kind> "<name>" with an error card. When Operator is enabled, the step offers Open In Operator.
Outcome Event The request completed Deployment completed for design '<name>'. at informational severity The request failed before applying (cluster client, dependency graph, malformed design) Failed to deploy design '<name>'. at error severity, with an error card A deployment in which some components failed in Kubernetes still raises the completed event. Read the per-component rows in the Finish step to see which ones failed.
Each persisted deploy event, including an error event, adds 1 to the design’s deployment count in Layer5 Cloud. Dry runs and undeploys do not change it. The count drives the catalog sort Most Deployed.
Error cards 🔗 An error card shows the event description, then Details, then Probable Cause and Suggested Remediation side by side. In the notification center, the Error Docs menu item opens the matching entry in the Meshery error code reference.
Code Meaning Fix meshery-server-1073 Unable to deploy the design. Wraps most hard failures; Details holds the inner error. Confirm the connection’s status is Connected or upload a new kubeconfig, and assign the connection to the selected environment. meshery-server-1096 Kubernetes cluster is unavailable: no selected context resolved. Upload a new kubeconfig, check the network and the cluster, and verify the server’s credentials. meshery-server-1095 Invalid kubeconfig. Upload a new kubeconfig and make sure the server can reach the API server. meshery-server-1070 Failed to parse the design file. Check the design definition. meshkit-11190 Error applying a manifest. The Kubernetes API’s own reason and remediation replace the generic text. Make sure the manifest is valid. meshery-server-1475 to 1480 A dependency problem in the design. Open the design, fix, rename, or remove the dependency, and retry. For 1480, resolve the dependency’s failure first. When nothing happens 🔗 The Finish step waits for the next deploy event from the server. If the request fails before the server raises an event, such as an expired session, a proxy error, or no provider, Kanvas shows no error and the Finish step keeps spinning. The step has no timeout. Close it, sign in again if your session expired, and check the notification center and the Meshery Server logs.
Related 🔗 Undeploy a Design removes what a deployment created. Troubleshoot Kanvas covers connection and loading problems.

body:
In this tutorial you put three Services in front of running workloads: a ClusterIP Service in front of a Deployment, a NodePort Service in front of one Pod, and a LoadBalancer Service in front of another. Pods come and go and change IP addresses every time they are replaced. A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable address and finds them by label, and its type decides who can reach that address. Building all three side by side makes the difference between the types concrete.
What you will learn 🔗 A Service selects its backend Pods by label, and any Pod whose labels match joins the Service automatically. A ClusterIP Service gets a virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster. A NodePort Service adds a port on every node, and a LoadBalancer Service adds an external load balancer provisioned by the cluster’s cloud provider. In Kanvas, the Network relationship documents which workload a Service sends traffic to, while the selector is what Kubernetes acts on. Before you begin 🔗 A cluster-backed environment. Use Meshery Playground (https://play.meshery.io), a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. An environment that holds your cluster’s connection. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. See Environments. Operator mode for the inspection phases, which needs Meshery Operator and MeshSync running in the cluster. Where Operator mode is turned off, its switch is disabled; the deploy summary still confirms each object. A unique prefix. Playground is shared. Use your own prefix in every name and label; this tutorial uses alex. The earlier tutorials. Explore Pods and Explore Deployments cover building, deploying, and inspecting workloads, which this tutorial uses without re-explaining. The scenario 🔗 You build one design with six components and deploy it in three rounds:
Service Type Selector Backend alex-api-cip ClusterIP app=alex-api Deployment alex-api, 2 replicas alex-np NodePort app=alex-np Pod alex-np-pod alex-lb LoadBalancer app=alex-lb Pod alex-lb-pod Every workload runs nginx:latest, which listens on port 80. Every Service listens on port 80 and forwards to target port 80.
What each type exposes, and what you can observe in Meshery Playground:
Type Reachable from Kubernetes allocates In Playground ClusterIP Pods inside the cluster A cluster IP Works fully NodePort Anything that can reach a node A cluster IP and a port on every node The node port is assigned; node IPs are often unreachable from your browser LoadBalancer Clients outside the cluster A cluster IP, a node port, and an external address from the cloud provider No external address is assigned; it stays pending Kubernetes request flow follows a single request from a client through a Service to a Pod, and Creating relationships covers every relationship you can draw between components.
Expose a Deployment with a ClusterIP Service 🔗 Create a new design named alex-services. Add a Deployment named alex-api with replicas 2, selector match labels app: alex-api, template labels app: alex-api, and one container named web with image nginx:latest and container port 80. Add the label app: alex-api to the Deployment itself in the Labels tab. Add a Service named alex-api-cip. Set its type to ClusterIP, add a port with port 80 and target port 80, and set its selector to app: alex-api. Add the label app: alex-api to the Service in the Labels tab so it shows up with the workload when you filter by label. Draw a Network relationship from the Service to the Deployment. Edge handles appear when you hover a component; choose the network option and drag to the Deployment. Compatible targets show a green outline while you drag, and releasing anywhere else creates nothing. Run Validate, Dry Run, and then Deploy from the Actions menu, selecting the environment that holds your cluster’s connection. What just happened. The Service’s selector, app=alex-api, matches the labels in the Deployment’s Pod template, so both Pods the Deployment creates become backends of the Service. The selector points at Pod labels, not at the Deployment: Kubernetes matches Pods, whoever created them. Port 80 is the port clients use on the Service’s address, and target port 80 is the container port that traffic is forwarded to.
The Network relationship records the same connection in the design so that anyone reading the diagram sees where traffic flows. Its edge shows the port values it reads from both components, and Kanvas evaluates relationships after every change; a relationship’s registry definition can copy designated fields from one component to the other. Kubernetes routes by the selector alone, so confirm the selector in the Service’s configurator after you draw the edge.
Check your work. The summary lists Deployed Deployment "alex-api" and Deployed Service "alex-api-cip". Switch to Operator, select the Service, and switch its details panel to Details. It shows the service type ClusterIP, a cluster IP, no external IP, and the selector app=alex-api. The cluster IP is reachable only from inside the cluster: any Pod can send requests to it, and the cluster’s DNS also resolves the name alex-api-cip.default.svc.cluster.local to it.
A selector that matches no Pods is not an error. The Service still deploys and gets a cluster IP, but it has no backends and requests to it fail. If you mistype the selector, nothing warns you; compare the selector with the Pod labels.
Expose a Pod with a NodePort Service 🔗 Switch to Designer and add a Pod named alex-np-pod with the label app: alex-np and one container named web, image nginx:latest, container port 80. Add a Service named alex-np. Set its type to NodePort, add a port with port 80 and target port 80, and set its selector to app: alex-np. Leave the node port empty so Kubernetes assigns a free one from the node port range (30000 to 32767 by default). Draw a Network relationship from alex-np to alex-np-pod. Run Deploy again with the same environment. What just happened. A NodePort Service is a ClusterIP Service plus one port opened on every node in the cluster. Traffic that arrives at any node on that port is forwarded to the Service’s backends, wherever they run. Deploying the design again created the two new objects; Kanvas also resubmitted the Deployment and the ClusterIP Service, which already exist, and those stay as they are.
Check your work. Switch to Operator and select alex-np. Its details show the service type NodePort, a cluster IP, the selector app=alex-np, and, under its connections, the ports including the node port Kubernetes assigned. The Service is reachable at http://<node IP>:<node port> from any machine that can reach a node; the Pod’s host IP is one node address. In Playground, node IPs are often not reachable from your browser, and the assigned node port still confirms that Kubernetes exposed the Pod. If you set a fixed node port and another user on the cluster already holds it, the dry run fails with a Field Value Invalid error on the node port; clear the field and let Kubernetes choose.
Expose a Pod with a LoadBalancer Service 🔗 Switch to Designer and add a Pod named alex-lb-pod with the label app: alex-lb and one container named web, image nginx:latest, container port 80. Add a Service named alex-lb. Set its type to LoadBalancer, add a port with port 80 and target port 80, and set its selector to app: alex-lb. Draw a Network relationship from alex-lb to alex-lb-pod. Run Deploy again. What just happened. A LoadBalancer Service builds on a NodePort Service: Kubernetes allocates a cluster IP and a node port, then asks the cluster’s cloud provider integration to create an external load balancer that forwards to those node ports. When the provider finishes, Kubernetes records the load balancer’s IP or hostname in the Service’s status. A cluster without such an integration, such as Playground, accepts the Service and never assigns an external address.
Check your work. In Operator, select alex-lb. Its details show the service type LoadBalancer, a cluster IP, and a node port under its connections. In Playground there is no external IP and no load balancer address, because no cloud provider fulfills the request. On a managed cloud cluster, an external address appears once the provider has created the load balancer; load a fresh snapshot to see it, because Operator does not update on its own.
Change a deployed Service 🔗 Deploy replaces an existing object in place, but Kubernetes rejects some changes to a Service, such as clearing the cluster IP it assigned. Kanvas reports those rejected changes as Deployed, and the Service stays as it was. To change a deployed Service’s type or ports reliably, undeploy the design and deploy it again.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu and select the same environment. Undeploy deletes each component’s object by kind, name, and namespace: the Deployment, both Pods, and all three Services. Kubernetes then removes the ReplicaSet and Pods the Deployment owned. Undeploy matches by name, not by the design label, so same-named objects that someone else created in the same namespace are deleted too. If the dry-run step reports objects as not found, they are already gone; select the bypass option to finish.
The design stays in your account until you delete it from the design’s file menu. Deleting a design never removes cluster objects.
What you learned 🔗 A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable address and finds them by label selector, not by owner. ClusterIP serves clients inside the cluster, NodePort adds a port on every node, and LoadBalancer adds an external load balancer that only a cloud provider integration can supply. A selector that matches nothing deploys without error, so checking it is your job. The Network relationship documents traffic flow in the design; the selector is what Kubernetes routes by. Next steps 🔗 Continue with ConfigMaps and Secrets to configure workloads without rebuilding images. Read Deploying designs for every option in the Deploy workflow. Read Operator to understand views, filters, and snapshots.

Each guide accomplishes one task for a reader who already knows the basics. If you are new to Kanvas, start with Getting Started. If you want the reasoning behind a behavior, read Concepts. For exact options, limits, and shortcuts, use Reference.
Every action in these guides runs under your permissions. Kanvas hides or disables an action your role does not allow. Validating, deploying, and undeploying a design also need a Meshery you run, because the hosted kanvas.new site does not run them. How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud lists what each environment supports.

Run the steps in this order. Validation catches configuration errors in the design, a dry run checks the design against the target clusters, and a deployment applies it.

body:
Evaluation is how a design stays consistent. After you change a design, Kanvas runs it through the policy engine, which applies the registry’s relationship definitions: it identifies relationships, writes configuration across related components, and drops relationships that no longer hold. The engine returns the whole evaluated design, and Kanvas applies it back to the canvas. This is why a value you did not touch can change a moment after you edit a related component.
Evaluation never blocks editing. You can keep designing while it runs, and a new edit supersedes the evaluation in progress.
What triggers evaluation 🔗 Evaluation runs after any of these changes:
A configuration value or a display name changes. A relationship is added or removed. A component is added, removed, duplicated, or merged. A design loads, or an import or merge completes. Kanvas waits until changes stop for about one second, then evaluates. Another change during evaluation restarts the cycle. Selecting the indicator icon forces an evaluation, and a new design resets evaluation state.
Two interchangeable engines 🔗 Engine Where it runs Properties Meshery server In your Meshery server Always available. Client-side (WASM) In a background worker in your browser No round trips to the server, so it is typically faster. A WASM evaluation times out after 10 seconds. Both engines apply the same policy engine and the same definitions. The choice changes where the work happens.
Choosing the engine 🔗 The Relationship Evaluation Engine preference lives in the Options dialog, which you open from the canvas right-click menu.
Value Behavior Automatic (recommended) The default. At load, Kanvas tries to start the WASM engine and waits up to 30 seconds for it to report ready. If it starts, WASM is used. If not, the Meshery server is used. Meshery server Always uses the server. Client-side (WASM) Always uses WASM. The preference is saved to your user preferences, so it applies on all your devices and designs. Kanvas chooses the engine once, when Designer loads, so reload Kanvas for a change to take effect.
Two behaviors to know:
Forcing Client-side (WASM) gives no fallback. If the engine fails to start, evaluations fail silently and relationships stop updating. Switch to Automatic or Meshery server and reload. Automatic checks only that the engine initializes. It does not fall back to the server later if the WASM engine fails after a successful start. Reading the indicator 🔗 The top toolbar shows an icon for relationship evaluation. Its state is in the tooltip.
State Tooltip Running “Evaluating relationships…” with a spinning icon Done “Relationships evaluated” and the time elapsed, a summary of the actions the evaluator applied, and a View Evaluation History button Nothing evaluated “No relationships evaluated yet” There is no error state. A failed evaluation clears the last-evaluation details, so the tooltip returns to “No relationships evaluated yet”, and the failure is logged to the browser console only. If relationships stop updating, check the engine first.
When Kanvas applies an evaluation result and decides to skip it, it shows the notice “Skipping evaluation application”, with a reason when one is known. A successful evaluation shows no message.
Diagnosing unexpected results 🔗 Turn on Enable Debugger in the Options dialog. It is off by default. Open the debugger and go to its Evaluation Engine tab. Read the status: Initialized, Not Initialized, or Not Available. Read the engine type, WASM or SERVER, and any initialization error. The tab refreshes every second. If WASM is not initialized, or results look wrong, set the engine to Meshery server, reload, and compare. Make any change to re-trigger evaluation. If the server engine also gives wrong results, file an issue that includes the engine type, any initialization error, the relationships you expected, and the design or a minimal version of it.
Large designs 🔗 Evaluation covers the whole design regardless of which relationship layers you hide. In Adaptive render mode, Kanvas can suggest cost-saving changes when a design grows: disabling TagSets when there are more than 5, collapsing parents when there are more than 10, hiding unused components when there are more than 200, and using Wireframe mode when there are more than 100 relationships. Each suggestion appears at most once per 60 seconds.
Related pages 🔗 Relationships: the kinds that evaluation applies. Create Relationships: what you create by hand.

body:
Operator mode shows a live picture of your clusters. A performance test adds the missing signal: how a service responds under load. You select a Service or Ingress on the canvas, Kanvas seeds a test from it, and Meshery runs the load and keeps the result as a reusable performance profile.
Before you start 🔗 Operator mode on a Meshery you run. The hosted kanvas.new site does not offer Operator mode. A target Meshery Server can reach. Meshery Server generates the load, not your browser and not the cluster. The address you test must be routable from wherever Meshery Server runs. A ClusterIP address is reachable from inside the cluster only. Performance permissions. The form needs View performance profiles to appear, and the Run Test button needs Run test. See Permissions by Role. Start a test 🔗 The action is named Initiate Performance Test and is offered on Service and Ingress resources only, the kinds that expose an endpoint. It is not offered on pods, deployments, or any other kind. Right-click the resource, or select it and use the action in the header of the Details panel.
The Performance panel opens on the canvas at 400 px wide, floating and minimizable. Only one performance panel exists: starting a test from a second resource replaces the target of the open panel. The panel hosts the Meshery performance test form, so the fields, profiles, and results are the same ones Meshery provides. Opening the panel generates no load. Nothing runs until you press Run Test.
What Kanvas pre-fills 🔗 Setting Seeded value Profile name <Kind> - <component name>, for example Service - checkout URL to test The first endpoint derived from the resource, or empty Concurrent requests 10 Queries per second 20 Duration 30s Load generator fortio Change any value before you run. The form also accepts request headers, cookies, content type, request body, additional load generator options as JSON, and a certificate for TLS endpoints.
How the URL is derived 🔗 For a Service, Kanvas builds an endpoint from the service’s type and ports and seeds the first one. A service with several ports yields several endpoints; edit the URL to test another port.
Service type Seeded URL ClusterIP (also when no type is set) http://<clusterIP>:<port> LoadBalancer http://<ingress IP or hostname>:<port>. Empty until the cloud assigns an address. ExternalName http://<externalName>:<port> NodePort Empty. Kanvas does not know node addresses. Enter http://<node address>:<nodePort>. Headless (clusterIP: None) Seeds http://None:<port>. Replace it with a real address. For an Ingress, the URL is always empty. Enter the host and path you want to test. The seeded scheme is always http; change it to https for TLS endpoints.
Run it and read the result 🔗 Edit the seeded values. Press Run Test. Meshery first saves the settings as a performance profile (the toast reads Performance profile <name> has been created), then submits the load test (Load test has been submitted). A countdown runs for the test duration. The results then render in the same panel, with a way back to the form. The same profile can be selected and re-run later, which is what makes a test repeatable before and after a change. Results are stored in Meshery’s performance results history, not in Kanvas. Profiles, schedules, comparisons between runs, and how results are interpreted are covered in Performance Management in the Meshery documentation.
Validation and failure modes 🔗 Message Meaning Please enter a valid URL along with protocol The URL needs a scheme such as http://. Please enter a valid JSON string The additional options field is not valid JSON. Duration rejected Duration must be positive and end in h, m, or s. Failed to create performance profile The profile could not be saved, so the test did not start. Load test did not run with msg: <message> The load generator reported a failure. The message names the cause, often an unreachable endpoint. Connection to the server got disconnected. Load test might be running in the background. Please check the results page in a few. The result stream dropped. The test may still finish; check the results page in Meshery. Permission denied block or disabled Run Test Your role lacks View performance profiles or Run test. Empty panel The host Meshery did not supply the performance form. Use a Meshery release that includes it. Kanvas does not pre-check that the endpoint is reachable.
Related 🔗 Resource Details shows the live state of the resource you are testing. Performance Limits covers the limits of Kanvas itself on large designs.
description: Generate load against a Service or Ingress from the Operator canvas using a performance profile, and read the results.

body:
Four actions take a design from the canvas to running infrastructure and back. Run them in this order. Each one is stricter than the last and costs a little more.
Action Checks or changes Needs a cluster Changes the cluster Validate Each component’s configuration against its schema, in your browser No No Dry run The design against the Kubernetes API of each target cluster Yes No Deploy Creates or updates every component’s object on the target clusters Yes Yes Undeploy Deletes every component’s object from the target clusters Yes Yes The deploy and undeploy flows are five-step wizards that run validation and a dry run for you, so you do not need to run them separately first.
Where these actions run 🔗 All four are Designer-mode actions in the design’s Actions menu. They run on a Meshery you run, with the Meshery Server’s kubeconfig doing the work. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run them and shows a self-hosted-feature prompt. See How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud for what each environment supports.
Who can run them 🔗 Action Permission Validate Validate Design (enforced on mobile only) Dry run Validate Design Deploy Deploy Design Undeploy Undeploy Design A denied action is hidden or disabled. The permission by role matrix is in Permissions by Role. Deploys, dry runs, and undeploys also appear in the notification center, where failures carry error codes and remediations.
For environment selection, connection problems, and loading failures, see Troubleshoot Kanvas.

body:
Whiteboarding in Kanvas (3:41) follows one late-night incident from page to postmortem on a single live design. Its page has chapters and a transcript.
Whiteboarding lets you diagram freely on the same canvas as your infrastructure. You draw shapes, text, freehand strokes, and lines to explain intent, and they sit beside real components in one design. It is on by default and available on every plan.
Drawn objects are saved with the design and shared live with collaborators. They are components marked as annotations, so they count toward your plan’s components-per-design limit. See Designs and Components.
This guide covers the drawing tools. For per-object operations such as copying, locking, and resizing, see Working with Canvas Objects.
The dock 🔗 The dock sits at the bottom of the canvas in Designer mode. Its tools, left to right:
Tool Shortcut What it does Select V Select, move, and configure objects. Hand H, or hold Space Pan the canvas. Components - Open the component palette. Kubernetes - Open every Kubernetes component. Shapes - Browse shape categories. Comment M Drop a comment thread. Image I Pick an image file and place it. TextBox T Add a text box. Section S Add a labeled, dashed region that holds other objects. Pen Ctrl/Cmd+E Draw annotation lines. Pencil Ctrl/Cmd+P Draw freehand. Help Center Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+/ Open help. The Pen and Pencil icons turn green while their mode is active. Press Esc to leave a mode. Pinned models appear after a divider at the right end. See Pin Models to the Dock.
The dock scrolls horizontally when it overflows, and it is greyed out while the app is in an error state, for example after a failed save. In Operator mode only the Select and Hand tools, Help Center, and minimized panels remain.
Turn tools on or off 🔗 The canvas right-click menu opens an Options dialog with these toggles, all on by default:
Enable Dock hides or shows the entire dock, including component pickers, not only the drawing tools. Enable Pencil and Enable Pen hide or show those two icons. Each change saves to your user preferences, so it applies to all your designs and devices. The toggles hide icons only. The keyboard shortcuts for Pen, Pencil, M, T, S, and I keep working.
No permission key gates drawing. Tier listings show Pencil, Pen, and 500 built-in shapes on Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise.
Draw freehand with the Pencil 🔗 Each stroke becomes one filled shape. Defaults are caribbean green, thickness 1, and opacity 1. There is no color or thickness control before you draw. Afterward, select the stroke and use its style toolbar to change fill color, opacity, and border.
Draw lines with the Pen 🔗 The Pen is Connector mode. Click empty canvas to place a small terminal point, then click elsewhere to place another and join them with a line. Repeated clicks draw a connected polyline. Starting from a component’s edge handle also works. Cancelling mid-draw removes the dangling point.
Pen lines are annotation edges. They explain flow and do not change any component’s configuration. Style them like any edge: color, line style, arrow and curve style, label, and animation.
Pan and box selection are off while you draw with the Pen or Pencil.
Add shapes, text, sections, images, and comments 🔗 Shapes. Choose from the shape categories. A shape carries no configuration and is never deployed. You can swap any object’s outline for one of 24 shapes while keeping its content, position, and size. Text boxes. Double-click to edit text inline. Text options include color, weight (regular, medium, semi bold, bold, black), underline or strikethrough, alignment, and font size. Sections. A section groups the objects dropped inside it, and they move with it. Images. Images up to 512,000 bytes are embedded in the design. Larger files are rejected. Comments. A comment opens a discussion thread on the canvas. Resolved threads disappear from the canvas until reopened. See Review a Design with Comments. Style objects and lines 🔗 Select an object to open its toolbar. Controls appear only when the object supports them.
Control Options Fill 13 swatches including transparent, with opacity from 0 to 1 Border Color, style (solid, dotted, dashed, double), thickness from 0 to 25 Layer order Move to front, forward, backward, to back Animation None, blink, ripple, bounce, pulse Line style Solid, dashed, or dotted; ten curve styles; eleven arrow heads Line animation Marching ants, which shows the direction of flow Collaborate 🔗 Every change, including drawn objects, syncs live between everyone in the design through a shared document over a peer-to-peer session. Each collaborator appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and live cursors and selections are shared. Undo and redo cover the shared document: components, configuration, styles, relationships, drawn objects, and layer toggles.
Limits and behavior 🔗 Drawn objects are saved with the design. Kanvas never deploys annotations. Images and text files over about 500 KB are rejected, whatever your plan.
description: Sketch freehand, draw annotation lines, and add shapes, text, sections, images, and comments alongside real components.

body:
A design is one record with one owner. These guides cover how other people reach it and how you discuss it with them. Access is per person and has no access level: everyone who can open a design can edit it. Comments are part of the design, and they work in Designer mode.
Goal Guide Give specific people access, change visibility, copy a link, or revoke access Share a Design Leave threaded comments, mention people, resolve threads, and control email Review a Design with Comments Live co-editing needs no setup. When two people have the same saved design open, they see each other’s cursors, selections, and edits. Collaboration Model explains how live editing, access, and comments fit together. To try all three with a teammate, follow the Collaborative Editing tutorial.
Sharing and comments run under your permissions. Sharing needs the Share Design permission, and the people picker needs View All Users. See Permissions by Role.

body:
Kanvas rests on one idea: a design is a declarative description of infrastructure. It records which components exist, how they relate to each other, how each one is configured, and any annotations that explain the intent. A design describes the state you want; it is not a script of steps to run.
Each part of Kanvas plays one role around that design:
Designer authors the design. You place components, connect them, and configure them on a shared canvas. Every save creates a new version, and collaborators can edit the same design at the same time. Meshery validates and deploys the design. It checks the design against component schemas, dry-runs it against target clusters, and deploys or undeploys it on the Kubernetes contexts you choose. Operator shows the running result. It displays live cluster state and links it back to the design: every resource Kanvas deploys carries the identity of its source design, so Operator can show exactly what one design produced. Layer5 Cloud, as the remote provider, stores designs and their versions and governs who can see them. Every new design starts public; Designs and Components explains visibility in full.
Concept pages 🔗 Designs and Components - what a design contains, how it is saved and versioned, what components are, and how a design maps to deployed resources. How Kanvas Works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud - the extension model, where designs live, what talks to your clusters, and what differs between kanvas.new and self-hosted Meshery. Relationships - how Kanvas maps the ways connected components interact. Collaboration Model - how live co-editing, design access, and comments work together, and what each one controls. Designer - the authoring mode: its purpose, scope, and tools. Render Modes - how Kanvas trades visual detail for canvas speed, and how Adaptive mode moves between modes. Operator - the operating mode: live cluster state and per-design views.
description: The core mental model behind Kanvas: designs, components, relationships, the two modes, and how Kanvas works with Meshery and Layer5 Cloud.
