title: Concepts

body:
In this tutorial you design a MySQL Pod that takes its database name from a ConfigMap and its root password from a Secret, deploy it to a cluster, and prove from inside the container that each value arrived. Separating configuration and credentials from the container image is how one image runs unchanged in every environment, and knowing exactly how Kubernetes delivers those values tells you why a changed setting sometimes reaches a running container and sometimes does not.
What you will learn 🔗 How a ConfigMap and a Secret store key-value data, and why a Secret’s values are base64-encoded rather than encrypted. The two ways a Pod consumes them: environment variables resolved once at container start, and mounted volumes that the kubelet keeps up to date. That a Pod refers to a ConfigMap or Secret by name and key, and that nothing checks the reference until the container starts. How Kanvas validates, dry-runs, and deploys a design, and what Operator shows for Secret data. Before you begin 🔗 A Kanvas environment with a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use Meshery Playground, a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a self-hosted feature prompt. Familiarity with Pods and the Kanvas Designer. If this is your first Kanvas tutorial, complete the Kubernetes Pods tutorial first. A short unique suffix for your object names and labels, such as your initials plus a number (jd42). Playground is shared with other users, so this tutorial writes names as mysql-<suffix>; replace <suffix> everywhere with yours. The scenario 🔗 You build three components and connect them by name references in the Pod spec:
ConfigMap mysql-config-<suffix> data: database = tutorialdb Secret mysql-secret-<suffix> data: root-password = <base64 of strongpassword> | | | env MYSQL_DATABASE | env MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD | volume at /etc/app-config | volume at /etc/db-secret v v Pod mysql-<suffix> container mysql (image mysql:8.0) The official MySQL image reads MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD to set the root password and MYSQL_DATABASE to create a database on first start, so a working login and a database named tutorialdb prove that both environment bindings work. The mounted files prove the volume bindings.
Create the ConfigMap 🔗 Start a new design and name it, for example configmaps-secrets-<suffix>. Kanvas saves the design automatically a few seconds after each change; there is no Save button. Add a ConfigMap component from the Kubernetes model. Its configurator opens beside it. Set the name to mysql-config-<suffix>. Leave the namespace as default. Under Data, add one entry with key database and value tutorialdb. On the configurator’s Labels tab, add the label owner with your suffix as the value. You use this label to find your objects in Operator. What just happened. A ConfigMap is a plain key-value object for non-sensitive configuration. It holds strings (or binary data under binaryData) up to 1 MiB in total, and it does nothing on its own: a Pod has to ask for its keys. Kanvas renders the configurator from the ConfigMap’s schema and checks your change against that schema in the background.
Check your work. The ConfigMap sits on the canvas with no warning badge. A yellow triangle badge means a schema warning; select it to jump to the field.
Create the Secret 🔗 Encode the password. In any terminal, run:
echo -n 'strongpassword' | base64 The output is c3Ryb25ncGFzc3dvcmQ=. The -n matters: without it, echo adds a newline that becomes part of the password.
Add a Secret component. Set the name to mysql-secret-<suffix> and the type to Opaque.
Under Data, add one entry with key root-password and value c3Ryb25ncGFzc3dvcmQ=.
On the Labels tab, add the same owner label.
What just happened. A Secret has the same key-value shape as a ConfigMap, and values under data must be base64-encoded. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone who can read the Secret object can recover the value with echo c3Ryb25ncGFzc3dvcmQ= | base64 -d. What protects a Secret in a cluster is RBAC on who may read Secrets, encryption at rest configured on the API server, and the kubelet keeping Secret volumes in memory instead of on disk. If you prefer not to encode values yourself, the stringData field accepts plain text and the API server encodes it for you.
The value is also stored in your design. Kanvas creates new designs with public visibility, so anyone who can open the design can read and decode the value. Use throwaway values like the one in this tutorial, and never put a production credential in a design.
Check your work. Decode the value you typed to confirm it round-trips to strongpassword. A value that is not valid base64 passes Validate but fails when the cluster checks the Secret in the next phase.
Build the Pod 🔗 Add a Pod component. Set the name to mysql-<suffix> and add the owner label on the Labels tab. Add one container with name mysql, image mysql:8.0, and a container port of 3306. Add an environment variable named MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. Leave its value empty and set Value From to a Secret Key Ref with name mysql-secret-<suffix> and key root-password. Add a second environment variable named MYSQL_DATABASE, with Value From set to a Config Map Key Ref with name mysql-config-<suffix> and key database. Use the ConfigMap reference here, not a Secret reference: each reference type looks only in its own kind of object. In the Pod spec, add two volumes: app-config, of type Config Map, with name mysql-config-<suffix>. db-secret, of type Secret, with secret name mysql-secret-<suffix>. On the mysql container, add two volume mounts: app-config at mount path /etc/app-config, read-only. db-secret at mount path /etc/db-secret, read-only. What just happened. The Pod now consumes the same data in two ways:
Delivery What the container sees When a changed value reaches the container Environment variable (valueFrom) MYSQL_DATABASE=tutorialdb, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=strongpassword Only when the container restarts. The kubelet resolves the values once, at start. Volume One file per key: /etc/app-config/database, /etc/db-secret/root-password Eventually, without a restart. The kubelet refreshes mounted files periodically (not for subPath mounts). Both deliver decoded values: the container never sees base64. Each binding is a reference by object name and key. Kanvas Validate checks each component against its own schema only, and a server-side dry run of a Pod does not look up the objects it references, so a misspelled name or key surfaces only when the container tries to start.
Check your work. The design holds three components and no warning badges. The Pod’s container shows two environment variables and two volume mounts.
Validate, dry run, and deploy 🔗 Run Validate from the Actions menu. Validate runs in your browser against each component’s schema and does not contact the cluster. Its findings are advisory; they never block a deploy. Run Dry Run. Kanvas sends each component to the cluster’s API server as a server-side dry run, which applies the cluster’s real validation without persisting anything. Run Deploy. Select the environment that holds your cluster connection, review the dry-run result, and deploy. What just happened. Deploy creates each object, or replaces it in place if it already exists, and labels it with the design’s id. Components with no declared dependency on each other are applied in parallel, so the Pod can reach the cluster before its ConfigMap and Secret do. In that case the Pod briefly reports CreateContainerConfigError and then starts on its own once the kubelet retries.
Check your work. The summary at the end of the deploy lists Deployed ConfigMap "mysql-config-<suffix>", Deployed Secret "mysql-secret-<suffix>", and Deployed Pod "mysql-<suffix>". A Failed to deploy row carries an error card with the cluster’s reason. A dry-run error names the component and field, for example an invalid label value or a Secret value that is not base64; select the error to open the configurator at that field.
Verify the bindings 🔗 Switch to Operator. Opening Operator with the design loaded shows a view scoped to this design, which lists the objects carrying the design’s id label: your ConfigMap, Secret, and Pod. Operator draws a snapshot, so if the Pod is still starting, change a filter or reopen the view to fetch fresh state.
Select the Pod. Its status chip reads Running once MySQL has started, which takes up to a minute. The container details list its environment variables and its volume mounts marked (RO). For variables set from a reference, Operator shows the reference, not the value.
Select the Secret. Operator shows its type, Opaque, and does not display its data values.
Start a terminal session on the Pod (Initiate Terminal Session). Kanvas opens a /bin/sh shell in the container. The terminal sends one line at a time when you press Enter, so run commands one per line:
printenv MYSQL_DATABASE cat /etc/app-config/database cat /etc/db-secret/root-password mysql -uroot -p"$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "SHOW DATABASES;" With kubectl access to the cluster, kubectl exec mysql-<suffix> -- printenv MYSQL_DATABASE and the equivalent commands give the same answers.
What just happened. The first two commands print tutorialdb: the ConfigMap reached the container as a variable and as a file. The third prints strongpassword, decoded, which shows that anyone who can exec into a Pod can read its mounted Secrets. The last command logs in with the password from the Secret and lists tutorialdb among the databases, which MySQL created from the ConfigMap value on first start.
Check your work. If the Pod reports CreateContainerConfigError and stays there, a referenced name or key does not match: compare the Pod’s references with the ConfigMap and Secret names and keys. If mysql answers Access denied, the stored password differs from what you expect, most often because the base64 value was encoded with a trailing newline.
Operator’s Download action saves the complete object as JSON, and for a Secret that includes its data. Treat downloaded Secret files as sensitive.
Change a value 🔗 Return to Designer and change the ConfigMap’s database value to otherdb. Deploy again. Deploy replaces the ConfigMap in place. After a minute or two, run the first two commands from the previous phase again. What just happened. cat /etc/app-config/database now prints otherdb, because the kubelet refreshed the mounted file. printenv MYSQL_DATABASE still prints tutorialdb, because environment variables are fixed when the container starts. MySQL also keeps its existing databases: MYSQL_DATABASE applies only to the first initialization. This difference is the main reason to mount configuration that must change at runtime as files.
Most fields of a running Pod, including its environment variables, cannot be changed in place. When you change the Pod itself, Deploy reports success but the running Pod keeps its old spec. To apply a Pod change, Undeploy and deploy again, or manage the Pod through a Deployment, which replaces Pods when its template changes.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu in Designer. Undeploy deletes each component in the design from the cluster by kind and name: the Pod, the ConfigMap, and the Secret. It removes nothing that the design does not contain, and it deletes any object of the same kind and name in that namespace, whoever created it, which is another reason for unique names on a shared cluster.
Because the design stores the Secret value, delete the design too if you no longer need it.
What you learned 🔗 A ConfigMap holds configuration and a Secret holds credentials, both as key-value data. Secret values are base64-encoded, which hides nothing; access control and encryption at rest protect them. A Pod consumes either one through environment variables, fixed at container start, or through mounted files, which update without a restart. References are by name and key and are checked only when the container starts, so a typo shows up as CreateContainerConfigError, not as a validation error. Kanvas Validate checks schemas in the browser, Dry Run checks against the cluster without persisting, and Deploy creates or replaces each object. Operator shows a Secret’s type but not its values. Next steps 🔗 Schedule Work with CronJobs - run a container on a schedule and watch the Jobs and Pods it creates. Deploy a Design - the full Validate, Dry Run, Deploy, and Undeploy reference for everyday use. Operator - how Operator discovers cluster resources and what its views show.
description: Inject configuration from a ConfigMap and a credential from a Secret into a MySQL Pod, as environment variables and as mounted files, and verify each binding in the running container.
excerpt: Inject configuration from a ConfigMap and a credential from a Secret …
title: Use ConfigMaps and Secrets

body:
In this tutorial you create a VPC network and EC2 instances in your AWS account without leaving Kanvas. You deploy three designs from the catalog, in order, to your own Kubernetes cluster: a controller that talks to AWS, a VPC network, and the EC2 instances that run inside it. Each AWS resource is a Kubernetes custom resource in the design, and a controller in the cluster turns that resource into real infrastructure.
The bridge is AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK). ACK lets you manage AWS resources with the same declarative model you use for Pods and Services: you declare the desired state in the cluster, and the controller makes AWS match it. The trade-off is that the cluster now holds AWS credentials and creates resources that cost money, so this tutorial runs only on a cluster you control and ends with a full cleanup.
What you will learn 🔗 An ACK controller watches custom resources in the cluster and creates, updates, and deletes the matching AWS resources. A custom resource can exist only after its definition (CRD) is installed, so designs that depend on each other deploy in a deliberate order. Deploy applies only the ordering a design declares; it does not sort designs or install CRDs ahead of the custom resources that need them. A Pod reads credentials from a Secret through environment variables that reference the Secret’s keys. Operator shows what Deploy put in the cluster, and the AWS console shows what the controller built in AWS. Before you begin 🔗 A self-hosted Meshery with a connected Kubernetes cluster. Install Meshery by following the Meshery installation guide. Minikube and Amazon EKS both work. The cluster must appear in Meshery as a connected Kubernetes connection assigned to a Meshery environment, because Deploy targets environments and the Kubernetes connections they hold. See Environments. Not Meshery Playground, and not kanvas.new. You put real AWS keys into a Secret in this tutorial. Meshery Playground is a shared cluster, so never deploy credentials there. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Deploy, Undeploy, and Operator open a prompt to self-host instead. Meshery Operator and MeshSync in the cluster. Operator reads the cluster through them. Deploy works without them; only the inspection steps need them. An AWS account and a dedicated IAM identity. Create an IAM user or role for this tutorial with the minimum permissions needed to manage VPCs, subnets, gateways, elastic IPs, route tables, security groups, and EC2 instances. Do not use root or administrator keys. You need its access key ID and secret access key. Budget for a short-lived bill. The VPC design creates a NAT gateway and an elastic IP, and both incur AWS charges for as long as they exist. EC2 instances incur charges while they exist too. Plan to finish the tutorial and its cleanup in one sitting. The scenario 🔗 You deploy three designs. Each one depends on the one before it:
1. EC2 controller design namespace ack-system +-- CRDs teach the cluster the AWS kinds (VPC, Subnet, Instance, ...) +-- Service account identity the controller Pod runs as +-- Secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY +-- Controller Pod reads the Secret, calls the AWS API 2. VPC workflow design region us-east-1 by default +-- 1 VPC +-- 1 internet gateway +-- 1 NAT gateway + 1 elastic IP +-- 2 route tables public, private +-- 2 subnets public, private +-- 1 security group 3. EC2 instances design instances placed in the VPC network At the end, the cluster holds the controller and a set of custom resources, and your AWS account holds the matching VPC network and running instances.
Clone the designs 🔗 The catalog holds the three designs this tutorial uses:
EC2 controller design VPC workflow design EC2 instances design Clone each design into your workspace from its catalog page, then open the clone in Kanvas on your self-hosted Meshery.
What just happened. Only published designs can be cloned. Each clone is a new private design named <name> (Copy), owned by you and placed in your selected workspace. It is independent of the catalog original: your edits never reach the source, and later changes to the source never reach your copy. That independence matters here, because you are about to put credentials into the controller design.
Phase 1: Configure the EC2 controller 🔗 Open your copy of the EC2 controller design. Its components deploy to the ack-system namespace: the CRDs that define the AWS resource kinds, a service account for the controller, a Secret for your AWS credentials, and the controller Pod itself.
Open the Secret component’s configurator by double-clicking the Secret. In its data, set exactly two keys:
Key Value AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID <base64-encoded-key> AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY <base64-encoded-secret> Secret data values are base64 encoded. Encode each value locally rather than pasting keys into a website, and avoid a trailing newline:
printf '%s' 'YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID' | base64 printf '%s' 'YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' | base64 Open the controller Pod’s configurator and inspect its container’s environment variables. You find two entries, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Each takes its value from a secretKeyRef that names the credentials Secret and one of its keys. The design already contains this wiring; you change nothing here.
What just happened. The controller never reads the Secret directly. When the kubelet starts the controller’s container, it resolves each secretKeyRef, decodes the matching value from the Secret, and sets it as an environment variable. The AWS SDK inside the controller reads AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY from the environment and signs every AWS API call with them. In manifest form, the wiring looks like this:
env: - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: <credentials-secret-name> key: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: <credentials-secret-name> key: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY The key names in the Secret and in the secretKeyRef entries must match exactly. A typo leaves the variable unset or the container unable to start, and the controller cannot authenticate.
The Secret’s values are now stored in your design, and Kanvas saves the design automatically. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption: anyone who can open the design can read your keys. Do not publish this design, do not share it, and do not keep it in a workspace other people use.
Phase 2: Deploy the EC2 controller 🔗 Deploy the controller design from the Actions menu. The Deploy stepper validates the design, asks you to pick the environment that holds your cluster’s connection, runs a dry run against that cluster, and then deploys.
On a first deploy, the dry run can report errors for objects in ack-system. A dry run creates nothing, including namespaces, so the cluster rejects objects aimed at a namespace that does not exist yet. If those are the only errors, tick the box that bypasses dry-run errors and continue. Deploy itself creates the missing ack-system namespace before it applies the objects.
The Finish step lists one row per component, such as Deployed Secret "<name>", or a failure row with an error card.
What just happened. Meshery Server turned each component into a Kubernetes object and applied it to every cluster in the environment you picked: create the object, or replace it in place if it already exists. Deploying the same design again therefore updates the cluster instead of duplicating objects. Deploy also labeled every object it applied with the design’s id, which is how Operator finds them next. The cluster now knows the AWS kinds through the new CRDs, and the controller Pod is starting with your credentials in its environment.
Phase 3: Verify the controller in Operator 🔗 Open the design-scoped Operator view with View in Operator from the design’s file menu. It shows only the objects this design deployed, because it filters on the design-id label that Deploy added. Confirm the Pod, the Secret, and the service account in ack-system, and open the controller Pod’s details to check that it is running.
As an alternative, open the Layers panel in Operator and filter on the ack-system namespace and the kinds you care about. The AWS kinds that the CRDs define appear under Custom Resources once MeshSync reports them.
What just happened. Operator draws a snapshot of what MeshSync reports from the cluster, not a live stream. It fetches a new snapshot when a view loads, when a filter changes, or when the selected clusters change, and it draws at most 100 resources per snapshot. If the Pod was still starting when the view loaded, change a filter or reload the view to fetch a fresh snapshot.
Phase 4: Deploy the VPC workflow 🔗 Open your copy of the VPC workflow design. It holds one custom resource per AWS networking resource: a VPC, an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, an elastic IP, a public and a private route table, a public and a private subnet, and a security group. The design targets the us-east-1 region by default. Adjust CIDR blocks or the region in each component’s configurator if your account needs different values, and keep all three designs in the same region.
Deploy the design to the same environment.
What just happened. This design contains no controller and no CRDs. It is a set of custom resources whose kinds exist only because Phase 2 installed their definitions. Deploy did not install those definitions for you and would not have reordered anything across designs: it applies only the ordering a design declares. Had you deployed this design first, the cluster would have rejected every component because it did not know their kinds.
Once the custom resources exist, the EC2 controller sees them and calls the AWS API to create each resource. The Finish step confirms that Kubernetes accepted the custom resources; AWS creation happens afterward, asynchronously, and can take several minutes for the NAT gateway. Open the VPC console in us-east-1 and confirm the VPC, both subnets, both route tables, the gateways, the elastic IP, and the security group.
Phase 5: Deploy the EC2 instances 🔗 Open your copy of the EC2 instances design and deploy it to the same environment. The design places its instances in the network you created in Phase 4.
What just happened. The same mechanism ran a third time. Kubernetes accepted the instance custom resources because the controller design installed their definition, and the controller created the instances in AWS inside your VPC network. The dependency chain is now complete: credentials, then controller and definitions, then network, then instances.
Verify 🔗 In AWS. Open the EC2 console in the region the designs use. Confirm that the instances are running and that they sit in the VPC and subnets from Phase 4.
In Operator. Open the design-scoped view for each design to see the custom resources it deployed. Each view shows only that design’s objects.
In the cluster. List the AWS kinds the controller installed, then read a resource’s status. ACK reports in each resource’s status conditions whether it has synced with AWS:
kubectl api-resources --api-group=ec2.services.k8s.aws kubectl describe <kind> <name> -n <namespace> Clean up 🔗 Remove everything in reverse order: instances, then the VPC network, then the controller. The order matters for the same reason it mattered on the way in. ACK deletes an AWS resource when its custom resource is deleted, and the controller is what makes that AWS call. If you remove the controller first, nothing is left to delete the instances, the NAT gateway, or the elastic IP, and they keep running and keep billing.
Undeploy the EC2 instances design, then the VPC workflow design, then the EC2 controller design, each from the Actions menu. Undeploy deletes each object in the design by kind and name on every cluster you select, and it ignores objects that are already gone. If Undeploy reports an error, delete the custom resources with kubectl instead, in the same order, while the controller is still running. Use kubectl api-resources --api-group=ec2.services.k8s.aws to find the kinds, then kubectl delete the instances first and the networking resources after them. Remove the controller design only when no AWS custom resources remain. Confirm in the AWS console that the instances are terminated and that the NAT gateway, the elastic IP, and the VPC are gone. The AWS console is the final word on what you are still paying for. Deactivate or delete the access key you created for this tutorial, and delete your copy of the controller design or clear its Secret values. Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix Deploy fails with meshery-server-1096 Kubernetes cluster is unavailable. No cluster in the selected environment resolves to a connected Kubernetes connection. Check that your cluster’s connection status is Connected and that the connection is assigned to the environment you picked in the Deploy stepper. Deploy fails with meshery-server-1073 Unable to deploy the selected design. This error wraps most hard deploy failures. Read the Details section of the error card for the inner error. The most likely cause is a connection that is not assigned to the selected environment. The dry run or deploy rejects the VPC or EC2 components because their kind is unknown. The CRDs are missing: the controller design was not deployed first, or it was undeployed. Deploy the EC2 controller design, confirm it in Operator, then deploy the dependent design again. Custom resources exist, but nothing appears in AWS and their status never reports synced. The controller cannot authenticate: wrong or badly encoded keys, a key name that does not match, or an IAM identity without the needed permissions. Re-encode both values without a trailing newline, check the two key names in the Secret and in the Pod’s secretKeyRef entries, check the IAM permissions, and deploy the controller design again. Read the controller Pod’s log for the AWS error. AWS resources appear in a region other than the one you expected. The designs target us-east-1 by default. Look in us-east-1, or set the region in each design’s configurators before you deploy. Operator shows Uh-oh. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster? Operator received no objects for the selected cluster. Confirm that Meshery Operator and MeshSync run in the cluster and that the cluster is selected in Operator. Undeploy reports an error. Undeploy failed for one or more objects. Delete the custom resources with kubectl in reverse order while the controller still runs, then confirm in the AWS console. Where to go next 🔗 Deploying designs covers the Deploy stepper, environments, and the deployment summary in full. Undeploying designs explains what Undeploy removes and what it leaves behind. Operator explains how Operator builds its view of a live cluster. Deploy Azure resources applies the same controller pattern to Azure. Kubernetes tutorials build the Kubernetes fundamentals this tutorial relies on.

body:
Designer mode is where you author a Kanvas design. You compose infrastructure from versioned components, configure each one against its schema, connect components with relationships, annotate the result, and validate or deploy it, all on one canvas that every collaborator edits at the same time. Designer works on intent: what you want to run. Operator works on live state: what is running.
Designer: the bottom dock holds the tools for adding components and annotations, and the Layers panel controls what the canvas draws. A design is a shared document 🔗 Everything on the canvas is an entry in one design document: every component you configure, every relationship, and every annotation you draw. The canvas draws that document. Moving a node, applying a layout, or hiding a layer writes into the design. As a result:
Collaborators see the same canvas, including positions, locks, and layer visibility. Undo and redo cover every change to the document: components, configuration, styles, relationships, annotations, and layer toggles. Hiding a component in the Layers panel changes only what is drawn. The component stays in the design and deploys with it. For what a design contains and how it is versioned, see Designs.
Designer and Operator 🔗 Designer Operator Purpose Author and change a design Inspect and act on resources running in connected clusters What the canvas draws Components, relationships, and annotations from the design document Kubernetes resources discovered in the selected clusters What you can edit The whole design: add, configure, relate, annotate, style, lay out, delete Nothing; live nodes are read-only Actions Validate, deploy, undeploy, share, reset design Open a terminal, follow logs, run a performance test, open the source design Selection, panning, zoom, the Layers panel, and undo and redo work in both modes. Keyboard shortcuts that add or change content, such as copy, paste, duplicate, delete, Pen, and Pencil, act only in Designer.
What you do in Designer 🔗 Compose from versioned components. The palette lists models from the Meshery registry by category, and each model offers a version selector with the newest version first. Add a component by dragging or clicking, nest it by dropping it onto a compatible parent, or drop YAML, JSON, or archive files to import infrastructure as code. Configure. A new component opens its configurator, a form rendered from the component’s JSON schema with the schema’s defaults. Edits write to the design after a short pause and trigger validation and relationship evaluation. Switching a component to another version keeps its configuration values; validation flags any that no longer fit. Relate. Drawing an edge or nesting one component in another creates a relationship when a registry definition matches the pair. A relationship can write values from one component’s configuration into another’s. Kanvas re-evaluates relationships about one second after changes stop, and evaluation never blocks editing. See Relationships and Relationship Evaluation. Annotate. Shapes, text boxes, sections, images, comments, Pen connectors, and Pencil strokes explain the design without configuring infrastructure. Lay out. Six layouts rearrange the canvas: Grid, Constrained (the default), hierarchical, star, bus, and ring. A design with no saved positions is laid out automatically when it opens; otherwise Kanvas keeps the saved positions. A layout changes positions only, never configuration. Validate, dry-run, deploy, and undeploy. Kanvas checks each changed component against its schema. A badge on the component counts its validation warnings and dry-run errors. Meshery Server carries out deployment. Share. A share gives others access to the design, and anyone with a share can edit it. What mode gates and what permission gates 🔗 Authoring is gated by mode, not by role. Adding, configuring, duplicating, deleting, and renaming work in Designer and are blocked in Operator. Resources synced from a live cluster are read-only in every mode. Within Designer, what you can change on a component depends on that component’s registry capabilities: a configurator tab or a style control appears only when the component declares it.
Only four actions are permission-gated: validate, deploy, undeploy, and share. When your role lacks one of these permissions, its control is hidden. The permission catalog also lists permissions for individual canvas gestures, such as adding shapes or resetting styles. Kanvas does not enforce those on the canvas, so withholding them has no effect. Users who are not signed in are prompted to sign in before sharing, and to sign in or run Meshery locally before validating or deploying. See Permissions.
How changes are stored and synchronized 🔗 Designer has no Save button. Every change to the design requests a save, and Kanvas sends it 3 seconds after the last change. A new design is not saved until it has a component or a name.
While a design is open, every change, drawn objects included, syncs live between collaborators through the shared document. Each collaborator appears as an avatar in the toolbar, and their cursor and current selection show on your canvas. Storage does not merge: each save sends the whole design, and the last save wins. Live co-editing in the open session is what reconciles concurrent edits. See Collaboration.
If a save fails, Kanvas enters an error state: the dock is disabled and edits are not applied while Kanvas retries the save with increasing delays.
Configurable components and annotations 🔗 Every object on the canvas is a component entry in the design. Annotations carry an annotation flag; configurable components do not. The Layers panel uses that flag to split the canvas into Annotations and Configurable Components, each with a count and its own visibility toggle. Pen connectors are non-binding annotation relationships: they draw lines without changing any configuration.
The distinction does not exempt annotations from your plan. When a design is saved, Layer5 Cloud counts every component entry, annotations included, against the components-per-design limit. The limit is checked on save, not when you add an object, so a design can grow past it on the canvas and then fail to save.
What Designer does not do 🔗 It does not operate live workloads. Terminal sessions, log streams, and performance tests are Operator actions. It does not filter components by label. Label filters exist only in Operator views. It does not set an access level on a share. Every share can edit. It does not narrow relationship evaluation by layer. Evaluation always covers the whole design. Where to go next 🔗 Reference: Canvas Objects, Tool Modes, Canvas Actions, Layout and Layers, Component Badges, and Keyboard Shortcuts. Build a design: Configuring Components, Creating Relationships, and Whiteboarding. Check and save a design: Validating Designs and Saving Designs. Give others access: Sharing Designs.

body:
Export writes a design out of Kanvas so you can back it up, move it between Meshery deployments, hand it to Helm or kubectl, or put it on a web page. Every export is generated from the current state of the design. You cannot export an earlier version.
Export is a File menu action, disabled on an empty design. In Operator mode, Export instead downloads the open view as <view name>.json.
Choose a format 🔗 Format Keeps layout, annotations, and metadata Use it for Design file (YAML) Yes Backups, moving designs, re-import into Kanvas Design (OCI image) Yes Storing and versioning a design in a container registry Kubernetes manifest No kubectl apply and pipelines that expect plain manifests Helm chart No Helm repositories, Argo CD, Flux, Artifact Hub Embed design (JavaScript) Snapshot of the canvas Showing a design on a web page Kanvas offers at least one of the first four. Which ones appear can depend on the capabilities of your Layer5 Cloud account. Per-format options and size limits are not exposed. To capture the canvas as a PNG picture, use Take Screenshot instead. See Canvas Actions.
Design file (YAML) 🔗 A complete copy of the design, including layout, annotations, component grouping, and configuration. The download is named <design name>.yml. Kanvas can import it back without loss.
Design (OCI image) 🔗 The same lossless content packaged as an OCI image archive. Push it with a registry tool such as docker push or oras push to version and distribute designs alongside application artifacts. Kanvas imports the archive back, taking the design file in its layers. See Import and Merge Designs.
Source-type formats 🔗 A design can be exported as the kind of source it was built from. Both formats are lossy: layout, annotations, and comments are dropped because neither format can carry them. To keep a design fully editable, export the design file instead.
Docker Compose is an import source only. A design cannot be exported to Compose.
Kubernetes manifest 🔗 Plain Kubernetes resource definitions, ready for kubectl apply.
Helm chart 🔗 A .tar.gz chart archive that contains the Kubernetes resource definitions. Install it with helm install <release> <chart>.tgz or place it in a Helm repository.
Re-importing a manifest or chart restores the resources, but not the layout, so the graph does not reappear as you drew it.
Embed design (JavaScript) 🔗 The Embed Design option downloads a JavaScript module and shows a two-line snippet to paste into an HTML page. The embed is a static snapshot, not a live view. See Embed Designs.
Access and tiers 🔗 Exporting needs no sign-in for a public or published design. Anonymous callers can download the design file of any public or published design, not just their own. A private design is downloadable by its owner, a provider administrator, a user the design is shared with, or a user holding the View Designs permission. Each download of the design file writes an audit event and raises the design’s download count. Anonymous downloads record as “Anonymous viewer downloaded”. No plan tier gates export, and exporting your own design needs no permission key. Layer5 Cloud’s catalog table shows its Download action to roles with the Download a Design permission. The browser either prompts for a save location or saves to your downloads folder. Success shows <name> design downloaded. Failure shows “Failed to download design”. Keep a version you can return to 🔗 A design has a single current version, and the save history is an event log, not a set of snapshots. To keep a restorable point, export a design file or an OCI image at that moment and store it. For an OCI image, push it to a registry under a tag.

Pinning a model puts its icon in the dock at the bottom of the canvas, so you can reach its components without opening the full palette. Pins belong to your account. They are not stored per design or in the browser, so they follow you across designs, browsers, and devices.
Pinning works in Designer mode. In Operator mode the dock does not show pinned models.
Pin a model 🔗 Hover a model row in the component palette and use the pin icon. Its tooltip reads “Pin To Dock”. The shape palette offers the same pin on each shape category row.
Only models and shape categories can be pinned. Individual components cannot. There is no limit on how many models you pin. Kanvas matches pins by model name, so pinning the same model at a different version is the same pin.
Use a pinned model 🔗 Pinned models appear after a divider at the right end of the dock.
Select a pinned model to open a picker with its components. Click a component to add it near the center of the canvas, or drag it to a specific spot. The picker has its own search box and a version selector with an “All Versions” choice. A pinned model whose lookup returns nothing is not drawn.
Remove a pin 🔗 Either of these removes the pin without affecting any design:
Select the pin icon again on the model row. Its tooltip reads “Remove From Dock”. Hover the pinned model in the dock and select the close (X) badge. Default dock 🔗 With nothing pinned the dock holds Select, Hand, Components, Kubernetes, Shapes, Comment, Image, TextBox, Section, Pen, Pencil, and Help Center. See Whiteboard on the Canvas.

body:
The canvas has four tool modes. The mode decides what a mouse drag does: move an object, pan the view, draw freehand or draw a connecting line. Select is the default. This page lists how to enter and leave each mode, what every mouse gesture does in it, and the wheel and zoom controls that work in all of them.
Modes at a glance 🔗 Mode Purpose Enter Leave Drag on empty canvas Box selection Select Select, move, configure and style objects. The default. V or Esc Choose another mode Draws a selection box On Pan Move the view without touching objects. H, or hold Space V, Esc, or release Space Pans the view Off Pencil Draw freehand annotations. Ctrl/Cmd + P, or the Pencil tool in the dock The same shortcut, V or Esc Draws a stroke Off Pen Draw connecting lines and annotation edges. Ctrl/Cmd + E, or the Pen tool in the dock The same shortcut, V or Esc Places points and lines Off The Pencil and Pen dock icons turn green while their mode is active. The mode shortcuts work in Designer mode. Select and Pan also work in Operator mode.
Releasing Space returns you to Select, not to the mode you held it from. If you were drawing with Pencil or Pen, re-enter that mode afterward.
Kanvas ignores single-key shortcuts while you type in a text field, so typing a label or a comment never changes the mode.
Select mode 🔗 Gesture Result Hover No effect. Click an object Selects it and shows its style toolbar, resize handles and connection handles. Drag an object Moves it. Locked objects do not move. Double-click a component Opens its configurator. Double-click a textbox or comment Edits its text inline. Right-click, or press and hold, on an object Opens the object menu. Right-click on empty canvas Opens the canvas menu. See Canvas Actions. Drag on empty canvas Draws a selection box that selects the objects it covers. Ctrl/Cmd + click Adds an object to the selection or removes it. The cursor shows an arrow while hovering, a move cursor while dragging an object and a crosshair while you draw a selection box.
Object actions are listed in Canvas Objects.
Pan mode 🔗 Pan mode turns a drag on the canvas into a pan. The cursor is an open hand, and a closed hand while you drag. Hold Space to pan for as long as the key is down, or press H to stay in Pan mode until you leave it.
Pencil mode 🔗 Pencil draws freehand. Each stroke you release becomes one annotation object on the canvas.
Gesture Result Press and drag Draws a freehand stroke. Release Completes the stroke and turns it into an object. A new stroke is caribbean green, with thickness 1 and full opacity. Pencil has no color or thickness control before you draw. Select the stroke afterward and change its fill, border and opacity in the style toolbar. See Canvas Objects.
Pencil strokes connect to nothing. They annotate. Pan and box selection are off while Pencil is active.
Pen mode 🔗 Pen draws lines. Each line is an annotation edge, a non-binding relationship that carries no configuration, so it explains a design without changing it.
Step Result Click on empty canvas Places a small point to start from. Click again elsewhere on empty canvas Places another point and draws an edge between the two. Repeating this draws a connected line of segments. Start from a component’s connection handle and release on another component or a point Draws an edge between them. Cancel mid-draw Removes the dangling point. Points are small borderless shapes. Edges drawn with Pen use the same style controls as every other edge: color, line style, curve, arrowhead, label and animation. See Canvas Objects. Pan and box selection are off while Pen is active.
Edges between registry-defined components, which configure the components they join, are drawn in Select mode from a component’s connection handle. See Relationships.
Wheel and zoom controls 🔗 These are registered in Designer and Operator mode.
Input Result Scroll wheel Pans vertically. Horizontal scroll, or Shift + scroll wheel Pans horizontally. Each Shift step moves 50 pixels. Ctrl/Cmd + scroll wheel Zooms toward the pointer. Each step changes the zoom by 0.1. Ctrl/Cmd + + and Ctrl/Cmd + - Zooms in and out by the same step. The Options drawer sets the zoom range: a minimum from 0.1 to 5 (default 0.1) and a maximum from 0.1 to 30 (default 30). Zooming the page itself is left to the browser.
Object controls and badges appear only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough. When you are zoomed out, Kanvas shows a hint to zoom in to interact with elements.
Related reading 🔗 Keyboard Shortcuts - every shortcut in one list. Whiteboarding - a task guide to drawing on a design. Designer - what Designer mode is for.

body:
Undeploying deletes the Kubernetes objects that each component in a design describes, from every cluster in the environments you select. It does not touch the design itself. The design record, its versions, and its Operator view are unchanged.
Before you start 🔗 The prerequisites match Deploy a Design: a Meshery you run with a connected cluster, a non-empty design, and the Undeploy Design permission. The hosted kanvas.new site does not run undeploy. See Permissions by Role.
The undeploy flow 🔗 Choose Undeploy from the design’s Actions menu. The Undeploy design "<name>" stepper has the same five steps and gates as the deploy stepper:
Validate Design. Runs validation inline. Identify Environments. Selects the environments, and so the clusters, to remove from. Dry Run. An undeploy-type dry run that deletes by name with server-side dry run. Because an absent object returns NotFound, a design that was never deployed, or is already removed, shows an error for every component here and needs the bypass checkbox to continue. Finalize. Confirms the environments and component count. The button reads Undeploy. Finish. Runs the removal and shows the results. What gets deleted 🔗 Behavior Detail What is removed One delete for each non-annotation component’s object, in its namespace, on every selected cluster. How it is matched By kind and name from the design, not by label. An object with the same kind and name that was created some other way is deleted too. Order Reverse dependency order. A component whose dependent failed to delete is withheld: Withheld <component>: <dependent> did not undeploy successfully. Objects already gone Ignored. Namespaces, custom resource definitions, volume claims, Secrets Deleted only when the design has a component for them. Dependency charts For components of non-Kubernetes models, Meshery uninstalls the model’s Helm chart: Undeployed dependent helm chart for <component>. This can remove custom resource definitions and operators that other designs on the cluster use. Missing namespace Created before the delete is attempted. Meshery always processes dependency charts on undeploy. The Include Dependencies checkbox in the dry-run step does not change this. Before you undeploy a design that uses custom resource models, check what else on the cluster depends on its definitions.
Read the results 🔗 Success raises the event undeployed design '<name>'. at success severity. Failure raises Failed to undeploy design '<name>'. at error severity, with an error card. The error codes match those in Deploy a Design. The deployment count of the design is not decremented.
In Operator mode, the resources leave the live view once MeshSync reports their deletion.
Limits 🔗 There is no undeploy-type dry run outside the stepper. Deleting a design does not undeploy it. Undeploy first if you want the resources gone. See Delete a Design. As with deploy, the Finish step waits for a server event. If the request fails before the server raises one, the step keeps spinning with no error. See Deploy a Design.

body:
Right-clicking an empty part of the canvas - anywhere no component sits - opens the Canvas Actions menu. Where the component context menu acts on one component, this menu acts on the canvas as a whole: undoing and redoing, pasting, selecting everything, capturing the canvas as an image, and reaching help.
The menu adapts to the mode you are in. Commenting and pasting, for example, are offered in Designer mode but not in Operator mode, where the canvas reflects discovered infrastructure rather than a design you are authoring.
Editing actions 🔗 Action Shortcut Behavior Add Comment M Drops a comment at the point you right-clicked. Designer mode only. See Review a Design with Comments. Undo Cmd/Ctrl + Z Reverses the last change to the design: components, configuration, styles, relationships, annotations and layer toggles. A message confirms the change was reverted, or reports that no changes remain. Redo Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Z or Cmd/Ctrl + Y Re-applies the last undone change. Paste Cmd/Ctrl + V Pastes the clipboard contents at the cursor position. Designer mode only. Select All Cmd/Ctrl + A Selects every component on the canvas. Reset Design Clears every component from the canvas. Designer mode only, and destructive - see below. Reset Design 🔗 Reset Design removes everything currently on the canvas. Kanvas asks you to confirm before it does, and the confirmation reminds you that undo is usually the better tool if you only want to step back a few changes. The confirmation dialog carries a “don’t show this again” checkbox; ticking it stores that preference against your user settings, and the reset then happens immediately on every subsequent use.
Screenshot Canvas 🔗 Take Screenshot captures the canvas as drawn - components, relationships and annotations - and downloads it to your machine as a PNG. The file is named Kanvas-<timestamp>.png, so repeated captures of the same design do not overwrite one another.
The capture is of the canvas, not your browser window: panels, the dock and the toolbar are not included. It records the canvas as currently viewed, so pan and zoom to frame what you want before you capture. Object controls and badges appear only when the canvas is zoomed in far enough, so zoom in first if you want them in the image.
This is the quickest way to put a design into a pull request, an incident write-up or a slide. When you need the design as data rather than as a picture - to hand to another tool, or to re-import later - use Exporting Designs instead.
Options 🔗 Options opens the canvas settings drawer. Each change saves to your user preferences on the server after a short pause, applies to every design you open and shows a confirmation message. Preferences belong to you, not to a design.
Option Default Effect Dark Theme - Switches the canvas between light and dark themes. Snap to Grid On Snaps objects to the grid as you drag. Hide Gridlines On Gridlines are hidden by default. Enable Dock On Off hides the whole bottom dock, including the drawing tools and pickers. Keyboard shortcuts still work. Show Reset Canvas Confirmation On Off makes Reset Design act immediately. Enable Pencil On Shows the Pencil tool in the dock. Enable Pen On Shows the Pen tool in the dock. Auto-pan on Drag Off Pans the view while you drag an object past the canvas edge. Kanvas turns it off on large designs, with a limit for each render mode. See Auto-pan on Drag. Max Canvas Zoom 30 Upper zoom limit, from 0.1 to 30. Min Canvas Zoom 0.1 Lower zoom limit, from 0.1 to 5. Enable Debugger Off Shows debugging aids. Relationship Evaluation Engine Automatic (recommended) Chooses how relationships are evaluated. Show Tutorial On Shows the in-app tutorial. Show Walkthrough On Shows the walkthrough. Render Fidelity - Sets how much detail the canvas draws, from full fidelity down to a wireframe, and can adapt as a design grows. See Render Modes. Operator mode offers only Show Tutorial and Show Walkthrough.
Shortcuts 🔗 Shortcuts (Cmd/Ctrl + /) opens the keyboard shortcut reference in the help drawer, listing the shortcuts available in both Designer and Operator modes.
View help center 🔗 Help Center (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + /) opens the in-app help modal. It gathers, in one place, every route by which you can learn more about Kanvas or reach someone who can help:
Card What it opens Documentation Guides, references and how-tos for Kanvas and Meshery. Video Tutorials Walkthroughs and demos in the Layer5 video library. Quick Tips An in-app tour of core Kanvas features, shown in a drawer beside the canvas. Academy Structured learning paths in Layer5 Cloud. Discussion Forum The Layer5 discussion forum, for questions and shared knowledge. Slack The Layer5 community Slack, for real-time conversation. Quick Tips and Keyboard Shortcuts open in a drawer alongside the canvas, so you can keep working while you read them. Support opens its form in a modal over the canvas. The remaining five cards open in a new tab. The Help Center is also reachable from the help button at the right-hand end of the dock.

body:
In this tutorial you design a CronJob that runs a small container every minute, deploy it, and watch Kubernetes turn the schedule into Jobs and the Jobs into Pods. Then you change the schedule in place and clean up. Scheduled work such as backups, report generation, and cache warming runs this way, and understanding the CronJob to Job to Pod chain is what lets you answer the two questions that matter in production: did it run, and where is its output.
What you will learn 🔗 How a CronJob creates a Job for each scheduled time, and how each Job creates a Pod that runs to completion. Why a Job’s Pod must use restartPolicy OnFailure or Never. How the history limits decide how many finished Jobs stay in the cluster, and what concurrencyPolicy and suspend control. Why the objects a controller creates are not part of your design, and how to find them in Operator anyway. Before you begin 🔗 A Kanvas environment with a Kubernetes cluster connected to Meshery. Use Meshery Playground, a shared live cluster, or a self-hosted Meshery with a connected cluster. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions: Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a self-hosted feature prompt. Familiarity with Pods and the Kanvas Designer. If this is your first Kanvas tutorial, complete the Kubernetes Pods tutorial first. A short unique suffix for names and labels, such as your initials plus a number (jd42). Playground is shared with other users; replace <suffix> everywhere with yours. About 15 minutes, most of it waiting for scheduled runs. The scenario 🔗 You build one component. Kubernetes builds the rest:
CronJob hello-<suffix> schedule "*/1 * * * *" (in your design) | at each scheduled minute, the CronJob controller creates v Job hello-<suffix>-<n> (not in your design) | the Job controller creates v Pod hello-<suffix>-<n>-<random> runs busybox, prints the date, exits Design the CronJob 🔗 Start a new design and name it, for example cronjobs-<suffix>. Kanvas saves the design automatically a few seconds after each change; see Save Designs for how saving and versions work. Add a CronJob component from the Kubernetes model. Set its name to hello-<suffix> and, on the Labels tab, add the label owner with your suffix as the value. Set the schedule to */1 * * * *, which means every minute. Under the job template, set the Job’s metadata label owner: <suffix>, and set the same label on the Pod template’s metadata. Labels on the CronJob itself are not copied to the Jobs and Pods it creates; the template labels are. In the Pod template spec, set the restart policy to OnFailure and add one container: Name: hello Image: busybox:1.36 Command: /bin/sh, -c, date; echo Hello from the Kubernetes cluster What just happened. A CronJob is a Job factory. Its schedule uses standard cron syntax (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and is evaluated in the time zone of the cluster’s controller manager unless you set timeZone, such as Europe/Berlin. Its jobTemplate is a complete Job spec, and the Job’s template is a complete Pod spec. A Job runs its Pod to completion, so the Pod’s restart policy must be OnFailure (retry in the same Pod) or Never (create a new Pod on failure); the Pod default, Always, is rejected.
Check your work. The CronJob is on the canvas with no warning badge. If a yellow triangle badge appears, select it to jump to the field that does not match the schema.
Validate, dry run, and deploy 🔗 Run Validate from the Actions menu. It checks the component against its schema in your browser and does not contact the cluster. Its findings are advisory. Run Dry Run. The cluster’s API server checks the CronJob with its full validation without persisting it. Run Deploy, select the environment that holds your cluster connection, and deploy. What just happened. The dry run is the first check that applies Kubernetes rules beyond the schema, such as the allowed restart policies and the cron syntax. Deploy creates the CronJob and labels it with the design’s id. Nothing runs yet: the CronJob controller creates the first Job at the next scheduled minute.
Check your work. The deploy summary lists Deployed CronJob "hello-<suffix>". If the dry run reports an error on the restart policy, set it to OnFailure. An error on the schedule means the cron expression is malformed. Select a dry-run error to open the configurator at that field.
Observe the Jobs and Pods 🔗 Wait two or three minutes, then switch to Operator. With the design loaded, Operator opens a view scoped to the design, and that view shows only the CronJob: Kanvas puts the design’s id label on the objects it applies, and the Jobs and Pods are created by Kubernetes, not by Kanvas. To see the whole chain, filter the view by the label owner=<suffix>, or search for hello-<suffix>, and include the kinds CronJob, Job, and Pod. Search matches part of a resource name, and Job and Pod names start with the CronJob’s name. Select one of the Pods. Its status chip reads Succeeded: the container printed its message and exited with code 0. Read the output of a run. Open a log session on one of the Pods (Initiate Log Session), or with kubectl access run kubectl logs job/<job-name>. The output is the date followed by Hello from the Kubernetes cluster. Operator shows a snapshot of the cluster, fetched when you open a view, change a filter, or change the selected cluster. To see Jobs created since the last fetch, change a filter or reopen the view.
What just happened. Every minute the CronJob controller created a Job named after the CronJob and the scheduled time, and the Job controller created a Pod for it. Wait five minutes and fetch again: no more than three completed Jobs remain. The CronJob keeps successfulJobsHistoryLimit (default 3) successful Jobs and failedJobsHistoryLimit (default 1) failed Jobs, and deletes older ones together with their Pods. Keep these limits low on a busy schedule: finished Jobs and Pods stay in the cluster and count toward any object-count quota in the namespace.
Three more fields shape a CronJob’s behavior:
Field Default Effect concurrencyPolicy Allow What happens when a run is due while the previous one is still running: Allow starts another, Forbid skips the new run, Replace stops the old run and starts the new one. suspend false true stops new runs without deleting the CronJob. Runs already started finish. startingDeadlineSeconds none How late a missed run may still start. A run that misses its deadline is skipped and counted as missed. Check your work. If no Jobs appear after several minutes, check the schedule and confirm the CronJob is not suspended. A Pod in Error or a Job that keeps retrying means the container failed: read its logs. A Pod stuck in Pending means the cluster could not schedule it or pull the image.
Change the schedule and redeploy 🔗 Return to Designer and change the schedule to */2 * * * *, every second minute. Set successfulJobsHistoryLimit to 1. Deploy again. What just happened. Deploy replaces an existing object in place, so the CronJob keeps its name and history and the controller uses the new schedule from the next run. After a few minutes Operator shows a new Job every two minutes and only one completed Job at a time. To pause the CronJob instead of changing its schedule, set suspend to true and deploy.
Changes to the job template apply only to Jobs created after the redeploy. Jobs and Pods that already exist keep the spec they were created with.
Check your work. In Operator, the CronJob’s newest Jobs are two minutes apart, and older successful Jobs disappear after the next run.
Clean up 🔗 Run Undeploy from the Actions menu in Designer. Undeploy deletes each component in the design by kind and name, which here is only the CronJob hello-<suffix>. The Jobs and Pods are not in the design. They are owned by the CronJob, and Kubernetes garbage collection removes owned objects after their owner is deleted. Fetch the Operator view again to confirm they are gone. If any remain, delete them with kubectl delete jobs -l owner=<suffix>.
Undeploy deletes any CronJob with the same name in that namespace, whoever created it, which is another reason to use unique names on a shared cluster. The design itself stays saved; delete it if you no longer need it.
What you learned 🔗 A CronJob creates a Job at each scheduled time, and each Job creates a Pod that runs to completion with restart policy OnFailure or Never. The history limits decide how many finished Jobs stay in the cluster; concurrencyPolicy, suspend, and startingDeadlineSeconds decide which runs start. Your design contains only the CronJob. Objects that controllers create carry the template labels, not the design’s id, so you find them in Operator by label or name. Deploying a changed design replaces the CronJob in place; the new schedule and template apply to future runs. Next steps 🔗 Deploying WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes - keep data across Pod restarts with PersistentVolumeClaims. Deploy a Design - the full Validate, Dry Run, Deploy, and Undeploy reference for everyday use. Operator - how Operator discovers cluster resources and what its views show.

body:
In this tutorial you install Azure Service Operator (ASO) in your own Kubernetes cluster, then design an Azure resource group and a storage account inside it, deploy both from Kanvas, and find them in the Azure portal. You manage real Azure infrastructure with the same design, validate, and deploy loop you use for Kubernetes workloads, and the cluster keeps that infrastructure matched to the design.
The trade-off is indirection. Kanvas never calls Azure. It applies Kubernetes objects to your cluster, and ASO turns those objects into Azure resources in the background. A successful deploy means the cluster accepted the objects; the Azure resources follow a little later, and Azure-side failures surface on the objects in the cluster, not in the deploy summary.
What you will learn 🔗 ASO is a Kubernetes operator that turns custom resources into Azure resources, authenticating to Azure as a Service Principal whose credentials live in a Kubernetes Secret. Kanvas components from the Azure model are those ASO custom resources in design form, and their configurator forms come from the ASO schemas in the Meshery registry. Deploy applies custom resources to the cluster in one pass; ASO then reconciles each one with Azure on its own schedule. Azure resources have owners: a storage account belongs to a resource group, so the resource group must exist in Azure before the storage account can be created. Deleting a custom resource is how you delete the Azure resource it manages, which makes cleanup order matter. Before you begin 🔗 Your own cluster, never Meshery Playground. This tutorial puts real Azure credentials into a Secret in the cluster. Playground is a shared cluster, so anyone with access to it could read them. Use a self-hosted Meshery with a Kubernetes cluster you control. Hosted kanvas.new has no cluster actions; Validate, Deploy, and Undeploy there open a prompt to self-host instead. To install Meshery, see https://docs.meshery.io/installation. A connected cluster assigned to an environment. Deploy targets Meshery environments and the Kubernetes connections assigned to them, so your cluster must be a connected Kubernetes connection that belongs to at least one environment. An Azure subscription and the Azure CLI. You need rights to create a Service Principal with the Contributor role on the subscription. Sign in with az login before you start. kubectl access to the same cluster. You install cert-manager and check ASO from the command line. Operator mode for verification (optional). Operator reads the cluster through Meshery Operator and MeshSync. Deploy does not need them; Operator does. A unique prefix. Storage account names are global across all of Azure. Pick a short prefix, such as your handle, and use it in every name. This tutorial uses alex. You need basic familiarity with Kubernetes and the Azure portal. You do not need to write YAML.
The scenario 🔗 You work with two designs. The first installs ASO; the second describes the Azure resources ASO creates.
Design 1: Azure Service Operator (cloned from the catalog) ASO operator, its custom resource definitions, and Secret aso-controller-settings ---- Service Principal credentials Design 2: alex-azure-resources (built by you) Resource Group alex-aso-rg location eastus ^ | owner | Storage Account alexasodemo01 location eastus, access tier Hot Kanvas Deploy --> Kubernetes custom resources --> ASO --> Azure subscription At the end, the portal shows resource group alex-aso-rg containing storage account alexasodemo01.
Phase 1: Create the Service Principal 🔗 ASO needs an Azure identity to act on your subscription. Create a Service Principal with the Contributor role scoped to the subscription:
az ad sp create-for-rbac -n azure-service-operator --role contributor --scopes /subscriptions/<AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID> Keep the output; you need three of its fields plus your subscription ID:
Output field Use it as appId AZURE_CLIENT_ID password AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET tenant AZURE_TENANT_ID (your subscription ID) AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID What just happened. You created a non-human identity in Microsoft Entra ID and granted it Contributor on the subscription. Everything ASO later does in Azure, it does as this identity, so its role assignment is the upper bound on what your designs can create. The password is shown only once; treat it like any other secret.
Phase 2: Install cert-manager 🔗 ASO serves admission webhooks that need TLS certificates, and it relies on cert-manager to issue them. Install cert-manager in the cluster before you install ASO:
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/jetstack/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.14.1/cert-manager.yaml Wait until the pods in the cert-manager namespace are running (kubectl get pods -n cert-manager) before you continue.
What just happened. cert-manager is now ready to issue certificates for any workload that asks. If ASO starts before cert-manager can serve its requests, the ASO webhooks have no certificates and the operator does not become ready.
Phase 3: Install ASO from the catalog 🔗 Find the Azure Service Operator design in the catalog and clone it. The clone is a private copy named Azure Service Operator (Copy), owned by you, in your selected workspace, and independent of the catalog original. Open the clone and select its aso-controller-settings Secret. Enter your four values under the keys AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_CLIENT_ID, and AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET. Follow the format the Secret already uses: Kubernetes expects base64-encoded values under data and plain text under stringData. Deploy the design to the environment that holds your cluster. The Deploy stepper validates the design, asks for target environments, runs a dry run against the cluster, and then applies every component. Confirm the operator is running: its pod reaches the Running state in the operator’s namespace (azureserviceoperator-system in ASO’s standard install). What just happened. Deploy turned each component of the cloned design into a Kubernetes object and applied it: the operator’s workloads, the custom resource definitions that teach Kubernetes the Azure kinds, and the Secret. On startup ASO reads aso-controller-settings and uses those credentials for every Azure call. From now on, creating one of its custom resources in the cluster is a request to create the matching Azure resource.
The Secret now lives inside your design as well as in the cluster. Do not publish the design, and do not share it: anyone you share a design with can read, edit, clone, and re-share it, credentials included.
Phase 4: Design the resource group and storage account 🔗 Create a new design and name it alex-azure-resources. Kanvas saves it automatically once it has a name or a component. Search the component palette for Resource Group from the Azure model and add it. Its configurator opens as soon as it lands on the canvas. Name the resource group alex-aso-rg and set its location to eastus. Search the palette for Storage Account from the Azure model and add it. Name the storage account with your prefix, for example alexasodemo01. Azure requires storage account names to be globally unique, 3 to 24 characters, lowercase letters and digits only. In the storage account’s configuration, set the owning resource group to alex-aso-rg, set the location to eastus, and set the access tier to Hot (frequently accessed data) or Cool (infrequently accessed data, lower storage cost). Run Validate from the Actions menu. It lists every required field you have not set, per component. Fill each one in the configurator and validate again until the list is empty. What just happened. Each component is an ASO custom resource. Its configurator form is generated from that resource’s schema in the Meshery registry, which is why the fields are ASO’s fields and required ones carry a red asterisk. ASO uses the custom resource’s name as the Azure resource name by default. The owner field on the storage account is what places it inside the resource group in Azure; it is a reference by name, not a drawing on the canvas. Validate runs entirely in your browser against those schemas. It catches missing and malformed fields, never blocks you, and does not check Azure rules such as name uniqueness.
Phase 5: Deploy and let ASO reconcile 🔗 Deploy alex-azure-resources through the stepper to the same environment you used for ASO. On the Dry Run step, the cluster checks each custom resource against the ASO definitions installed in Phase 3. Fix any errors it reports before you continue. Finish the deployment. The summary lists a row per component and cluster, such as Deployed ResourceGroup "alex-aso-rg". What just happened. Deploy applied both custom resources in one pass. Kanvas orders components only by dependencies a design declares, so the storage account can reach the cluster at the same moment as the resource group. That is safe: ASO retries a resource whose owner is not ready yet until the owner exists in Azure, then creates it. The deploy summary reports what the cluster accepted. The Azure resources appear a minute or more later, once ASO has completed its calls to Azure. Every object Deploy applies carries a label with the design’s ID, which is how Operator finds them.
Deploy is idempotent: if you change the access tier and deploy again, Kanvas replaces the custom resource in place and ASO updates the storage account in Azure.
Verify 🔗 Check three places, from closest to the design to closest to Azure.
Operator. Open the design-scoped view from the design’s file menu (View in Operator). It filters on the design’s ID label, so it shows only the objects this design applied. Kinds outside the built-in Kubernetes lists appear under Custom Resources in the Layers panel. Operator draws a snapshot, not a live stream; reload the view or change a filter to fetch a fresh one. The cluster. kubectl get resourcegroups.resources.azure.com,storageaccounts.storage.azure.com -n default lists both custom resources. ASO reports progress through each resource’s Ready condition; kubectl describe shows the reason when a resource is not ready. The Azure portal. Open resource group alex-aso-rg and confirm that storage account alexasodemo01 is in it, in East US, with the access tier you chose. Clean up 🔗 These resources cost money while they exist. Remove them in this order.
Undeploy alex-azure-resources. Undeploy deletes each component’s custom resource from the cluster. ASO deletes the Azure resource when its custom resource is deleted.
Confirm in the portal that the storage account and the resource group are gone. Azure deletions take a few minutes.
If Undeploy reports an error, or the custom resources are still in the cluster, delete them directly and confirm in the portal again:
kubectl delete storageaccounts.storage.azure.com alexasodemo01 -n default kubectl delete resourcegroups.resources.azure.com alex-aso-rg -n default Undeploy the Azure Service Operator design last. It removes the operator and its custom resource definitions. If you remove the operator first, nothing is left to delete the Azure resources, and you must remove them in the portal yourself.
Remove the credentials. Delete the Service Principal in Azure if you no longer need it, and delete your cloned operator design so the credentials no longer live in your workspace.
Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix Dry Run or Deploy fails with meshery-server-1096 Kubernetes cluster is unavailable. None of the selected targets resolves to a connected Kubernetes context. Confirm the cluster’s connection status is Connected and that the connection is assigned to the environment you selected. Upload a fresh kubeconfig if the credentials changed. Deploy fails with meshery-server-1073 Unable to deploy the selected design. This error wraps most hard deploy failures. A common cause is a connection that is not assigned to the selected environment. Open the error’s Details to read the inner error. Assign the connection to the environment and confirm it is Connected. The resources design fails dry run or deploy because the cluster does not recognize the Resource Group or Storage Account kind. ASO’s custom resource definitions are not installed, or the operator design has not finished deploying. Deploy the Azure Service Operator design first and confirm the operator pod is running, then deploy the resources design again. Operator shows Uh-oh. Is MeshSync healthy on the selected cluster? Operator has no MeshSync data for the selected cluster. Confirm Meshery Operator and MeshSync are running in the cluster. Deploy does not depend on them; verify with kubectl and the portal in the meantime. The deploy succeeded, but nothing appears in Azure and the custom resource’s status reports an authorization error. The Service Principal lacks rights on the subscription, or the Secret holds wrong values. Check the Contributor role assignment and the four Secret values. Correct the Secret in the operator design and deploy it again; if ASO keeps reporting the old error, restart the operator pod so it rereads the Secret. The storage account never becomes ready and its status reports a name error. The name is taken elsewhere in Azure or breaks the 3 to 24 lowercase letters and digits rule. Choose another name with your prefix, update the component, and deploy again. Where to go next 🔗 Deploying designs covers the Deploy stepper, targets, and the deploy summary in full. Undeploying designs explains what Undeploy removes and what it leaves in place. Cloning a design describes how catalog clones are owned and stored. Operator explains how Operator draws what runs in your cluster. Deploy AWS EC2 instances applies the same operator pattern to AWS. The official ASO documentation at https://azure.github.io/azure-service-operator/ lists every Azure resource kind ASO supports and its fields.

body:
An embedded design is an interactive picture of a design on your own page. Readers can pan and zoom it, but cannot edit it. It is a static export: Kanvas gives you a JavaScript module file and a snippet that loads it. How an embed works 🔗 It is a snapshot. The file holds the canvas as it was at export time: node positions, element styles, and inline background images converted to data URLs where the fetch succeeded. Later edits to the design do not change an exported file. Re-export to refresh it. It needs no Layer5 Cloud at view time. The page makes no request to Layer5 Cloud, so the embed works for private designs and keeps working if the design is deleted. Anyone who can read your page can read the embedded design data. It is view only. Layout is fixed to the exported positions. Selection and box selection are disabled, zoom is limited to 0.5x to 6.6x, and there is no editing, component configuration, relationship evaluation, or live cluster data. It loads one library. The page fetches the Cytoscape library (version 3.27.0) from a public CDN, so viewers need outbound access to it. A Meshery logo link, which opens meshery.io, is drawn at the bottom right of the canvas. No option removes it. It has no parameters. Width, height, theme, background, and zoom are not options. The container’s CSS sets the size. There is no iframe embed. Kanvas offers no embed URL for the app itself. Embedding needs no permission key and no paid plan. Embed a design in an HTML page 🔗 Open the design, choose Export, and select Embed Design. Kanvas loads the design if it is not the open one, waits for it to render plus 3 seconds, and then generates the file. A failure shows “Failed to generate Embed Code for ”. Download the JavaScript file, then copy the embed code. Place the file next to your page, or anywhere your page can reference, and paste the snippet:
The container id is embedded-design- plus the design id, lowercased, with spaces replaced by hyphens. The script file name is embedded-design- plus the design name, lowercased, with spaces replaced by hyphens, plus .js. Other characters in the name are not changed, so avoid unusual characters in design names. Keep the id in the snippet equal to the id the script expects. Two requirements follow from this snippet: Serve the page over HTTP or HTTPS. Module scripts do not load from file://. Give the container a real height. The div fills 100 percent of its parent, which collapses to zero in a parent with no height. Embed in WordPress 🔗 WordPress has no Kanvas-specific plugin. You add the script to your theme and the snippet to a Custom HTML block. Create a js folder in your active theme and copy the downloaded file into it. Enqueue the file as a script module from the theme’s functions.php, replacing design.js with your file name: function kanvas_design_script() { $script_uri = get_template_directory_uri() . '/js/design.js'; wp_enqueue_script_module('kanvas-design', $script_uri, array(), '1.1.0'); } add_action('wp_enqueue_scripts', 'kanvas_design_script'); In the post, add a Custom HTML block containing only the
from the snippet. Because the theme already loads the module, leave out the Parameter Required Meaning src Yes Path to the exported JavaScript file. id Yes Unique container id for this embed on the page. size No full (default, 80 percent wide) or half (50 percent wide). Ignored when style is set. style No Inline CSS for the container. Overrides size. Place the exported file near the page and reference it: {{< meshery-design-embed src="../path/to/your-design.js" id="your-unique-design-id" size="half" >}} A live example, rendered from a design exported from Kanvas: Open Design Related 🔗 Export Designs covers the other formats. Share Designs covers live access to a design for specific people.
